ROY J. DENVILLE
Grand Masters come and go, each leaving a bit of himself in the annals
of Freemasonry in California and Hawaii. Roy J. Henville, the 119th Grand
Master, is certainly no exception.
Born in Rockville, Missouri, on August 11, 1913, he came to California
at an early age, attending public schools of Los Angeles and South Pasadena.
He graduated from South Pasadena High School, where he competed in track
and established a cross country record that stood for over 20 years.
Undaunted by the economic problems of the Great Depression, he married the charming and supportive Elinor Phares on March 7, 1935. She was
his sweetheart since the fourth grade. She has proven and continues to prove
his wisdom in this choice. A daughter, son and two grandsons enhance his
immediate family.
While working hard as a salesman and, later, as a food broker, to sustain
his family during the hard times, he soon became a Mason, being raised in
Three Pillars Lodge No. 613 in Sacramento on September 29, 1944. Two years
later, he demitted to Las Palmas Lodge No. ·366 in Fresno where his work
had taken him. Nine years later, finding himself in Southern California and
unwilling to accept a lapse in his Masonic activity, he joined San Marino Lodge
No. 685 and became immersed in community and Masonic activities, reaching
the Oriental Chair in 1964.
As a member of the San Marino Congregational Church, he served progressively as usher, Head Usher, Chairman of the Board of Deacons, and
on the Board of Trustees, greeting all who entered the door of the church.
With his characteristic warmth, friendliness, and sincerity, he convinced
everyone that "there were no strangers in that church." He expanded his field
of community service as a director of the highly respected and dedicated Midnight Mission in Los Angeles, the institution that provides so many meals
and shelter for homeless men.
He rendered additional service through his Masonically related offices of
President of the Pasadena Masonic Service Bureau; San Marino Lodge
Trustee; and member of the Advisory Board of the San Marino Chapter, Order
of DeMolay. He is a recipient of the DeMolay Legion of Honor Award.
He is a member of the Southern California Research Lodge, Southern
California Past Masters Association, Al Malaikah Shrine Temple, Past Masters
Shrine Club, San Marino Chapter of the Order of the Eastern Star, San
Gabriel Valley High-12 Club, Allied Masonic Degrees, the Saint Gabriel Conclave of the Red Cross of Constantine, Honorary Member of the National
Sojourners and its Heroes of '76, the York Rite Bodies of Alhambra, and
the Royal Order of Scotland.
Originally joining the Scottish Rite in Fresno in 1946, he demitted to the
Pasadena Scottish Rite Bodies in 1960, where he served as Venerable Master
in 1976, and where he was honored in 1975 with the rank of Knight Commander Court of Honour, and in 1981, coroneted with the 33rd Degree, Inspector General Honorary. Recognizing Brother Roy's talents, the Sovereign
Grand Commander appointed him Assistant Chairman of the Inspector
General's Advisory Conference for the Pasadena Scottish Rite Bodies.

ROY J. BENVILLE
Grand Master
October 11, 1984-0ctober 16, 1985

iii

His services to Grand Lodge began in 1963 when he was appointed to the
Jurisprudence Committee. In 1976, he was a member of the Committee to
Select the Junior Grand Warden. From 1969 to 1978, he was the Inspector
of the 532nd Masonic District, after which he was appointed Assistant Grand
Lecturer for Division V.
The Brethren recognized his abilities and services by placing him on the
first step to the ultimate office in California Masonry. They elected him Junior
Grand Warden in October of 1981, at which time he began his membership
on the Masonic Homes Board of Trustees. Successively, for the next three
years, the Brethren, convened at each Annual Communication of Grand
Lodge, advanced him up the steps to Senior Grand Warden, Deputy Grand
Master (during this year he was a member of the Masonic Memorial Temple
Board of Trustees of Grand Lodge) and finally, to the office of Grand Master
in 1984.
Brother Roy's greatest legacy and the part of himself that he has given to
Masonry in California and Hawaii has been the example and instruction of
his great measure of social intelligence and the ability to deal successfully
in interpersonal relationships.Enlisting the traits which have combined to constitute this enviable ability, there are such elements as warmth, friendliness,
humility, sincerity, kindliness, and resourcefulness. These traits have enabled
him to be comforting, generous, gracious, self-effacing, and hard working.
In short, his gift to Masonry has been his exemplification and personifica•
tion of Peace and Harmony.

TRIBUTE TO THE AMERICAN FLAG

By R. Stephen Doan, Grand Orator
When we present with honor the starry
emblem of our own beloved Land, we are stirred by
that patriotism which is graven upon the heart of every
true American. Old Glory, emblem of Liberty
symbol of Freedom under constituted authority;
Old Glory, beneath whose protecting shadow, the weary
and oppressed of every land have found opportunity
and peace; Old Glory, beneath whose tattered,
blood-stained folds so many of our Brethren have
surrendered their lives in defense of Justice,
Truth and Right; Old Glory, flying proudly above
the land of the free and home of that democracy
which we shall ever strive to preserve: of the
people, by the people and for the people.

Devotional Message
Most Worshipful Grand Master and Members of the Grand Lodge:
If I may ask your indulgence for a few moments I would like to take advantage of this opportunity to express my heartfelt appreciation to our Grand
Master, the Most Worshipful Roy J. Henville, for having appointed me to
this position for the past Masonic year. It has been a most gratifying and
rewarding experience, and one that I shall cherish for the remainder of my
life. I also want to express my warm and sincere regard for the other members
of this year's Grand Family, who collectively have made this such a thoroughly
enjoyable experience and whose acquaintance and friendship have come to
mean much to me. It has been a year that has enhanced my appreciation of
our Fraternity immeasurably and afforded me insights that I would otherwise have never had. For all of this I am most grateful.
My remarks today are an expression of some of the thoughts evoked as
a result of my experiences this past year and my reflections on them. Basically,
they are an effort on my part to consider at least some aspects of the meaning of Masory for me and to express them in such a way as may give them
a more general significance.
First of all, I spent some time in reading and rereading portions of Morals
and Dogma, one of the great beacon lights of Masonry. Like the sacred volume
that lies open upon our altar, it is a distillation of the highest thoughts and
noblest aspirations of the hearts and minds of men of noble character. In
short, both of them hold up before us a standard of excellence which we are
encouraged to emulate as being the only basis for a life well lived.

8

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

We are all conscious of living our moral life as if it were in a two-storied
house. Downstairs goes on what has too evident a claim to the painful label:
ordinary. Upstairs we have a different outlook and associate with better company. Not that our everyday routine should be called ordinary. It, too, can
be representative of upstairs living, depending upon the thoughts and motives
that direct us as we go through our daily routine. The intention of our thoughts
and motives are the soul of action and behaviour.
We know perfectly well when and how we can be upstairs and when and
how we linger downstairs. The precepts of Masonry are an attempt to draw
us upstairs. I believe that for most men, at least at some time in their life,
there is a desire to live as spiritual aristocrats. We have no doubt in our hearts
that true happiness is inseparable from distinction, and when we enjoy cheap
good times downstairs we never cease to be aware that there could be a different kind of happiness upstairs. Masons, I believe, are characterized as "Men
of Desire" ... the desire to live life upstairs.
As Masons we do not claim to be a religion; in fact, we reject the allegation when it is made. We do, however, claim to be religious, which is to say
we believe there is a spiritual nature in man as well as a purely physical nature.
As men who profess a religious faith we ascribe to the belief in an all-powerful,
all- knowing, beneficent Diety. Few of us would make the claim that our comprehension of Diety is perfect, unflawed, needing no correction ... like Paul
we would say, "Now I see imperfectly, as one seeing himself in a flawed mirror." We claim to be in search of further light, which is to say we acknowledge
that we do not yet possess full illumination. We can admit, can we not, that
as individuals our moral and spiritual development is imperfect, unfinished ... but, at the same time, we desire further light that we may become
more fully human.
If Freemasonry has a mission and a future, it must not content itself with
merely a beautiful ritual flawlessly rendered. If the noble ideals and teachings
of the Craft are limited only to dramatic and colorful performances in our
Lodge rooms, then there is little place or use for our Fraternity in the daily
affairs of men.
As a member of the Craft each of us is either an asset or a liability. We
are either part of the problem or a part of the solution. We cannot imitate
certain politicians, who have a liking for straddling fences and for sitting on
the center of the beam. Every member of a Lodge who is not a real benefit
to his fellow-man is a liability and not an asset, and if the majority of members
in any Lodge answer to that description, then the Lodge itself becomes a drag
on the community and an embarrassment to the Craft. Service is a fixed law
of nature, and a fundamental command of the Judea-Christian
faith ... "Learn to do good, to be fair and to help the poor, the orphan,
and widows", (Isa. 1:17). "Whoever will be great among you, let him be your
servant; And whoever will be chief among you, let him be your servant", (Mt.
20:26,27). We need always to live in a house by the side of the road, always
on the lookout for opportunities for service, not only to the Brethren of the
Craft, but to those outside as well. Consecrated service is the need of the
moment; it is always the need of every moment - labor and service are two

of the dominant keynotes of Masonry. Masonic service is not servile, for it
is based upon fraternity of the highest order - Brotherhood springing from
Fatherhood.
We all know that in most organizations promotion to higher office carries
with it increased salary or benefits: as a consequence there is always a sufficiency of applicants for advancement in these. But progress in Masonry
accomplishes none of these small-minded ambitions. Rather it calls for an
expenditure of time and effort which, if put into the commercial affairs of
life, would reap a compensating financial harvest.
There are other harvests of ultimately greater value which can only be reaped
by first sowing the good seed of service to one's fellowmen and assisting
generously and ungrudgingly in such ameliorative plans and endeavors as are
likely to leave a world a better place for one's having passed through it. Is
not this latter the harvest we Masons most desire to be remembered by? For
the exercise of benevolent motives and the full and free activity of charity
towards others, free from the destructive influence of partisanship, our history
as Freemasons is one that few, if any other, such organization can compare.
Within the Lodge the symbolism of our ritual and ceremonial is intended
to convey nuances of meaning that defy our efforts to put into words alone.
Not all truth is verbal...one has only to meditate upon a great painting to
realize that. The symbolism points us toward heights as yet unscaled, a splendor of spiritual and moral challenge that towers over us like some majestic
Mount Everest, beckoning our spirits upward. Realistically, we know that each
man ascends this Everest of the spirit to a level commensurate with his desire
for the fullness of human perfection, and his understanding of what comprises that perfection. Inevitably this implies a certain aristocracy... not all men
respond the same. For some, ascending the foothills is quite enough. Others
more diligent will scale the middle heights. Only those who are most passionate in their pursuit of such excellence will persevere in the struggle for
the greater light of truth and clarity of moral vision that comes from attaining
the summit. Few indeed are these, but it is to these great souls that we are
indebted for the inspiration they afford us when they recount the glory of
the vision of the promised land.
Masons understand, therefore, that not all men are open to the challenge
of Masonry and that none can be compelled. Therefore, it is the individual
who must first reveal his readiness by inquiring about the benefits of Masonry,
and he is likely to do that only when he has reached a stage where moral
and spiritual values become important to him and he sees those values
demonstrated in the life of another whom he comes to know is a Mason.
In short, men want to see the virtues of moral and spiritual achievement
displayed, not merely talked about, or, as the prayer puts it..!'not only with
our lips but in our lives." Herein lies the secret of Masonry's success.
Those who, over the years, have been most admired in our Fraternity and
have tended to fill the highest offices have been men who, by-and-large, have
not only been imbued with those high qualities and noble virtues proclaimed
within the confines of the Lodge, but demonstrated in their daily living. A
litmus test of greatness is when it can be said of a man that he left the world
a better place than he found it.

9

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

It follows, does it not, that proclamation and practice are both needed:
the latter validates and confirms the former. Where the instruction is inadequate, inept, or uninspiring there will be little encouragement for the neophyte
just beginning his ascent to persist. Where the example is lacking demonstration in the life of the instructor there is no credibility in the message and
discredit is brought upon the moral philosophy or religion being proclaimed.
Within the Lodge, those who would teach must first be learners, and then
they must put into practice that which they have learned.
Although we would hope for the day when all men would aspire to such
an aristocracy of the spirit, and, therefore, be potential candidates for the
instruction our Craft can offer, realism compels us to recognize that day has
not arrived. Troubled as we may be over the decline in numbers, it needs to
be said that in a hedonistic, even narcissistic culture (such as characterizes
much of Western culture today) with its stress upon "rights" and "doing one's
own thing" there is little inclination on the part of many to accept the discipline
of self that is necessary for the development of moral virtues exemplified by
Masonry and the higher religions. Unless and until our general moral climate
changes for the better, I am convinced that we will not be inundated with
applicants.
Like the ancient pagan Roman world where men had become sick of their
own corruption and so were compelled to turn to the cleansing, purifying
power of a higher faith for their healing, so must today's culture come to
the same realization; then, men will again seek the light of our Craft for
guidance in their lives. In the meantine, we must be faithful in our own individual and collective pursuit of the integrity of excellence.
Any desire to spread superficially and win over an immense number of men
by any lowering of our standards needs to be resisted. The ancient Church
made that mistake when pagans in great numbers came into the Church, not
so much because they were convinced of the rightness of its faith, but because
it was made the legal faith of the Empire. Well-intended though the edict may
have been, it resulted in the corruption of the Church. The supreme goal of
our ancient Order and of the higher religions is the moral improvement of
the individuals comprising our membership by a sincere and enlightened
personal commitment, and not the more or less indifferent obedience of
external forms and rites performed perfunctorily without thought as to their
deeper meaning and the obligation they impose. There is a direct relationship between that which an individual truly believes and his subsequent
behavior. The old folk adage puts it well: "What you do speaks more loudly
than what you say!" Unless our professed belief and our daily conduct are
in harmony, the profession we make is nothing but "sounding brass and
tinkling cymbal."
Any man in his right senses will realize that the cause of man's higher aspirations, and Masonry is but one manifestation of such aspiration, is something
that transcends our scientific concepts or our efforts at rationalization. Our
sincere desire to progress morally and spiritually...the efforts made in this direction to erect that inner temple of the spirit, "not made with hands;• without

which the outward manifestations of faith become meaningless, can only come
about through a determined application of the will, and the aid of the Supreme
Architect.
I do not imply that effort of the will alone is sufficient. It is not. I mean
only that it is necessary that we make the effort. To say that the human will
alone is sufficient is to say that man can achieve by his will alone the heights
of moral and spiritual perfection towards which the Master Architect of the
U~iverse is.summoning all of us. The real truth is that we can only collaborate
with the D1ety who made us all and calls us to a higher degree of perfection
that He alone can enable us to achieve. Our part is to acknowledge the impulse and to seek further light while imploring Divine guidance.
This is not easy, for the ordinary man (and all of us have some of the ordinary ~n us) know~ well that the flattering title of being a morally upright
person is only acqmred at the cost of restrictions in numerous activities from
which he. ordi~arily derives all his pleasures. When we speak of the fight of
man agamst his own lower nature, we think not only of the temptations of
the flesh, but also of the perversions of the mind born of life in common.
There are many of them, but let us take one example: the desire to shine
to preen in the attention of others, to be the admired center of adulation'.
All of us are afflicted with it in some measure. As long as it confines itself
to an effort to better ourselves, to outdo our brothers in good deeds it is
a virtue. However, it often overshoots the mark, and becomes a goal in itself.
It may assume various aspects; greed, authoritativeness, desire for acclaim all o~ which are vices detrimental to the improvement of the self. It may even
turn mto one of the most dangerous vices of intelligence, the lust for power.
~ ?umber of us are would-be dictators in our own small spheres, and amb1t1ous men are all the more eager to play a flattering, leading part when their
professional abilifies alone would not qualify them to outshine the others.
The only way in which religion or moral philosophy can be of genuine
assistance to mankind is to the extent to which those professing it perfect
th.emselves, by building an inner temple, by judging themselves soberly and
w1t~~ut compl~cency. In so doing that individual is unconsciously shaping
a spmt that radiates to those around him, influencing others to seek that which
has so blessed him.
One cannot but be struck by the disproportion between the duration of
~ man's life .and the duration of his influence on future generations. History
1s replete with examples. The destiny of man is not limited to his time on
earth. A man exists less by the actions performed during his life than by the
effect he leaves behind him. He may be unaware of it himself. He may think
that his death is the end of his reality in this world, whereas, it may well be
t~e beginning of a grea~er and more significant reality. Each of us may be
hkened to a comet flashmg through the heavens, leaving a trail that is either
modest or brilliant in its effect upon others. That which was best in each
of us, which we may have given unconsciously to our circle of friends and
relations will never completely die. An impressive trail has been left by the
founders of the higher religions, by the prophets, by the thinkers, those to
whom we owe the unalterable framework of our moral life. Our intellectual

10

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

endeavors, our whole structure of speculative Masonry will be of no real
significance if they do not lead us, and through us others, to a better comprehension of ourselves, of the meaning of our lives, and the resources and
the potential buried deep within each of us.
The extraordinary strides made in the conquest of disease and of nature
will not bring to man the happiness he has a right to expect, unless there
is also a corresponding moral development. To do this we need enlightenment which we receive from our religious faith and from the teachings of
this Ancient and Honorable Order of Freemasons, the encouragement of our
mutual fellowship, the advice of our wise leaders, the inspired traditions
represented by our religious heritage, heirs to all the spiritual treasurers of
mankind and keepers of the eternal flame which the greatest and noblest of
men have passed on to one another, from time immemorial.
Today, my Brethren, the torch is in our hands; it is up to us to pass it on
to those who will follow after. May we ever hold it high that its light may
be a guide to others who would seek further light and truth in our Fraternity.
And now it would be appropriate for us to set aside time in which to
remember those members of this Grand Lodge, each of whom has been a
light in his generation and now has "traveled to that undiscovered country
from whose bourne no traveler has returned."

MEMORIAL TRIBUTE

Memorial Message
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
Most Worshipful Grand Master, Distinguished Guests and Brethren all.
It is fitting and proper that we pause a few moments, early in this 136th Annual Communication, to pay respect to the memory of our Brothers who have
laid down their burdens to rest for awhile. During this past Masonic year,
there have been 565 members of this Grand Lodge who have passed away.
Our Grand master, Most Worshipful Roy J. Henville, has been called upon
to offer the Masonic funeral service for one of his appointive Grand Lodge
Officers, two past Grand Masters and several others who were members of
his Lodge.
We are indebted to the Lodges and Brothers of Hawaii for the theme for
this Memorial Service. On the occasion of the Grand Master's visit to Hawaii,
this past July, one of his first activities was a visit to the National Memorial
Cemetery of the Pacific. There, under the watchful approval of the statue
of Columbia, your Grand Master, with the aid of the other Grand Lodge
Officers present, placed a wreath at the Dedicatory Stone in memory of all
Masons who have gone before as well as those from the Armed Forces who
gave their lives for our freedom.
·
The Grand Lodge Officers attended the Central Union Church on the last
day of their visit in Honolulu. There, on the reredos behind the altar, the
words "Love Never Faileth" are engraved. Those words are the title of the
solo which will conclude this Memorial Service following the Memorial Devotional by the Grand Chaplain.
Members of this Committee will now present the Past Grand Masters who
will give a Memorial lfibute and two Eulogies.

KERN HADLEY COPELAND
By Chester R. MacPhee, P.G.M.
The Grand Lodge of California has lost another pillar of strength in the
passing of one of our most revered Grand Lodge Officers, Brother Kern
Hadley Copeland.
Born in Denver, Colorado on May 1st, 1919, he is survived by his beloved
wife Laura, two sons, Kern Copeland III and Todd Copeland, and a daughter
Allison, as well as two grandchildren.
Our Brother was a graduate of Pepperdine College and the University of
Southern California, and finished among the top 10 at the Graduate School
of Indiana University. He was a retired Captain of the U.S. Army in World
War II. In 1964 he joined Glendale Federal Savings, was appointed an Assistant Vice- President in 1969 and Senior Vice President, Property Service Division in 1973. He was a member of the Glendale Chamber of Commerce, the
Glendale Adventist Hospital and a Board member of the Los Angeles Midnight Mission. He was Chairman of the Design Advisory Board of the City
of Glendale in 1979-80 and Treasurer of the Friends of Burbank Airport.
Brother Copeland was raised to the sublime degree of Master Mason on
March 8th, 1957 in Alexander Hamilton Lodge No. 535. In 1964 he served
as Master of the Lodge and President of the 560th Masonic Officers
Association.
Appointed by Most Worshipful Grand Master Kermit A. Jacobson, as
Assistant Grand Treasurer in 1977, he gave substantially of himself in that
capacity. I can testify to his outstanding ability and concern for our Fraternity for I was Grand Treasurer at the time. We worked well together and I
admired him greatly. In 1978 and 1979 he served as an outstanding Chairman of the Temple Properties Committee. For five years, from 1980-84, he
served as a knowledgeable and prudent Chairman of the Finance Committee of this Grand Lodge.
Our present Grand Master, the Most Worshipful Roy J. Henville, recognizing the financial acumen of Brother Copeland, appointed him for the second
time as Assistant Grand Treasurer of this Grand Lodge to serve during the
current year. That service was interrupted by his death, and we mourn that
passing today.
He was a man for all seasons, certainly one of California's best, and he
will be sorely missed by this Grand Lodge.

MEMORIAL TRIBUTE

LOUIS ROBERT MITCHELL
By Raymond A. Ebbage, P.G.M
Junior Grand Deacon of the Grand Lodge of California for the year
1984-1985.
Born in Salt Lake City, Utah on October 22, 1924 into a Masonically
oriented family. His father lived to receive his 50 year Masonic pin, and both
father and mother were members of the Order of Eastern Star.
After moving several times Lou finished high school in Grass Valley, California. Lou also joined and participated in DeMolay for over three years.
He graduated from high school into the United States Navy during World
War II and served as a radar man for three years on supply ships in the South
Pacific.
Lou returned home and entered college to study engineering under the G.I.
Bill. However, after a couple of years in college, he decided to finish his studies
on his own and with correspondence courses which he completed while being employed by the State of California. He started with the Department of
Architecture and ended with the Department of Water Resources as a Civil
Engineer. Lou retired after 25 years with the State in 1983.
He married his wife of 18 years, Betty Jean, in 1967. His twin daughters
Janice and Joyce have been a constant source of gratification, Janice providing him with even more joy through three children of her own.
Lou petitioned Masonry in 1976, and was raised December 17, 1976 in Three
Pillars Lodge No. 613 in Sacramento. Almost immediately he went to work
as an officer and served his Lodge with distinction as Master in 1982.
Lou was an active Mason. He joined the Scottish Rite and Ben Ali Shrine
in Sacramento, played trombone in the Ben Ali Band and was a working
member of the Ben Ali Keystone Cops.
Lou was appointed Junior Grand Deacon of the Grand Lodge of California, installed in October 1984 and served until his death October 2nd, 1985.
An avid reader, specializing in history, he also enjoyed photography and music,
especially playing Dixie Land Jazz on his trombone.
As an outdoors man, his pursuits were hiking and fishing - hiking to where
the fishing was good.
He passed into that land from whose bourne no traveler returns on October
2, 1985.
His presence will be sorely missed.

16

There are five grandchildren, whom Ellsworth loved dearly. His beloved
wife Hazel, who was so devoted to him preceded him in death several years ago.
Ellsworth's remarkable speaking and acting ability, for which he has been
so distinguished, became apparent at a very early age. In 1911 and 1913 he
appeared in juvenile roles in Mack Sennett Comedies and in films which starred Charlie Chaplin, Mable Norman, and Ford Sterling.
Ellsworth's formal education began in the Los Angeles public school system,
followed by attendance at Long Beach Polytechnic High School, where he
graduated in 1923. While in high school, he was a member of the tennis and
the debating teams, and was one of six finalists in a state-wide oratorical contest on the Constitution of the United States.
Upon his graduation from Long Beach Polytechnic High School in 1923
Ellsworth entered Pomona College, where he was prominent in college
activities:
-

-

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

He won a letter as Captain of the Freshman tennis team.
He played football.
He captained the Freshman debating team.
He made the Varsity debating team and toured Northern California successfully meeting Stanford, the College of the Pacific and other univ~rsity
teams.
He won in 1925 the Southern California Oratorical Contest and the
Southern California Extempore Contest.
He won in 1926 the Southern California and the Pacific Coast finals in
oratorical contests on the United States Constitution. He achieved second
place in the National finals. [Parenthetically, one of the U.S. Constitutional
oratorical judges was Joseph H. Joplin, himself a learned Consititutional
authority, who subsequently became my father-in-law. And a $1,000 prize
which Ellsworth won in the National finals made financially possible
Ellsworth and Hazel's marriage in 1930.]
He won the 1927 Southern California Peace Contest.
He was elected to membership on the Student Body Council.
He was made President of Delta Sigma Rho honorary forensics fraternity
in 1926-27.
He was appointed by Pomona College as Student Coach of the Women's
Varsity and Freshman debating teams, the former winning second place
and the latter the Southern California championship.
He acted in several college plays, in one of which Joel McCrea participated.
He became a member of Kappa Delta fraternity.

Ellsworth's professional schooling was obtained at the School of
Jurisprudence, University of California, Berkeley, and the University of
Southern California School of Law, where he received his LLB degree in 1930.
Ellsworth's law school activities, like his college activities, were outstanding:

-

17

He was elected President of the Student Body of the U.S.C. School of Law.
He was made President of Gamma Eta Gamma legal fraternity.
He was elected to Skull & Scales, a law school honorary fraternity.
He was elected to Skull & Dagger, an all University honorary fraternity.

Throughout his law school career, his fellow students admired and respected
him for his remarkable intellectual skills and his inspiring leadership.
His graduate activities were many:
- He became President of Pomona College (Alumni) Men's Club in 1944-45.
- He served as President of the Pomona College General Alumni Association in 1945-46.
- He was a member of the Pomona College National Committee in 1964.
Among his civic activities has been his participation since 1943 as an active member, and during his illness as an Emeritus member, of the Board
of Directors of The Midnight Mission, which ministers to the needs of
homeless men in the City of Los Angeles and where today an average of more
than 40,000 free meals are served to the destitute each month.
In 1938 Ellsworth was President of Wilshire Men's Club. Also, at Wilshire
United Methodist Church (across Wilshire Blvd.) he was a member of the
Official Board while his long-time friend, the Reverend Dr. Willsie Martin
was the minister. On becoming Grand Master, Ellsworth appointed Dr. Martin
as Grand Chaplain of the Grand Lodge. How appropriate it was that Dr.
Martin took as his theme for the Grand Lodge Devotional Services "Give
me men to match my mountains" and as a text from the Holy Word, that
Magna Charta declaration of man's true greatness found in the 8th Psalm:
"When I consider Thy heavens, the moon and the stars which Thou hast
ordained, what is man that Thou are mindful of him, or the son of man that
Thou visitest him. For Thou hast made him but a little lower than God. Thou
crownest him with glory and honor. Thou hast made him to have dominion
over the works of Thy hands. Thou hast put all things under his feet." And
as a keynote, that bugle call by Paul to the early Christian Church: "Quit
·
you like men. Be strong."
After being admitted to the California State Bar in 1930, Ellsworth received
an appointment as a Deputy City Attorney for the City of Los Angeles,
specializing in civil litigation. In 1935 he transferred to the legal division of
the Department of Water and Power where he handled many important cases.
In 1945 he became Judge of the Municipal Court in Los Angeles and in 1949
was made Judge of the Superior Court where he served until his illness of
recent years. Frequently, on assignment by the Chief Justice of the State
Supreme Court, he was called upon to sit on the Appellate Department.
As a judge, Ellsworth was greatly honored and respected. In the courtroom,
attorneys often stood in awe of his phenominal photographic memory,
whichenabled him to quote at will the testimony of witnesses who had testified
before him. At his request, the most complicated cases were assigned to him,
particularly those involving matters of first impression. Administratively, he

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

participated in resolving important operating procedures for the court system
and was a member of the judicial group which assisted in the design of many
court buildings throughout the County of Los Angeles. His tremendous
knowledge of the law, his legal and judicial ability, and his wide experience
were superb. In spoken or written word, his expression of the law had a clarity
rarely equaled.
As a Master Mason, Ellsworth was particularly active:

As Venerable Master for more than two decades, Ellsworth has been diligent
and untiring in his devotion to the Scottish Rite. His achievements have been
truly magnificent and he has been an inspiration to all around him and near
him.
In degree work, his faultless memory often has achieved what to others
would have proved an impossibility. Across the years, when an emergency has
occurred and an actor could not be present at the last moment, it has been
Ellsworth who at one reading could photograph in his mind the script and
go on stage with such perfection that it seemed as though he always had performed the assigned role of the absent actor.
In truth and in fact, Ellsworth was the real architect of the beautiful Scottish Rite Masonic Temple, in which his funeral services now are being held.
Hour after hour, day after day, week after week, month after month, and
year after year, he devoted himself to the design, construction and operation
of this magnificent edifice. With Millard Sheetz, the artist and designer, he
journeyed to Italy where together they selected in the quarries the marble to
be cut and polished for the walls. He guided personally the sculptor who
created the statues which adorn the exterior. He alone composed the quotations and prescribed exactly how the Masonic symbols would be placed for
all to see. He it was who counseled Millard Sheetz in content and design of
the beautiful mosaics which adorn the building and the graphic Masonic story
they portray.
There is not a cubic foot of the building which has been unknown to him.
Even the door knobs and hardware were selected individually by him, such
was his attention to detail. He specified the design and painting by the artists
of the more that 100 drops which grace this stage, including this beautiful
Cathedral Scene. Small wonder that this Temple has received international
acclaim.
•
From this podium, we have listened to our Brother teach us the great lessons
of Masonry and the wisdom of all nations and generations. Here, he has
helped us to understand the better the great religions and philosophies of the
world. His was the priceless ability to correlate and explain Biblical and secular
history. Of him, a member of the Class - Mayor Bowron - once marvelled
how one man's mind could hold so much knowledge and share it so generously
with others.
In retrospect, how appropriate now are Daniel Webster's classic words:

In Scottish Rite Freemasonry, in the Valley of Los Angeles, Ellsworth

GUY BOYD MIZE, P.G.M.
By Kermit A. Jacobson, P. G.M.
"The steps of a good man are ordered by the Lord; and he delighteth in
his way." - Psalm 37:23. This beautiful passage was well-known to the great
and good man whose memory we here honor.
Our dear friend and Brother, Guy Boyd Mize, was born on April 21, 1901,
in Ullin, Illinois. At an early age the family moved to St. Louis, Missouri,
where he studied accounting and auditing and became a cost accountant.
In 1921 Guy moved to Glendale, California and immediately joined the
Central Christian Church where he met Ruby Evelyn Eubanks, who became
his wife on June 20, 1925. To this marriage one son was born, Guy, Jr.
Guy's remarkable professional and business talents brought early recognition as he joined the John M.C. Marble Company in 1929 and became President in 1959.
As a leader in his profession, Guy served on both state and national
mortgage banking associations. He was admired and respected throughout
the profession; and his business acumen and qualities of leadership found
expression in all areas of his life.
As a churchman, Guy was a devoted servant of the Lord. He was looked
up to as an elder statesman of insight, gracious spirit, broad sympathy, sound
judgment, faithful stewardship, and fairness. He served his church for many
years as its Treasurer.
As a Master Mason Guy's influence reached no less than 237,000 Master
Masons and their families, when in 1961~62 he was Grand Master of Masons
in California and Hawaii.
He was raised a Master Mason in Unity Lodge No. 368 on November 23,
1928 and served as Master in 1939.
He was made Inspector of the 86th Masonic District in October 1944, and
appointed Assistant Grand Lecturer in October of 1950.
In addition to serving in our highest office, that of Grand Master in 1961,
Guy was recognized nationally by being elected a member of the Board of
Directors of the George Washington Masonic National Memorial Association, Alexandria, Virginia in 1962, in which capacity he served for many years.
He was honored with the 33rd Degree of the Scottish Rite and the Honorary
Legion of Honor, Order of DeMolay. He was a member of the York Rite
and Red Cross of Constantine.
There were three characteristics ever present in Guy's life.
The first was courage. There was a fearless forthrightness about his speech.
He spoke with authority, for he made certain of his facts before he spoke.
He was open, frank and direct but there was ever present a warmth and
kindness.
The second characteristic was peace. It was good to be near him and with
him. Guy was at peace with himself and with his Creator.
The third was strength. Guy's whole personality possessed a granite-like
strength that was impressive. How wonderful his strength of character was

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

evidenced in his practice of the principal tenets of Masonry - Brotherly Love,
Relief and Truth, and the domestic and public virtues of Temperance, Fortitude, Prudence and Justice.
We have been better men and better Masons because of the life of our Most
Worshipful and Illustrious Brother Guy. No higher honor, nor more sincere
tribute, can be paid to him. May we all honor his memory by heeding the
example and advice of his life.

"But when the great and good depart,
What is it more than thisThat man, who is from God sent forth,
Doth yet again to God return?Such ebb and flow must ever be,
Then wherefore should we mourn?"
-(William Wordsworth)

Memorial Devotional
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A.M. of California:
As we direct our attention to the remembrance of those of our members
who have departed this life we do so not so much to mourn their demise,
but rather to pay tribute to their memory and in the assurance of a faith that
"the souls of the righteous are in the hands of God."
"Man comes and tills the soil and lies beneath." In one short, poignant
sentence the poet sums up the life and death of mortal man. We who are
gathered here today know that "a time will come for each of us, and the wisest
know not how soon, when all distinction save that of goodness shall cease,
and, death, the mighty leveler of human distinctions, reduce us to the same
state."
Masonry is an institution; those of us who comprise it in any generation
are but mortal, and one by one, year after year, individual members must
obey the solemn summons and lay down their tools for the last time and depart
for that celestial Lodge, while other workmen from the quarries come forward to take their places and to carry on their works.
"They are passing away, these dear old friends,
Like leaves on the current cast;
With never a break in the rapid flow,
We watch them as one by one they go
Into the solemn past."
The roll call of those departed in a Fraternity with the number of members
of this Grand Lodge of California and Hawaii is inevitably long. Time does
not permit more than a few eulogies of our departed Brethren, yet all are
worthy.
In the democracy of the dead, all men are equal. The poor man is as rich
as the richest, and the rich man as poor as the pauper. The creditor loses
his usury, and the debtor is acquitted his obligation. There the proud man
surrenders his pomp; the politician his honors; the worldling his pleasures;
the invalid needs no physician; the laborer rests from toil. The wrongs of time
are redressed; injustice is expiated, and the irony of fate is refuted.

My Brethren:
I stand before you today, as I did a year ago, with a profound sense of
humility, gratitude, and apprehension. No man can serve as your Grand Master
without feeling how small and insignificant he is without the generous help
and support of all of you. The resultant humility is real; it is constant!
Your response and strength have been most effective and gratifying. For
this, I shall be everlastingly grateful. The measure of this gratitude., I am sorry
to say, I cannot express in words. Throughout the year, I have tried to express
it in and by my actions.
Now, I stand before you as the defendant in a court of law stands before
the judge and jury. My apprehension stems from the fact that I realize you
are the ones to judge my actions of the past year; you are the jury scrutinizing what I have tried to do; you are the ones who will determine the verdict.
I hope and pray that I have served you well. I assure you that I have made
every effort to be true to our Masonic principles, fair to everyone at all times,
and sincere in each personal relationship. As you review the events and
activities that have transpired this past year, I ask only that you judge my
role in them with fraternal understanding and compassion.
When I stood before you last year, I was fully aware that, while the office
of Grand Master is the highest honor that can be conferred upon an individual
Mason, it is also the challenge of a massive responsibility! Just as each Mason
is an ambassador of Masonry, a public relations committee of one, a builder
of goodwill, so is the Grand Master all of these things. However, because
of his greater exposure, the responsibility for being faultless is maximized.
I have kept this t.hought before me at all times.
INTER-JURISDICTIONAL DISPUTE

At the very outset of this administration, we faced an extremely serious
and potentially explosive situation.
The Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of New Jersey knowingly and
arbitrarily had violated the long respected and basic American Masonic
principle of territorial sovereignty. He initiated, passed and raised a California resident in a Lodge in that Jurisdiction without following long established
rules and procedures.
Despite the very courteous, low key, but repeated efforts of both our Grand
Master, E. Arthur Haglund, and Grand Secretary, Robert A. Klinger, to rectify
the situation before it was too late, the recalcitrant Grand Master stubbornly
pursued his course. Finally, with complete reluctance, our Grand Master was
compelled to issue his proclamation severing fraternal relations and withdrawing official recognition of the deviate Grand Lodge and its Constituent
Lodges. This is a dreadful action with countless ramifications and resultant
problems - not the least of which was the embarrassment to the California
resident - the kind of action no Grand Master or Grand Lodge will take
without the most serious consideration and widespread consultation, both
of which our Grand Master earnestly and conscientiously pursued.

37

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Upon my coming into the office of Grand Master last October, the new
Grand Master (since April of 1984) of New Jersey, recognizing the impact
and import of the withdrawal of recognition, took advantage of the changes
in administration in both his and our Grand Lodges and made an honest
and sincere effort to correct the situation. He even traversed the continent
and personally visited with us in order to restore friendly fraternal relations.
Not only did he defuse the explosive situation and assuage our feelings, but
more importantly, he made sure that Masonic protocol was followed in every
detail.
Thus the California resident, Danny Thomas, a universally known entertainer and philanthropist, who was recently awarded a Medal of Honor by
President Reagan for his humanitarian activities, has become a dual member
of our Palisades Lodge No. 637. Peace and harmony have been restored among
and between our two Masonic Jurisdictions with the traditional American
Masonic principle of territorial sovereignty reaffirmed! This joyous ending
enabled us to go on to our other duties and responsibilities with a great sense
of relief and renewed energy. (Treated as Grand Master's Decision No. 4)

Almost from its inception in England in 1717, Grand Lodges have pursued
the policy of refraining from response to criticism and refusing to be drawn
into a fight.
The list of both political and religious entities opposed to Masonry is surprising. Even more amazing is the fact that our Fraternity has survived them
all, despite its unwillingness to respond to all critics.
We managed to grow stronger after the very severe anti-Masonic period
in the United States, ranging from 1826 to 1840. We were very badly crippled,
but undaunted!
The most recent attack is that of the British Methodist Conference censuring
the Fraternity as a "threat to Christianity" and urging its communicants to
withdraw from Freemasonry. This follows the statement of a few years ago
by Scotland Yar~ requesting its members not to join a Lodge and, if already
a member, to resign. The Church of England had previously issued a similar
statement.
The f~ct ~hat the Duke of Kent, like so many of the nobility and royalty
before him, 1s the Grand Master of the United Grand Lodge of England raises
a few questions. Has he or have his constituents strayed from our fraternal
tenets? Have the Methodists and other dissidents become disloyal to the
Crown? Is there an incipient dissatisfaction expressing itself in England? Is
anti-Masonic criticism justified?
What should we do about all this criticism? Our office has received a flood
of mail on this subject, indicating extensive concern, not only among the
Brethren, but also among some non-Masons, family members, and others.
There are several courses to pursue. One is to ignore all of it and to go
about our work as usual. The other extreme is to declare war upon our
attackers and to fight back, item by item.
Somewhere in between are such approaches as: l) to dedicate ourselves to
a better performance in our respective communities; 2) to develop a firm wellstructured program of public relations; and, 3) to reach out into our
community by: a) fulfilling local needs with more widespread, selfless service;
b) openi~g our meeting places to more community groups; c) inviting
commumty leaders to our activities; d) demonstrating a sincere and dedicated
d~votion to the people in our community; e) giving more time to working
with and for all young people, when and wherever we can; f) improving our
individual and Lodge behavior to create an impeccable public image.
Years ago, I was taught that to argue is fruitless because, "everything you
say merely convinces your antagonist how wrong you are and how right he is!"
In short, I suggest our best response is to expand our horizons, to arrange
to include more family and friends in our activities, and to develop more pride
in ourselves and our beloved Fraternity. We are definitely NOT a religion,
but we should demonstrate more clearly that we are devoutly religious! We
have so much to give; we have so many capable people to help in so many ways!
Let's get out of the Lodge Room and do what we are taught to do in it!
Let us exemplify and personify our lessons and our precepts!! Let us divest
ourselves of all unnecessary or imagined secrecy and prove to the world that
we are NOT a secret society!!!

36

ANTI-MASONRY DEVEWPMENTS

An irritating problem that has recently reappeared is the anti-Masonic expressions reported in the press. As you know, this is not a new problem. It
has reared its ugly head from time to time since before the formation of the
first Grand Lodge in London, England in 1717. King Henry VI, in 1425, was
one of the earliest to rule against the Masons in England. He was followed
with anti-Masonic sentiments and regulations by King George III, in 1799.
In between, during 1738, Pope Clement XII issued his famous, or infamous,
Bull entitled, "In Eminenti", in which he declared "excommunication, ipso
facto, for all Freemasons of Catholic persuasion."
About 20 or more other Papal pronouncements against Masonry have been
issued since then, most quoted of which is the "Humanum Genus" proclaimed
by Pope Leo XIII in 1884. He declared that the "human race is divided into
two opposing parties, the kingdom of God and the kingdom of Satan." As
might be expected, he relegated Freemasonry to the latter kingdom. He went
on to say that, "By opening their gates to persons of every creed, they promote, in fact, the great modern error of religious indifference and of the parity
of all worships, the best way to annihilate every religion, especially the
Catholic, which being the only true one, cannot be joined with others without
enormous injustice."
Another of his accusations against Freemasons was that we contend, "the
peoples are sovereign, those who rule have no authority but by the commission and concession of the people."
While most Masons ignored this diatribe, Albert Pike, the eminent leader
of the Scottish Rite, Southern Jurisdiction, responded publicly, calling it a
"declaration of war" against democracy and the principles we hold so dear.
These Papal attacks have been accompanied by numerous others; by
political leaders, other religious antagonists, and by individuals, all motivated
by a variety of reasons.

STATUE OF LIBERTY

Chairman of the important life-sustaining Investment Committee of Grand
Lodge. His dedication and service to Freemasonry and especially to the Grand
Lodge of California is an inspiration to all.

Lest you get the idea that we have had nothing but negative problems, let
me tell you about our commitment to the renovation of the Statue of Liberty.
With so many of us being descendants of immigrants who literally poured
across the Atlantic Ocean and caught their first glimpse of this Land of Hope,
Freedom, and Prosperity through a porthole or from the overcrowded decks
of ships, I need not recount the joy, the tears of happiness, and the prayerful
expressions of gratitude they displayed and expressed!
The Statue of Liberty has been a beloved symbol to uncountable millions,
not least of whom are the Freemasons. Only here are we guaranteed, in writing,
the right to meet as we are doing today, unmolested and respected.
Furthermore, Masons played such well known and prominent roles in conceiving, sculpturing, and delivering the famous Statue that I shall not take
the time to enumerate them now. Suffice it to say that for many reasons, the
Masons in the United States have pledged to support the renovation project.
We are no different, except that we, of the California and Hawaii Juris~ic­
tion, have set a goal to contribute $1,000,000 to the project, a sum far exceedmg
that of any other Jurisdiction. I am proud to report that with your generous
support, we are approaching the $800,000 mark in less than a year, without
infringement upon any other program. Our goal remains the same .$1,000,000! We have only $250,000 or less than one-quarter to go. I am confident that you will find this sum within our capability and that you will share
in the pride of accomplishment!
The California Masonic Foundation is still receiving contributions. Please
make it your earnest desire, your wish, and your duty to contribute whatever
you can without injury to yourself or your family. This is one opportuni ty
to create a very favorable public image, a chance to receive national publicity,
telling the world that the Masons of California and Hawaii are literally saying,
"Thanks a Million!"

GRAND MASTER'S RELIEF

From time to time, our Brethren in other Jurisdictions encounter
catastrophic misfortunes. Earthquakes, fires, tidal waves, hurricanes, volcanic
eruptions and other disasters leave these Brethren devastated, homeless and
hungry, with their meeting places destroyed. Masons from many Jurisdictions
respond with financial or physical help.
Some of our older members will remember the San Francisco earthquak e
and fire of 1906 and the assistance provided by Brethren in other areas. Japan
has received such aid more than once. Not too many years ago, the Lodges
in Guatemala weFe similarly helped.
The Masonic Service Association monitors such calamities and serves as

that derived from family support and encouragement!
This year, we have been blessed by a very generous demonstration of such
family unity. Wherever we have gone, Eastern Star, Scottish Rite, York Rite,
Shrine, Hi-12, and Youth Orders, we have been invited and received in a most
cordial fashion with the greatest courtesy and respect. Receptions have been
numerous, well planned, and obviously warm, gracious, and charming. Very
frankly, it takes a man with big feet and a lot of weight to keep from flying
into Cloud 9. With all the compliments, generous remarks, and tokens of
affection so kindly proferred to us this past year, it would not be difficult
to develop a big head, so full of air that it would be easy to take off and
go into orbit!
It is difficult and unfair to try to single out any particular group or organization for specific mention on this subject. All have been equal as integral
members as a family should be. All have been supportive; all have been
thoughtful and helpful.
Although the Shrine is the most visible, exciting, and best known segment
of our Family, I have been impressed by their humility and determined efforts to be "just one of the family." Unfettered by some of the restraints under
which we operate, and therefore, able to expand their membership and build
financial resources, nevertheless they insist upon conforming to our standards
with dignity, bearing in mind that they are Shrine Masons.
Their efforts to build a stronger Masonic Family unity is international in
scope. At the Imperial Shrine level, they have a Masonic Relations Committee. Perhaps, we, as Symbolic Lodge Masons, can learn some valuable lessons
from our Shrine Brethren, particularly in the areas of public relations and
personal enthusiasm.
While many of our Brethren worry and lament about our declining
numbers, I am more concerned about the causes of that decline, among which,
the chief culprit is apathy!
With a stronger Masonic Family, reciprocally encouraging each other, I
believe we can defeat our worst enemy. How can anyone be apathetic when
he knows what the family expectations are and that the family is constantly
watching and encouraging him?
We need more expressed appreciation of each other; more joint activities
to build a closer "togetherness"; we need to have more FUN together, rather
than going in different directions; we need more cooperation and less competition for members, for dollars, for programs; we need more family spirit,
leading us to more Masonic Family Unity!

PROFICIENCY FOR CONCORDANT AND APPENDANT BODIES

At the conclusion of the Master's congratulations to the newly raised Master
Mason, he is told that by signing the Lodge By-laws it will subject him to
its burdens and responsibilities, as well as entitle him to its benefits and its
privileges.
However, there are some rights and privileges as a Master Mason that are
witheld for a certain period of time or for qualificaton. For instance, under

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

"Rules Governing Admission to the Home at Union City" for a member,
his wife or widow, and for admission of children of a member to the Home
in Covina, that member must have been a Master Mason in good standing
continuously for at least five years before making such application.
Under the five years of membership requirement for making application
to either Masonic Home, Grand Lodge has established recognition of the
member's sincerity, dedication, and support of Freemasonry to warrant
granting such admission, providing a need for either Home has been
demonstrated.
The privilege of making application to a concordant or appendant organization by a Master Mason is restricted under Section 2635 of the C.M.C .. Such
restriction involves waiting at least one year following the conferring of the
Master Mason degree and also having passed a satisfactory examination in
the Candidate's Lecture of that Degree.
I wholeheartedly support Grand Master Haglund's carry over Recommendation No. 3, entitled "Proficiency for Concordant and Appendant Bodies",
that the restriction in making application to concordant or appendant
organizations should apply only for a period of time not to exceed five years
after which the Master Mason would be eligible to make such application.
I think the precedent set by Grand Lodge in adopting a period of five years
of membership to establish the sincerity, dedication, and support of a Master
Mason for admission to our Masonic Homes should apply in this case and
suffice in lieu of having passed the Third Degree proficiency.

Speakers and discussion groups among the Grand Masters continue to seek

training for officers to stimulate interest. Some have adopted some drastic
changes in reducing the Candidate proficiency requirements for advancement
through the Degrees. Some have instituted aggressive programs to induce nonMasons to inquire about membership. Careful observation of the results of
such changes will eventually indicate the value of such changes.

Most Worshipful Gene Ross, Grand Master of Masons in Illinois in discussing a problem common to most Jurisdictions, that of "Unfinished' Work"

those Brethren who have stated they are no longer interested and do not desire
to complete their work. What has happened? Did the Investigating/Interviewing Committee fail in their duties? Was the Worshipful Master lax in

voted to accept him? How well was the First Degree performed? Don't we
all have a certain responsibility to our Lodge and our Fraternity to see that
only those who ale sincere should enter our door?"
Every applicant for the Degrees of Masonry is entitled to an explanaton
of the action he is taking. Every Lodge should have a Personnel Committee
tha~ meets with eac~ applicant, before his petition is read in Lodge, to explan~ that :v1asonry _is taug.ht by Degrees, that there is some memory work
re~mred with coac?mg available, what Masonry is and what it is not, along
with an opportumty for the Candidate to ask questions. Getting better

~ctivit~ does not replace the work of the Committee of Investigation. That
is very important and necessary, too. Such a preliminary meeting may reveal
to the applicant that Masonry is not what he expected. If so, it is better for
him t~ know this be~or~ ~oing any further. On the other hand, it is an opportune time to sell the md1v1dual the merits of Masonry and increase his interest
in receiving the degrees. This approach can help reduce the 200/o of these applicants who receive the First Degree and do not continue further. We are
presently losing 20 out of every 100 applicants who receive the Entered
Apprentice degree and then continue no further. The Ritual of the Several
Degr~es must be performed as nearly to perfection as possible to impress the

to believe that every Lodge officer is a good ritualist. Many sideliners are

Last, but certainly not least, Candidate coaching is very critical! Some of
the best memories of Masons are the enjoyable times spent with their coaches.
Friendships have been established that have been lasting. Our Candidate's
Coaches are entitled to far more recognition than has been afforded them

material in the "Handbook for Candidates Coaches" that explains the symbols, terms, furnishings, and other subjects.
I quote from the Handbook, "In this chain of instruction, the most intimate
contact of the Candidate is with his coach. His view of Masonry as a strong,
virile and worthwhile institution is more likely to be gained through evenings
spent with a strong and knowledgeable coach, than through the actual work
in the Degrees themselves. It is the coach who makes things come alive. It
is the coach who imparts life and meaning to a lecture. It is the coach who,
by answering questions and discussing ideas, may lead the Candidates to new
ideas and new interests in the tremendous pattern of Freemasonry." Candidate
Coaches have a great opportunity to sell Masonry to the Candidates.

Summarizing this topic, I firmly believe that a positive interest shown in

GRAND LODGE OFFICE COMPUTER NEEDS

HAWAII VISITATIONS

Past Grand Master E. Arthur Haglund, in his Message last year, indicated
a need to continue the effort to get a .well-planned and well-defined scope
of overall computer equipment to accommodate cost control for our two
Masonic Homes, non-financial data on membership, word processing, and
eventual replacement of the present good, but inadequate, equipment.
To proceed with this recommendation, I took advantage of Past Gra?d
Master Haglund's expertise and appointed him Chairman of a Special
Committee to determine the total Grand Lodge computer needs and to make
recommendations. Assisting him on this Committee were: Very Worshipful
Robert A. Klinger, Grand Secretary; Hugo Delfin, Accounting Manager;
Adrian West, Charitable Gifts; Francis Lewis, Membership Department;
Ronald Sherod, Masonic Homes Trustee; Herbert Pompey, Chairman of
Finance; and David Shampay, Master, Liberal Arts Lodge No. 677.
.
The Committee reviewed the control, information, and word processmg
needs of the Grand Lodge office, as well as those of the Union City and Covina
Masonic Homes.
Only basic financial systems are on the existing computer in San Francisco.
This computer is too small, slow in processing, and incompatible with any
other system to allow for the required expansion.
The primary needs identified are: 1) to establish a satisfactory data base
for membership records, with the accompanying output support for the
Lodges, as well as mailing labels (which will save $10,000 per year now spent
for the California Freemason Magazine) and membership statistics for the
Executive Committee and others; and, 2) to provide the capacity to establish
small data bases and to produce statistical and word processing applications,
without the added expense of employment of professional programming
talent. These procedures include preparation of the Annual Proceedings, the
Grand Lodge Roster, Annual Inspectors' Report Analysis, control and information systems for each of the Homes, Grand Lodge Library, Memorial
Temple Management, and others.
.
The Grand Secretary inquired of all large Grand Lodges as to their computer status. California is the only large Grand Lodge in the United States
without a complete computer-based membership administration system.
The Committee recommendation is based upon using the latest technology
which is more "user friendly" than previous systems and for a lower cost than
processing by service bureaus or companies
The Grand Treasurer, Very Worshipful John A. Sickenberger, approves of
the recommendation. With the cost spread over several years, the per capita
addition of 17 cents per member will be recommended in the Finance report
to cover the capital expenditure.
I extend my sincerest thanks to the Committee and Past Grand Master
Haglund for the time and effort spent in the study and recommendation on
this very important technological subject.

One of the most memorable and enjoyable occasions for a Grand Master
is the Annual Official Visitation to the Lodges in the Hawaiian Islands.
The friendliness and hospitality of the Hawaiians are just as warm,
spontaneous and sincere as they must have been when Captain LeTellier sailed
his small bark, Ajax, into the harbor of Honolulu on March 30, 1843 - 142
years ago. Within a few days, on April 8, 1843, he organized the Lodge "Le
Progress de l'Oceanie, U.D.'?...the first Masonic Lodge west of the Missouri
River, a notable distinction.
We enjoyed all this warmth and charm while carrying out a busy and eventful schedule. We celebrated the 75th Anniversary of Honolulu Lodge No. 409;
laid a wreath at the National Cemetery in honor and memory of our departed
Brethren; instituted King Kalakaua Lodge, a new Daylight Lodge in Honolulu;
shared in the pleasure and relief of the Mortgage Burning Ceremony of
Schofield Lodge No. 443, always a delightful occasion; and attended a very
successful Leadership Workshop.
Following all of these events in Honolulu on the Island of Oahu, we visited
the Islands of Hawaii, Kauai, and Maui, where we found the same traditional
friendly and gracious hospitality.
We learned that the Lodges in the Islands face the same problems,
challenges, and successes as do the Lodges in California. There are now 12
Lodges there with a total membership of just under 3,000.
We returned to the Mainland refreshed, invigorated, and with a rich collection of life-long memories. We cannot help but be proud of our Lodges
and the Brethren and their families in the Hawaiian Islands. They are a real
credit and asset to this Jurisdiction!

HISTORY
One recommendation to all of our Lodges that I fervently hope you will
implement is the development of an on-going history of each of our
Constituent Lodges, with a narrative about its members. "HistorY,' as one
college professor maintained, is "his story" or the story about people! the
mere record of dates, events, and places becomes vapid and boring. People
like to learn about other people!
I am aware that a history of the Grand Lodge is being planned. My recommendation concerns the individual Lodges and their respective members. There
really are two seperate histories involved.
Each Constituent Lodge should have a Lodge Historian whose duty it would
be to submit an annual report to our Grand Lodge History Committee. This
Committee, under the Chairmanship of Brother John Nocas, has compiled
considerable information but has not been supplied with funds to publish it.
Many of us remember the overwhelming task so ably performed by Past
Grand Master Leon 0. Whitsell, Chairman of the Grand Lodge Committee
on Masonic History, when the four-volumne set entitled, One Hundred Years
of Freemasonry in California, was published during our centennial year of
1950. Some of our Lodges cooperated beautifully, others contributed little
or nothing. The results are clearly and permanently recorded.
.
I firmly believe that we owe it to posterity to leave a complete and interesting
history of our Lodges and their outstanding members. I hope you and my
successors will agree with me.
U.S.S. ARIZONA MASONIC MEMORIAL PLAQUE
Grand Master Haglund noted last year that there are many plaques at the
U.S.S. Arizona Memorial in Pearl Harbor commemorating those who made
the supreme sacrifice, but no plaque bearing the Square and Compass.
Through the assistance of the National Sojourners and the Masonic Service
Association of the United States we received approval from the U.S. Department of Interior to place a commemorative plaque at the U.S.S. Arizona
Memorial.
This was accomplished during the first week of October when I was privileged to deliver the Masonic Plaque to the Ranger in Charge.
The Plaque is inscribed: "In memory of those true Patriots who lost their
lives defending our Country here at Pearl Harbor, December 7, 1941. All
Freemasons gratefully acknowledge their unselfish sacrifices and forever will
remember their heroism."
A Masonic Square and Compass emblem is in the Center of the Plaque.
We invite you to look for it the next time you visit this sobering memorial.
We hope you will share in the pride and gratitude of all Freemasons.

DECISIONS
Decision No. 1 - Use of Masonic Insignia
The California Association of High Twelve Clubs has requested permission to use the Masonic Insignia, the Square and Compass, on their printed
material.
Annotation la of the California Masonic Code reads as follows: "Grand
Lodge is entitled to sole use of its name and insignia. The name and emblem
have been registered with the Secretary of State pursuant to the California
Corporations Code, and the unauthorized wearing of fraternal organization
insignia is prohibited by Penal Code Section 538 (b)."
The insignia is used to identify Lodges and members of the Fraternity of
Free and Accepted Masons. Literature or printed material of Lodges and
Grand Lodge use that insignia as a mark of identification.
All concordant and appendant organizations of Freemasonry have their
own insignia of identification, and are set apart as separate organizations
by these individual insignia.
I am a member of High Twelve and support the purposes of High Twelve.
I commend the support and close association of High Twelve with Masonry
in California, yet I believe the purpose of the Masonic insignia is for identification of each organization. If High Twelve is permitted to use the Masonic
insignia, then all concordant and appendant organizations should be permitted
to do the same. If this should occur it would give the appearance that all
such organizations are a part of Grand Lodge, which they are not.
It is my decision, therefore, that the Masonic insignia should be restricted
to Grand Lodge and the constituent Lodges exclusively.
Decision No. 2 - York Rite Sovereign College
I have been asked to sanction a York Rite Sovereign College chapter in
California.
The applicable Section of the California Masonic Code is 2068 and the
question is whether the York Rite Sovereign College was in existence in California prior to September 27, 1957.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

After considerable investigation and with the assistance of the Committee
on Jurisprudence I have determined that a charter existed prior to September
27, 1957 for Chapter No. 12 of the York Rite Sovereign College, even though
an inactive chapter.
Therefore, it is my decision that the York Rite Sovereign College exists within
the Jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of California and Chapter No. 12 may
be reactivated and new chapters may be formed within our Jurisdiction.

I recommend that the Grand Lodge of California sponsor a float on New
Year's Day in 1987 in the Pasadena Tournament of Roses Parade. The cost
would be about half of the cost of the newspaper insert, or 60 cents per
member to be added to the per capita assessment as of June 30, 1986, on
a one time only basis. This would be a $100,000 entry, with Masonic Youth
Groups helping in the construction and decoration of the entry.
The participation would not only reach the great numbers in attendance
at the Parade, but also, the many millions throughout the world who would
watch it on television.
Our involvement in this project would build morale among our youth groups
and would tell the world that California Freemasons are indescribably grateful
to our forefathers who produced the U.S. Constitution. Furthermore, the accompanying publicity could certainly emphasize the important role of Masons
who participated at the Constitutional Convention in 1787. This is a rare,
once-in-a-lifetime opportunity at a cost that is minimal, with so many
advantages, that I fervently hope you will act favorably upon it.

Decision No. 3 - Interpretation of C.MC. Section 2050
I have been asked to render a decision as to whether the tenants of the
Masonic Memorial Temple property on Pine Street in San Francisco are forbidden from serving liquor therein.
Section 2050 of the California Masonic Code controls the serving of liquor
at social functions. The particular clause in question reads:
"Provided, however, that, except for ritualistic purposes, no liquor, wine
or beer may be served in a Masonic Temple or in any building or structure
owned or operated by a Masonic Temple or any organization a prerequisite
of membership wherein is that a person be a Master Mason."
It is my Decision that the above Section with respect to the specific question was not enacted to prohibit the tenants of the Pine Street property from
the serving of alcoholic beverages where there is no exterior Masonic identification on the buildings.
RECOMMENDATIONS

Recommendation No. I - Application of C.M.C. Section 2050
It is my Recommendation that the Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes
of California be authorized to determine whether Section 2050 of the California Masonic Code shall apply to the private individual residences of its

Recommendation No. 2 - Pasadena Tournament of Roses
In 1982, we took advantage of the opportunity to observe the 250th Birthday of our famous Brother George Washington, by producing an 8-page insert
about Freemasonry for the newspapers of our Jurisdiction at a cost of $1.13
per member approved for inclusion in the per capita assessment.
Making Freemasonry more visible to the public is most desirable. There
are many ways to accomplish this, one of which would be to have a flowerdecorated float in the Pasadena Tournament of Roses Parade. It would provide a world-wide exposure for California Freemasonry.
The year 1987 will offer an opportunity for us to take advantage of this
as it is the Bicentennial of the U.S. Constitution. We are proud to say that
we have steadfastly supported each year, by Proclamation of the Grand Master,
the Anniversary of this great document.

51

Recommendation No. 3 - Admission of Children into the Home at
Covina
The present rules for admission of children to the Masonic Home at Covina
require, among other qualifications, that the child be the "minor next of kin"
of a Master Mason of this Jurisdiction, and under certain additional restrictions of other jurisdictions. These rules limit the eligibility for admission to
the children, nieces, nephews, grandchildren and great grandchildren of Master
Masons, including those legally adopted by them. Although the Trustees of
the Masonic HomfS have the power to adopt rules for admission, such rules
must be in accordance with the Constitution and Regulations of Grand Lodge.
The Trustees, therefore, have no power to change that basic requirement
without Grand Lodge approval.
In the experience of the Trustees of the Masonic Homes, it has become
evident that many Master Masons have responsibilities to children who are
related to them by marriage rather than by blood, and who are either needy
or require the services provided by the Home for Children. Applications from
such Master Masons in need of the services which can be provided by the
Home for Children are being rejected in those cases where the minors involved
are not next of kin, even though the Home for Children has the capacity to
render the required services. Unlike the Home for Adults at Union City, which
is filled to capacity and in many cases persons admitted are subject to a waiting
period, there are vacancies in the Home for Children at Covina. There has
been a marked increase in the number of residents now living at the Home
for Children over and above the number living there a few years ago when
the population dropped to an alarming low of 32 children. The number of
residents is now about 55 and seems to have stabilized at that figure. While
this is a substantial increase, the fact that it remains constant at this number
means that there is room for 25 more children who could be provided with
needed services.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

For this reason I am making the Recommendation to the Grand Lodge that
the present provisions regarding eligibility to apply for admission to the Home
for Children at Covina be modified to include the term "minor relatives by
blood or marriage of Master Masons" in lieu of the term "minor next of
kin of Master Masons." This would make available the advantages of our
Home not only to next of kin but also to stepchildren and nieces and nephews
of a Master Mason by marriage. By so doing, in many cases we would at
the same time be relieving the distress of a worthy Brother Master Mason
who may not be in a position either financially or physically to care for a
child for whom he is responsible although that child is not related to him
by blood. A number of applications for such needy children have been
presented to the Board of Trustees in the past, but due to our present rules
could not be approved. This Recommendation is intended to be operative
only when there are sufficient facilities available to accommodate such needy
children, and, in any case, the children of Master Masons of this Jurisdiction
would have prior consideration.
