Recommendation No. 5 - Special Committee to Study and Clarify
C.M.C. Sections 2048 and 2050
I was asked to rule on whether a chapter of the National Sojourners may
properly hold a meeting in an Officers' Club within California or Hawaii.
It is my understanding that a room is rented in an Officers' Club for the
meeting and during the time the meeting is in progress the bar in said club
is open - selling, dispensing and serving liquor.
Section 2048 - "Meeting Place Limitations" says, "A Masonic Lodge or
organization the prerequisite of membership wherein is that a person be a
Master Mason, shall not hold a stated or special meeting in, or own or rent
a building, or be a tenant in a building, containing a bar", which in effect
would prohibit the National Sojourners from meeting in the above described
Officers' Club.
However Section 2048 goes on to say that "this section shall not prevent
a Masonic related organization from holding a meeting in a hotel, restaurant
or club where intoxicating liquor is sold."
As I understand it there is a general rule of law that if a specific provision
in the latter part of a document is contrary to a general provision in the earlier
part of the document, then the latter provision prevails.
The complication for me in this section is that the first provision spells
out that the persons attending the Meetings are Master Masons, but the provision at the end of the Section says "Masonic related organization". If a
Masonic related organization is Eastern Star, Daughters of the Nile, or others
whose members are not Master Masons, then there would be no contradiction.
In light of the difficulty in interpretation of Sections 2048 and 2050 of our
Masonic Code relating to Meeting Places and the Serving of Liquor at Social
functions, I recommend that the incoming Grand Master appoint a special
committee to restudy these two Sections for possible modifications and
clarification and that the Decision on the question of National Sojourners
meeting in Officers' Clubs be held in abeyance until such clarification and/or
modification is made.

In drawing this Message to a close, I beg your forgiveness for taking so

As every Grand Master learns first hand and with some measure of shock,

widespread geographic territory, could not be handled efficiently by one man
if it were not for the incredible support and assistance of so many people!
Therefore, I must pay tribute to some of them - with the fervent hope that

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Grand Master's Decision No. 2 approved the re-activation of Chapter 12
of the York Rite Sovereign College, allowing new chapters of that body to
be formed in our Jurisdiction.
This organization was issued a Charter on May 11, 1957. Its purpose was
not to confer degrees, but to stimulate interest in Masonry generally. At some
later date, it was de-activated.
California Masonic Code Section 2068 states, in part, "A Mason residing
within this jurisdiction shall not become a member of any organization, or
unit thereof, being newly formed in this jurisdiction, by whatever name or
character, which requires Masonic affiliation as a condition to membership,
unless such organization existed in this jurisdiction on September 27, 1957."
In view of the fact that Chapter 12 of the York Rite Sovereign College was
issued its charter prior to that date, the Committee recommends the adoption of Grand Master's Decision No. 2.
The Grand Master's Decision was approved.

to relax the requirements for admission, at least to this extent. The increase

The Masonic Homes Trustees:

by blood or marriage of Master Masons" in lieu of the term "minor next
of kin of Master Masons" has been referred to the Board of Trustees of the

C.M.C. SECTIONS 2048 AND 2050

The Committee on Jurisprudence:
Your Committee on Jurisprudence, to which this Recommendation No. 5
of the Most Worshipful Grand Master has been submitted, reports as follows:
The Grand Master has received many requests for interpretation of Sections 2048 and 2050 of the California Masonic Code, including a request from
the National Sojourners. During his review of these sections he has discovered
ambiguities and inconsistencies which have rendered interpretation difficult
or impossible when directed to specific circumstances. The Grand Master
believes that these sections need to be reviewed.
Therefore, the Grand Master recommends that the incoming Grand Master
appoint a special committee to study Sections 2048 and 2050 for possible
modification(s) and clarification and that the specific question as to the
meeting place of National Sojourners be held in abeyance until the special
Committee renders its report to Grand Lodge and action is taken thereon.
Your Committee on Jurisprudence has determined that no enabling legislation is necessary to carry out Recommendation No. 5. A majority vote is
necessary to carry out the Recommendation.
To place this matter before Grand Lodge, we move the adoption of the
Recommendation.

The Grand Master's Recommendation No. 5 asks the incoming Grand
Master to appoint a Special Committee to study Sections 2048 and 2050 of
the C.M.C. for proper interpretation and possible modification and
clarification.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes is constantly appraising
and reappraising its position on what it believes to be a sound and acceptable policy of this Grand Lodge. We believe, therefore, that any and all studies
of this nature are invaluable, not only to this committee, but also to the General
Assembly in making thoughtful and progressive policy decisions.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a "Yes" vote
on Grand Master Henville's Recommendation No. 5.

Annual Communication, Grand Lodge of Wyomin!'•

In this significant Masonic year we face an unusually important opportunity - and a
tremendously large need. At every turn and from every direction, our world is in a
rapid s.~ate of change and appears nearly every day to be in turmoil.
If the world appears such to us, just imagine how difficult it is for the young person
of today. The same turmoil, the same changes impact them but they must deal with them
without the benefit of the history, tradition and experience which you and I have.
There is an extremely important opportunity for us to he important in the lives of
young people of today in general, particularly those associated with our fine Masonic
Youth Orders -- Job's Daughters, Rainbow for Girls and DeMolay.
Nicely enough, the time has never been better for us to tighten our affiliations and
strengthen our relationship with these fine young people. On every front, there is a
swing "back to the basics". We see this in economics, education, social structures,
entertainment and societi in general. The "brief" fling at an open, permissible,
liberal way of life where anything goes has been tested and found lacking and all of
our institutions are enjoying a wave of nostalgia. We should recognize that this
brings the world back toward the things Masons have always stood for.
While we cannot yet boast of a rising membership either in our Fraternity or in the
Masonic Youth Orders, there are signs that the rapid declines of recent years are
slowing and there is some hope that the corner will be turned and our nunbers will
begin.to grow again.
While it should be a regular part of the activities of each of our constituent Lodges
to plan, promote and take part in Fraternal intercourse with these fine young people
at every opportunity, I proclaim the Month of March, 1985, as
MASONIC YOUTII ACTIVITIES MONTI!.
in the Grand Jurisdictions of California and Hawaii and encourage each Lodge to make
special efforts to promote a closer relationship with the young people in their local
Masonic family. Further, I direct that such emphasis and effort not be confined merely
to this official month, but should be made a part of the entire Masonic yea.r by including the members of the Masonic Youth Orders in such activities as Public Schools
Observances, U.S. Constitution Observances, Layman's Nights, Hiram Awards, Installations and any and all other public events.
Further, I direct that this Proclamation
should be read at the March Stated Meeting and, where possible, published in the Lorige
Trestle Board for the Month of March.
Sincerely and Fraternally,

MASONIC HOMES ENDOWMENT MONTH

PUBLIC SCHOOLS WEEK - 1985
''Public Schools
For Unlimited Opportunities "
America is on the move! From its bold, yet frail, beginning a little over
200 Years ago, our country has grown with such astonishing rapidity that it now
occupies a place of ·prominence among the nations of the world.
There was no way our founding fathers could have foreseen America's magnificent destiny, yet they, themselves, were the ones who made it possible by establishing a system of free public education • • • a system that provided unlimited
opportunities for the youth of this nation to develop their talents and use them
for the advancement and growth of our great country.
The unlimited opportunities offered by our public schools has provided America
with a vast reservoir of talented citizens who are competent in leadership, proficient in the professions, astute in business, outstanding in the sciences and
skilled in the crafts. The end result is a standard of living judged by many co be
the highest in the world.
If this standard is to be maintained, our schools muse have the whole-hearted
support of the entire community. I therefore call upon all members of society,
especially our Brethren in Freemasonry, to support our schools in their endeavor
to continue providing unlimited opportunities to the youth of our country. To
this end I do now Proclaim
PUBLIC SCHOOLS WEEK during APRIL 1985
throughout California and Hawaii, and I call upon all Masonic Lodges to arrange
with the schools in their area for a mutually convenient week in the Month of April
to be sec aside for appropriate ceremonies and programs particularly aimed at the
concept of PUBLIC SCHOOLS FOR UNLIMITED OPPORTUNITIES.
Furthermore, I direct that no Lodge programs or meetings, other than Stated
Meetings, be held during the designated week which might conflict with local Public
Schools Observances; and

Brotherly Love, Relief, and truth cannot be better exemplified than through the
existence and support of our Masonic Homes. Since 1906, the Masonic Home for
Adults in Union City has provided security and loving care for our elderly,
fostered feelings of individual self-worth, and encouraged societal interests
among the residents. The Masonic Home for Children in Covina has, since 1909,
aided youngsters to rebuild their shattered lives by providing an atmosphere of
family love and understanding while preparing them to become responsible adults.
The operational expenses necessary to maintain the existing grounds and structures
as well as to provide personnel and services are rising annually at a steady rate.
The average monthly number of residents at Union City will be raised to exceed 400
adults who require one of three levels of care - residental, personal, or skilled
nursing care. Over the last three years, the average number of children at Covina
has increased by 66%, Freemasonry serving mankind is essential to assure continued
quality for those to whom we provide relief,
In the 1983-84 Endowment Year, 75th year of this program, 51% of the Masons in
California and Hawaii gave their support by contributing to the Homes Endowment
fund. If we could increase the participation to 70%, we could reach our goal of
two million dollars this year.
"To relieve the distressed is the duty incumbent on all men but particularly on
Masons who are linked together by an indbsoluble chain of sincere affection." My
Brethren, won't you open your hearts to our elderly and our children?
With the aforementioned in mind, I proclaim the Month of May 1985, to be
MASONIC HOMES ENDOWMENT MONTH
in California and Hawaii and I invite every Mason to share in the support of our
Masonic Hornes Endowment Fund.
Send in your contributions today. Many Brothers match their dues as contributions .
Let us not forget that the opportunity is present to give throughout the year as
memorials to our loved ones.
I direct that this Proclamation be read by the Master at the May Stated Meeting and
also be published in the Lodge bulletins or distributed to each member.

distributed to each member.

PROCLAMATION
U, S. CONSTITUTION OBSERVANCE MONTH
The Chairman of the convention that framed our Constitution was
George Washington.
On the back of hie chair, there was a painting of the
sun as it appeared just above the horizon, When, after many months of
wrangling and discussions which often threatened to break up the convention
entirely, the Constitution was finally signed by the 39 delegates, Benjamin
Franklin, then 83 years old, who had been a great stabilizing force in the
convention, arose and said: "I have looked at that painting again and ap;ain.
I have wondered whether it was a rising or a setting sun. But, now I know it
is a rising sun."
Now, we must see to it that this sun that has shone upon us with
such favor, that has seen America grow from a weak little group of colonies
into the greatest of all nations, does not set.
Now, 198 years later, we must continue to see to it that that rising
sun will forever shine on this Country of the People, by the People, and for the
People,
NOW, THEREFORE I Proclaim the Month of September, 1985, to be
U, S. CONSTITUTION OBSERVANCE MONTH
in the Jurisdiction of California and Hawaii; and I direct all l.Ddges to arrange
and perform, or actively participate in, patriotic exercises to which the public
is invited, with the objective of demonstrating faith in our Nation, intensifying
our allegiance to it, denouncing its enemies within or without and pledging that
justice without undue delay or unconscionable interruption will always prevail.
I further direct that this Proclamation be read at the Stated Meeting
next following its receipt, and that wherever feasible it be printed in the
l.Ddge bulletin,

RJH:mlw
Dated:

July 15, 1985

REPORT OF THE GRAND TREASURER
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
The usual examination of our year-end financial results was conducted by
our Certified Public Accountants, Lindquist, von Husen and Joyce, of San
Francisco.
Their reports are reproduced in the pre-printed Grand Treasurer's report,
now available for your examination.
As you peruse the Grand Lodge financial data, please refer again to the
concerns expressed by our Committee on Finance in their report last year,
pages 268 and 269 of our 1984 Proceedings.
The unhappy fact that we are now losing two members for every one we
raise should be a compelling motive to closely scrutinize all levels of Grand
Lodge expenditures, without further delay.
The evident divergence in two significant trends - escalating costs and
diminishing membership - can only be counter-productive when reckoning
its continuing effect on the sole source of Grand Lodge income - the per
capita assessment levied upon our constituent Lodges.
On a more positive note, we are indeed fortunate that our accumulated
assets appear to be safe and secure, also productive, as evidenced in the Homes
and Temple operational reports.
We again extend thanks for the continuing generosity of our Brethren; also
for the devoted attention of our Board members and Trustees.
I must repeat, it is a pleasure and a privilege to serve.
Respectfully submitted,
JOHN A. SICKENBERGER, Grand Treasurer

Referred to the Committee on Distribution. The Committee on Distribution referred the entire report to the Committee on Finance.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

REPORT OF THE GRAND SECRETARY
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
In compliance with Section 1108-15th of the Supplement to the California
Masonic Code, I am pleased to submit to the members of this Grand Lodge
my annual report on the transactions and business which have occurred during
the year ending June 30, 1985.
The past year has been one of much activity in the Grand Lodge office,
and it is hoped that the actions and efforts of the office personnel in the
performance of their individual responsibilities have met, and will continue
to meet, with your approbation.
The responsibility of receiving all monies due the Grand Lodge and paying
the same to the Grand Treasurer has been faithfully executed, and these monies
have been credited to the appropriate accounts and are reflected in the published report of the Grand Treasurer. All supporting vouchers, receipts, records
and books are on file in the office of the Grand Secretary.
Also on file in the office are the minutes of all meetings held by the Masonic
Homes Board of Trustees, the California Masonic Memorial Temple Board
of Trustees, the California Masonic Foundation Board of Trustees, the
Investment Committee of Grand Lodge, the Retirement Committee of Grand
Lodge and the Executive Committee of Grand Lodge - some forty meetings
in all.
Your Finance Committee has continued to work in close cooperation with
the Executive Committee, the Grand Treasurer, the Grand Secretary, the Grand
Lecturer and the Manager of Accounting in diligently reviewing all items and
amounts which have been submitted to this committee in preparation of the
1985-1986 budget of Grand Lodge. Their report and their recommendations
will be presented to you during the course of this Annual Communication.
I would be remiss if I did not again express my continuing admiration for
those members of the Boards and Committees of Grand Lodge with whom
I have the privilege of working on a continuing basis. These Master Masons
fully understand and practice the tenets of our Fraternity.

During the past year several new people joined our office staff. These
additions were necessary due to two persons leaving our employ for other jobs
and another due to the desire of the Masonic Homes Trustees to employ an
additional field representative occasioned by a retirement. These new people
have assumed their respective job functions and have become valuable additions to our staff.
It is most gratifying indeed to be the recipient of many complimentary
remarks tendered by the Brethren concerning the efficiency and courteousness
of our office personnel, and I can assure those who are kind enough to express
these remarks that they are passed on to those concerned. Rarely do I hear a
negative comment and therefore I can only conclude that we enjoy a fine "batting averagC:' one which I can assure you we will do our utmost to maintain.
Again, I offer a sincere and appreciative "Thank you" to our office staff
members.

MEMBERSHIP QUESTIONNAIRE

Included as a part of the Summer issue of the California Freemason
Magazine was a membership survey questionnaire consisting of twenty
questions.
The general membership was asked to participate in this survey by merely
checking the box appropriate to their status and belief. In addition a blank
page was provided for any comments the respondents might care to make. Approximately 7,000 responses were received, most of which contained the sought
for comments. These responses were tabulated by computer and the results will
be published in a future issue of the Freemason Magazine. As to the comments submitted, these have been made available to several of the Grand
Lodge committees and they are currently being analyzed and compiled. The
results of the many ideas, beliefs and thoughts of those who took the time to
express themselves will be made available to your Executive Committee for
their guidance in their future planning.

SPECIAL ELECTIONS

Elsewhere in this report you will find that 59 Lodges requested dispensations
from the Grand Master to hold special elections for Lodge officers at times
other than the annual Stated Meeting of the Lodge. These requests, for the
most part, were occasioned by the resignation of the Master or one or both of
the Wardens. Many of these applications to hold a special election were received in a faulty condition in that they were not presented as a result of Lodge action being taken or they failed to state the reason why the special election was
being requested, or they did not state that the necessary two- thirds of the
members present at the Stated Meeting approved of the application. In addition, many Secretaries neglect to affix their Lodge's seal to the request. These
applications, therefore, had to be returned for appropriate and required information thereby resulting in extra work for all concerned and the resultant loss
of time. It is suggested that the Lodge Secretary make certain that all the required information is contained in the request prior to it being submitted for
approval by the Grand Master.

85

Again this year, as in past years, many Lodges have come to the realization
that they cannot continue to pay their necessary operating expenses based
upon a dues structure which is unrealistic. Consequently Resolutions have been
introduced to increase the dues to afford these Lodges the income which is
needed to allow them to operate on a sound financial basis. In a few Lodges,
fees for the degrees have also been raised to produce additional income.
The raising of fees and dues requires the Lodge to amend the Uniform Code
of By-laws. T~is action necessitates a Resolution to be presented in writing at
a Stated Meetmg and a Lodge vote taken to accept or reject the Resolution at
the very next Stated Meeting. Following the acceptance of the Resolution by at
least two-thirds of. the members present at the Stated Meeting, the Lodge
Secretary must certify under seal that the law has been complied with and the
amendment to the By-laws has received the necessary vote.
Too often, the Secretary's certification indicates that the Lodge vote on the
~mendment was n?t taken at the next Stated Meeting following the presentation of the Resolution, therefore it must be returned and the proper steps again
be taken. It should be noted that any amendment to the Uniform Code of Bylaws must be approved by the Grand Master or his designee before such
amendment can become effective.

you as your Grand Secretary, and I thank you for this great honor and
privilege.

ACTION BY GRAND LODGE

The Committee on Jurisprudence:
Your Committee on Jurisprudenc e has reviewed one hundred thirty Dispensations and thirty Resolutions and finds that Grand Master Henville acted

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

properly in granting all Dispensations and approving all Resolutions. The
Dispensations are categorized by subject matter in the Grand Secretary's
Report. The Resolutions all concerned Life Membership fees.
Due to the fact that Grand Secretary Klinger and his staff make available
the Applications for Dispensation and the Life Membership Resolutions as
they are received in the Grand Lodge office, we have been able to review the
documentation on a current basis. This allows us to obtain further information or clarification in those cases requiring further review prior to approval.
There are two particular areas which all too often result in tentative disapproval. The first is the Application for Dispensation to hold Special Elections of officers. In a significant number of cases, the reason necessitating
a Special Election is not stated. As a result, we are unable to determine whether
the Special Election is necessary because of a vacancy occurring in the offices of Master or Warden after an officer has been elected and installed in
that office (thereby making the provisions of C.M.C. Section 2502 applicable)
or if a Lodge has failed to install an officer within a period of 60 days subsequent to the election (thereby making Section 2524 applicable). If the latter
is the case, the Grand Master should previously have had applicaiton made
to him for a Dispensation authorizing additional time for qualification of
the officer, or the Lodge should not have been at Labor. Inspectors, as ~he
direct representatives of the Grand Master, as well as Masters and Secretanes,
should be particularly alert in this area and make certain that application
is timely made for proper Dispensations.
The second largest problem area is the Applications for Dispensation to
participate in a parade. Here, all information concerning the purpose of the
parade, the date, whether or not white aprons are to be worn, the manner
of participation such as a float or otherwise, what Masoni~ emblem ?r ot~er
designation is to be used, the source of funds for expenses m connection with
the Masonic participation in the parade and all other facts upon which the
Grand Master may make his determination should be furnished. On several
occasions, these applications have been made upon short notice. In order to
avoid disapproval by the Grand Master, the Lodges should be certain to provide in their applications all pertinent information.
Again we appreciate the assistance of the Grand Secretary and his staff
for their cooperation, particularly in assisting in those cases requiring further review.

In 1984 a Lodge in California, exercising jurisdiction over the accused
because he resides in this state, instituted a trial charging him with unmasonic
conduct as evidenced by the conviction of the accused in the California State
Courts for embezzlement from his employer.
Upon recommendation of the Trial Review Committee, which recommendation was based on the record in the Masonic trial proceedings, this Grand
Lodge at its 1984 Annual Communication reversed the findings of the Trial
Commission, found the accused guilty, and fixed the penalty at expulsion.
This application for restoration, like the preceding trial, has received more
notoriety than usual by reason of the extensive interest displayed by members
of the Coachella Valley Masonic organizations in which the accused and his
wife were very active.
The record, however, reveals that the accused is on probation by the California State Court until May 1986 for the crimes of which he was convicted.
The crimes of which he was convicted were of a serious nature and involved
moral turpitude.
Thus, while we appreciate the interest of each and every person involved
in urging restoration, we find no evidence in the application by the accused,
in any letter urging restoration, or otherwise, of any feelings of remorse or
acts of atonement on the part of the accused.
Your Committee therefore submits the following resolution:
RESOLVED, that the Petition for Restoration in Trial Record No. 2200
be denied.

TRIAL RECORD No. 2229

In Trial Record No. 2229, a member of Menorah Lodge No. 623 was charged
with unmasonic.conduct on the grounds that he, without authorization, took
checks from a Brother Master Mason with whom he was living, utilized these
checks to transfer funds from the Brother Master Mason's bank account to
his own, and applied the unlawfully obtained funds for his own personal use.
The accused did not formally respond to or defend against the charges and
the Trial Master found him guilty of unmasonic conduct and fixed the penalty
at suspension.
Your Committee on Trial Review believes that the acts of the accused are
of sufficient severity that the penalty should be raised from suspension to
expulsion.
We therefore submit the following resolution:
RESOLVED, that the findings of the Trial Master in Trial Record No. 2229
be affirmed, but the penalty be raised to Expulsion.
TRIAL RECORD NO. 2199

In this case a member of Yorba Linda Lodge No. 469 was charged with
three specifications of unmasonic conduct.
Charge 1) He smuggled high technology electronics overseas.
Charge 2) He falsified documents.
Charge 3) He conspired, aided and abetted to violate federal export laws.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Upon Trial by Commission, the accused was found not guilty of specification one, and guilty of specifications two and three. The Trial Commission
determined that the accused should be expelled.
The Trial Review Committee found that the Trial Record as submitted to
Grand Lodge did not contain the court documents to sustain the charges as
relied on by the Commission. After careful review, your Committee was unable
to sustain the findings of the Trial Commission based upon the partial record.
Your Committee therefore offers the following resolution:
RESOLVED, that the finding of guilty of unmasonic conduct in Trial
Record No. 2199 be reversed and that the matter be remanded to Yorba Linda
Lodge No. 469 to provide Grand Lodge with a record containing sufficient
evidence to sustain their findings.

The Brother Master Mason was awarded ten percent (10%) recovery along

The Committee is of the opinion that the loan was a personal business contract between two parties which might have been enforced by legal action prior
to the filing of bankruptcy. The Committee found that the filing for bankruptcy was a personal right authorized under the law, therefore, did not involve
moral turpitude. While the Committee was not unsympathetic to the Brother
who sustained the loss, we do not believe that the failure to repay a debt was
unmasonic conduct in these circumstances. Your Committee therefore submits the following Resolution:
RESOLVED, that the findings and penalty in Trial Record No. 2220 be
reversed and a not guilty verdict entered.

SPECIFICATION 2) He swore, under oath, before a U.S. Bankruptcy

would be paid when his home was sold, knowing
full well that it was already over-encumbered and
was in danger of foreclosure.
The accused did not respond to the charges. The Trial Master found the

The Committee finds no fault with the Trial Master's decision regarding

three should be reversed and the accused should be found not guilty. Based
on the facts in the Trial Record, the Committee finds that Specification three
does not involve moral turpitude, therefore, there is no unmasonic conduct.
The Trial Master's report regarding Specification three indicates that on
November 6, 1981, the accused borrowed $10,000 from a Brother Master
Mason. The accused on numerous occasions promised that he would repay
the debt. On July 3, 1984, the accused filed a petition for debt re-organization

TRIAL RECORD NO. 2213

Trial Record No. 2213 came to your Trial Review Committee as a result
of charges filed against a member of Tuolumne Lodge No. 8. The allegations
of unmasonic conduct were based on alleged violations of California Penal
Code, Section 647A, that is, wilfully and unlawfully annoying and molesting
a minor. Although originally pleading "not guiltY,' the Brother withdrew that
plea. The result was a finding by the Trial Master, without commission, of
guilty, fixing the penalty at expulsion.
In considering this matter, your Committee found two possible, and likely, failings. First, it appeared that many of the available records and documents
were not, despite their availability, before the Trial Master. They were not,
as a result, before your Committee. Underlining our concern is the well known
fact that these particular charges are, especially in marital dissolution proceedings, easily brought and difficult to disprove. Second, it is evident from
what is before us, that the decision by the accused to withdraw his not guilty
plea was made only after several conversations with the Lodge Secretary. This
Secretary later became the Trial Master. We find this a substantive violation
of equity and due process, as these conversations may have been material in
the Brother's conviction and sentence. Your Committee requires additional
confirmation that a just ruling exists.
Your Committee submits the following resolution:
RESOLVED, that the Trial Master's verdict of guilty and the penalty of
expulsion in Trial Record No. 2213 be reversed, and that this matter be remanded for further investigation, findings, and verdict by a different Trial
Master.
TRIAL RECORD NO. 2227

Trial Record No. 2227 involves a member of Hanford Lodge No. 279.
Charges of unmasonic conduct consisting of trespass, drunk in public, driving under the influence, and the use of foul and abusive language to another
Mason's wife were brought. The Trial Master, acting alone, returned a finding
of Guilty as to all charges, fixing the penalty at Expulsion.

96

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

In considering this matter, your Committee noted that the first two charges
were based on alleged conduct occurring approximately one year prior to the
third charge, the one of using foul and abusive language. No facts were
presented, nor foundation laid, for the Guilty finding on those first two
charges, except a brief heresay statement to the effect that they were a matter
of public record. We respectfully state that more evidence and substantiation
is required if, in fact, they do amount to unmasonic conduct.
The third charge, foul and abusive language to a Brother Mason's wife,
if true, is deplorable. It is questionable, however, that it is of the gravity contemplated in the California Masonic Code as constituting unmasonic conduct. Additionally, the Trial Master's findings seem completely founded on
a third party's oral statements, allegedly, but not in writing or completely,
confirmed by the lady at whom the allegedly foul and abusive remarks were
directed. The facts presented to your Committee do not support the findings.
Your Committee submits the following Resolution:
RESOLVED, that the verdict and penalty submitted in the Trial Master's
Report in Trial Record No. 2227 be reversed and that the accused stand
acquitted.

The Committee on Trial Review deems the penalty as inadequate. The actions of the accused constitute, in our view, betrayals of the trust confided
in him. As Secretary of his Lodge he owed a fiduciary duty to it specifically
and to Masonry in general. We, therefore, offer the following resolution:
RESOLVED, that in Trial Record No. 2219 the finding of guilty of unmasonic conduct be affirmed but that the penalty be raised to Expulsion.

TRIAL RECORD No. 2216

In Trial Record No. 2216, a member of El Cajon Valley Lodge No. 576
was charged with unmasonic conduct in that he did conspire to defraud the
United States by making and using false documents at various times while
performing welding services on ship repair contracts for the United States
Navy. He was found GUILTY on all twenty-two (22) charges in the United
States District Court for the Southern District of California and was ordered
to pay a fine of $15,000, be imprisoned for a period of eighteen (18) months
and placed on probation for five (5) years. On appeal, the United States Court
of Appeal for the Ninth Circuit affirmed the conviction and penalty. In
response to the notice that unmasonic charges were being preferred, the accused responded by letter denying each and every charge. The Masonic Trial
by Commission resulted in a verdict of guilty and imposed a penalty of
reprimand.
Your Committee feels that offenses of this kind are such serious violations
as to merit a greater penalty than Reprimand.
RESOLVED, that the finding of Guilty of unmasonic conduct be affirmed,
and that the penalty be raised to Expulsion.

TRIAL RECORD NO. 2221

EXHIBIT D

In this case, a member of Trana Lodge No. 684, was charged with four
specifications of unmasonic conduct relating to improper sexual conduct. The
accused being a young Methodist minister in a small community, and because
of its possible repercussions to the church, the Lodge and the community,
our Committee recommended to the Grand Master, E. Arthur Haglund that
the matter be transferred to San Bernardino for trial with a "neutral" Trial
Master and Commission.
After Trial by Commission, the accused was found guilty of two specifications and in part of a third. Suspension was determined as the penalty by
vote of 8-1.
The accused has been reassigned by his presiding Bishop to Arizona and
most probably will not return to this Jurisdiction. If he did return it is doubtful
that Trana Lodge, under the circumstances, would ever reinstate him. The
penalty imposed therefore, that of suspension by the Lodge, thereby permitting
the Lodge, at its option, to reinstate the Brother, in essence is an expulsion.
We believe that the offense charged justified the penalty of expulsion and
that the penalty therefore be raised to Expulsion.
We therefore submit the following Resolution:
RESOLVED, that the finding of guilty in Trial Record No. 2221 be affirmed
but that the penalty be raised to Expulsion.

TRIAL RECORD NO. 2198

Your Committee has considered a Petition for Restoration in Trial Record
2198 by a former member of Solano Lodge No. 229 who was expelled by this
Grand Lodge at our last Annual Communication after pleading guilty to insurance fraud.
Membership in our Fraternity must be jealously guarded and once membership is lost by an act of unmasonic conduct, restoration for the rights and
privileges of Freemasons should be granted only on clear and convincing
evidence of atonement and rehabilitation.
The former member has expression of support from his former Lodge and
from members of the community. However, your Committee does not feel
that sufficient time has elapsed to allow for the required showing.
Your Committee therefore submits the following Resolution:
RESOLVED, that in Trial Record 2198 the Petition for Restoration be
denied.

REPORT OF GRAND LECTURER
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
As the sands of time sift their way through the hourglass of life, so, too,
has another year carved its niche upon the annals of Freemasonry in this
Jurisdiction and I herewith submit my report on the labors of the year just
past in compliance with those areas of the California Masonic Code.
While this report should speak only to those areas with respect to ritual
because of the minor word changes in the C.M.C. relative to the Grand Lecturer's duties in 1981, I beg to inform you that it is entirely impossible to
separate those areas of ritual and administration if I am to comply with my
duty as Grand Lecturer.
As I pointed out in my report of 1982, the action of Grand Lodge left a
void of responsibility regarding the reporting to this Grand Lodge on the condition of the Lodges in regard to administration. This information is received
both by the Grand Master and the Grand Lecturer, but our Code fails to
delegate the responsibility of this report to the Grand Lodge. This legislation
has not provided or assigned responsibility for the guidance and counseling
of our Inspectors in areas of administration. The preparation of questionnaires for Officers of Lodges in order to qualify in administration for advancement has not been addressed and is apparently no longer the responsibility of the Grand Lecturer and his assistants.
It is the duty of each Assistant Grand Lecturer to assist the Grand Lecturer in the discharge of his duties; to examine and instruct the Inspectors
within his Division in the performance of their respective duties with respect
to ritual. My question is, who now should assist the Grand Lecturer in those
areas of "administmtive" instruction, which all Inspectors and Lodge Officers
must have? My duties speak to qualifying the Assistant Grand Lecturers and
Inspectors and to assist them in the discharge of their duties. I cannot do
this alone, but I merely point this out to you to show the mistaken action
of this Grand Lodge in 1981 when they added these simple words to two sections of the Code, "with respect to ritual."
The writing of this report is not ritual. Approval and segregation of expense claims for Inspectors and Assistant Grand Lecturers is not ritual. The
preparation of an annual budget for the Grand Lecturer, the Assistant Grand
Lecturers and Inspectors is not ritual. The long range planning and preparing
for Grand Lodge Ceremonies, Receptions for the Grand Master, Anniversaries of Lodges, room accomodations, meals and transportation for traveling
Grand Lodge Officers is not directly related to ritual. Those areas I previously spoke to are not ritual.
Your Grand Lecturer and the Assistant Grand Lecturers have continued
to work with the Inspectors and Officers of the constituent Lodges in areas
of administration, even though the Code indicates it is no longer our responsibility. I recommended at the 1982 Annual Communication that the 1981
legislation did not address and did not specify as to where these responsibilities
lie and that the matter be referred to the incoming Grand Master for clarifica-

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

tion. This matter continues to be an area of consternation and concern with
the Ritual Committee and at times with the Executive Committee.
I therefore make the following recommendation:
That the two areas of the California Masonic Code relating to the Grand
Lecturer and the Assistant Grand Lecturers which were changed at the 1981
Annual Comunication be rescinded, removing the words "with respect to
ritual" from Section 1114. 4th. and Section 1116.

Vacancies in this five-man line amount to four percent and will continue
to plague some of our Lodges for a considerable length of time. A vacancy
can be caused by many things - a person having a job transfer, a death, a
person not qualified to perform, plain old drop-out, and many, many other
reasons. Vacancies cause some officers to advance too fast. Skipping a portion of the line moves a person through in a very short time. However, for
the most part, it moves an inadequate officer into a place or station without
proper preparation. In almost all cases, this officer is not prepared for the
position or the responsibility applied to that position within the Lodge. The
officer suffers and, so, too, my Brethren, does the Lodge.
Past Masters filling a vacancy to alleviate the acceleration of an officer's
advancement is sometimes the only answer. When a Past Master accedes to
the request of the members of his Lodge to fill a vacancy, he is saying, "I
have done this before, but you need my help and I am willing." Many of these
Past Masters do a very good job the second time through. My admiration
and respect goes out to those Brothers who unselfishly offer themselves that
second, third or fourth time around. This is true dedication. However, quite
a number are not willing to dedicate themselves as much the second or third
time as they were the first. This is unfortunate, for any Brother that accepts
an office in any of our Lodges should be willing and able to give the best
he has to offer, not just a token involvement.
Again this year the total number of Funeral Certificate holders has declined.
What I personally believe has happened, is that we are now receiving a better, or more true and proper count of those Brethren qualified to do the service. The numbers are near 1800 which amounts to almost three for every Lodge
within the Jurisdiction. The action taken by this Grand Lodge to approve
the certification P.rocedure and the printing of the new book, which outlines
the various ceremonies in 1983, is doing the job and will result in more truly
qualified Funeral Service officiants, within the Jurisdiction, even with the
declining number of Lodges and membership.

Early in the year it was pointed out to our Committee that the Grand Lodge
Supply Room was running short of printed Monitors. We reviewed the book,
made the necessary corrections and it has been available for a number of
months now in its new blue cover. The Inspectors Manual has been a major

RITUAL

Requests do come to the Ritual Committee, from time to time, to allow
or permit various changes in the conferring of degrees - requests such as permitting twelve Fellowcrafts in the third degree and costumes for degree participants. Reasons given for the requests are that it would create more interest
and attract more members to our meetings.
We can easily understand how such innovations might create a temporary
interest and for a time increase attendance, but fortunately for the ritual, no
one person or persons have the authority to sanction such changes and the
ritual must remain as it is until such time as this Grand Lodge recognizes
the need for change.
To all of these requests we have replied that we have no authority in the
matter, except to see that the ritual adopted by Grand Lodge be adhered to
by all Lodges and officers in the Jurisdiction.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

To those who may disagree with this I offer the following quote from a
previous Grand Lecturer, "We do not think that its most important work the preservation of its Ritual in its integrity - should be neglected in any event
for upon that depends its honor and reputation."

HAWAIIAN MASONRY

It was again my privilege to visit our fiftieth State in early July. My primary
purpose for the visit was to conduct a School of Instruction for all Lodges
in the Hawaiian Islands. This was accomplished and I am proud to announce
that the Officers, Officers Coaches and Inspectors of the eleven Island Lodges
displayed a great desire and eagerness to perform the ritual in a most creditable
and efficient manner.
The secondary purpose for my visit was to assist the Grand Master in the
Mortgage Burning Ceremony of Schofield Lodge and the Institution of our
newest Lodge, King Kalakaua Daylight Lodge U.D.
A practice was held for those Past Masters of Schofield Lodge filling places
that were not occupied by our Grand Lodge Officers for both the opening
of Grand Lodge and the Mortgage Burning Ceremony. This was accomplished
one week previous to the actual ceremony and resulted in near perfection for
both the opening and the ceremony. I am most pleased with those fourteen
Past Masters for filling these vacancies and also for an almost flawless
performance.
Many thanks are extended to my Hawaiian Brothers for their efforts and
the many kindnesses shown to me on my visit to that beautiful paradise in
the Pacific.
INSPEClORAL CORPS

Section 1122 of the California Masonic Code sets forth the many required
duties of the Inspector. Over the years many additional burdens and duties
have been added to their responsiblilties even though they are not listed in
the Code. Words alone cannot express the gratitude that the Grand Jurisdiction owes to these great performers. Their diligence to duty and the thousands
of hours put forth for the betterment of our Fraternity should bring them
our highest praise and respect for their limitless devotion to duty.
Turnover is at or near an all time high. Thirty out of the 165 Inspectors
have chosen retirement for one reason or another. Nineteen percent have
chosen other areas of responsibility. My sincere thanks, on behalf of the Grand
Lodge and the Ritual Committee, to those who have sought retirement for
their untiring efforts and undaunted love of our order.
To those newly appointed Inspectors, it is a distinct honor and pleasure
to welcome you to the team and I will be looking forward with great enthusiasm to working with each of you.

109

CONCLUSION

As I conclude this report I do so with mixed feelings about the accomplishments and differences of the year just past. The Grand Lodge year
preceding this one was one with a number of frustrations of which no benefit
will be derived by dwelling upon those uncertainties, insecurities, and lack
of assurances that existed during that period of time. However, a great deal
of credit needs to be given Grand Master Henville for the re-establishment
of understanding and the return to fraternalism that has developed. There
are many ways in which to accomplish good under a declining membership
and uncertain future. Regardless of which path we choose, the survival of
our Fraternity and our fraternal ideals are of utmost concern.
To the 1984-85 Grand Lodge Officers for their great friendship and efforts
put forth in the performance of their respective duties at all Grand Lodge
openings and Ceremonies, my sincere thanks.
To Robert A. Klinger, Grand Secretary, and his very able staff in the Grand
Lodge office, thanks for your ready assistance to help in any situation.
In closing, I must express my gratitude to those seven Assistant Grand Lecturers for their strength, support, and warm bond of friendship provided
during our year. of. service together. If it were not for that closeness that
develops between a group of people working together, the burdens and responsibilities would be most difficult to deal with. I am sincerely and deeply
obligated to each of them. And to you, my Brethren, my humble thanks for
affording me the opportunity to offer another year of service to this great
Fraternity of ours.
Respectfully submitted,
JOE HAMMOND, Grand Lecturer

I move the adoption of this report and that the recommendation included
therein be considered by this Grand Lodge as an emergent resolution.

Jurisprudence, Policy and General Purposes and Finance.
As to the Grand Lecturer's recommendation included in his report be considered as an emergent matter, this was not Adopted by Grand Lodge.

MEETINGS
The Board of Trustees meets on a monthly basis at the Masonic Homes,
alternating between the North and the South. Meeting at the Homes provides a closer look at and better understanding of the operations of each
Home.
This is a working Board dedicated to providing the facilities, staff and
environment essential to the security and happiness of our elderly at Union
City and to the health, education and development of our children at Covina.
Many hours are spent in Committee meetings on rehabilitation, long range
planning, scholarship grants, special projects, budget and finance. lfustees
and Administrators present special reports on operations of the Homes,
resulting in a broader understanding of these complex units and improved
guidance and management of the Homes.
Representatives from the Masonic Homes Endowment Board are invited
to attend the monthly Board meetings. This interchange of information is
invaluable in communicating our needs to the Brethren through this important
Board charged with the responsibility of raising funds for our Homes.
You will note that the Administrators and members of the Board of Trustees
have been given the opportunity to participate in the preparation of this
Annual Report as follows:

UNION CITY STATISTICS
by J. Burton Brown, Administrator
As the fiscal year ended, our population totaled 378 which consisted of
133 men and 245 women. These figures include 40 couples. The monthly
averages consisted of 131 men and 238 women for a total of 369.
During the year, 23 men entered the Home with the average age being 83.4
years; there were 39 new ladies with an average age of 82.5 years.
The number of deaths came close to the number of entries: twenty-eight
men with an average age of 87.4 years and an average period of residency
of 3 years and 5 months, and thirty women with an average age of 87. 7 years
and an average period of residency of 6 years 6 months. One of our oldest
residents, a lady who had reached her 102nd birthday, died on April 16, 1985.
One of the ladies had resided at the Home since 1965 or a period of 20 years.
The three levels of care of the Home and their respective populations were
as follows:
RESIDENTIAL CARE has 49 men and 82 women, with
only five rooms unassigned.
PERSONAL CARE lists 37 men and 75 women and there
were 7 rooms unassigned.

SKILLED NURSING CARE had 47 men and 88 women
being cared for on an Extended Care basis, plus an average
of 16 temporary patients who retained their assigned rooms
in the Residential or Personal Care section during this short
term stay in the Nursing section.

of residents and a considerable amount of inconvenience. With the residents
adjusting to those items quite readily and accepting the delays and disruptions satisfactorily, it was decided to schedule the South Elevator for an
overhaul within this year. This is in process now, and it is expected to be back
in service by Christmas when we will welcome the gift in the same way we

The heating system was converted from steam radiators to a circulating
hot water system with individually controlled heat convectors. A number of
residents participated in "musical chairs (rooms)" as some of them had to
be relocated during the operation as the workmen converted 8 - 12 rooms
at a time. This work was scheduled during the warmer months to lessen the
inconvenience for the residents.
A welcome addition was received this year in the form of a piece of rolling
stock. Money authorized in the budget allowed us to purchase a GMC 39
passenger bus equipped with recliner seats, air conditioning, and rest rooms.
It is greatly appreciated by the residents and has proved to be extremely
beneficial for trips and transporting The Hilltoppers to their off grounds
performances.
Another additional feature which adds to the attractiveness of the Home
appeared near the South Wing of the Main building. It is a landscaped and
paved area that can be used for picnics or barbeques by the residents, visitors,
Lodges and/or groups from the community.

Although our capacity of 433 appears to offer a large number of unassigned
rooms for approved applicants, we must maintain a certain number of
rooms/beds in reserve for flexibility of assignments and for restricted uses.
These reserve figures total 25 from the three sections, and when added to our
population plus the number of beds in the Nursing Section that are needed
for temporary patients, our capacity of 433 is seriously threatened.
As of June 30, there were 37 approved applicants on the Waiting List, some
of whom are couples who have been unable to enter since their approval in
the last part of 1983.
UNION CITY OPERATIONS
by J. Burton Brown, Administrator
Emphasis during this past year has centered upon the continuing work on
the Acacias project. Due to some delays in construction, they will be completed within the next sixty days. These additional accommodations for
couples will be occupied as soon as the department of Social Services of the
State approves them and increases our license from 142 to 190 for the
Residential Section. Our overall capacity will then be 481 which includes the
Personal Care Section and the Skilled Nursing Facility.
Consequently, some of our plans regarding an increase in population have
not materialized. There are several couples on the approved list who have been
patiently waiting for as long as eighteen months. Currently, all approved applicants are assigned to a Waiting List, and those who are determined to have
the greatest need, are given priority in consideration for entry to the Home.
For some of these applicants there may be an interim period of 60 to 90 days
due to certain sections of the facility not having vacancies or being close to
capacity; and it is not unusual for some approved non-married applicants
to have their entry delayed for 8 to 10 months.
As we continue to draw closer to our capacity in the Skilled Nursing Facility
and Residential section, the Trustees are ever mindful of the potential needs
and are exploring various alternatives to what appears to be both short range
and long range concerns.
UNION CITY - SPECIAL PROJECTS
by J. Burton Brown, Administrator
Two mechanical improvements at the Home provide the residents with much
more reliable services than before. The North Elevator was completely
renovated and the revision of the heating system in the Residential Section
was realized during the year. Each of these projects took approximately three
months to complete. Each was also accompanied by temporary relocation

113

UNION CITY FACILITIES
by Stanley L. Channon, Chairman Facilities Committee
The conversion of two former dormitory buildings, apartments for
ambulatory residents, are expected to be completed ready for occupancy in
October. The apartment complex, known as the Acacias, will accommodate
up to 24 couples. Each apartment contains a bedroom, sitting room,
kitchenette and bathroom. Common lounge areas and activity rooms are also
provided in each building. Residents will have access to the main dining room
and other buildings at the Home via a covered walkway and elevator. The
apartments are a welcome addition to our facilities and willreduce the waiting
list of applicants considerably.
The Board is continually reviewing the facilities required to satisfy the needs
of our members and spouses, and has engaged an architect to prepare a master
plan which will consider the various options for future facilities' requirements.
During the past year, many improvements have been made for increased
operating efficiency, for the safety and security of the residents, and for the
overall appearance and enjoyment of the Home. A barbecue and picnic area
has been provided in front of the South wing of the main building and an
access pathway has been paved and landscaped. This attractive setting may
be enjoyed by visitors, staff and residents in future years. The 33 year old
elevators in the main building are being replaced with more modern, faster
and more reliable cars and controls. The antiquated nurses' call system in
the Skilled Nursing Facility is being replaced with a modern two-way communication system; three of the four floors have now been converted to this

COVINA OPERATIONS
by John A. Rose, Administrator
The population of our Masonic Home for Children at fiscal year end is
55. Four children have graduated and are now living independently. Three
of these young adults are attending college. One has joined the United States
Navy. Nine children have been able to return to their natural families as their
respective family situations improved.
In reviewing and evaluating our goals set for the past fiscal year, we see
significant improvement in each area. (1) Our academic and tutorial program
has significantly improved the overall school grade point averages of the
children in our care. (2) The staff of our Masonic Home has submitted to
your Board a draft of our proposed discipline policy, procedures and
methodolgy. Our early review of this valuable material suggests that our standards of discipline could well be a model system for other group homes .as
well. (3) Our staff continues to attend to the "whole" child. The same tenets
and virtues of this Masonic Fraternity are the same basics of our child care
program in guiding the physical, emotional and spiritual development of
children. (4) In an effort to teach the "whole" child, attention is given not
only to the physical health, but the mental health of each child; (5) more and
more, qualified volunteers have been most useful in areas such as tutoring,
big brother and sisterprograms, choir and equestrian instruction. We envision even a more comprehensive program in the coming years.
As a result of your Trustees' continued inspections, and as reported by your
Administrator, we continue to provide a quality environment in which children
thrive and develop. The management of our personnel, property and finances
is professional and sound.
We are most appreciative of our Grand Master, Most Worshipful Roy J.
Henville, who has encouraged donations toward special projects at Covina,
rather than accepting personal gifts for himself. This source of funds has
resulted in the purchase of two educational Apple Ile computers and learning
software. College bound students are expected to be computer literate. We
are now able to provide assistance to their studies and in learning about computer science. The Grand Master's special project fund also provided for the
purchase of sidewalk benches soon to be placed on the grounds.

COVINA FACILITIES
by Stanley L. Channon, Chairman Facilities Committee
As part of the on-going maintenance program at Covina, new standard
drapes were installed to replace the worn and various colored materials in
all of the residential cottages and in the parlor. Vertical blinds were also
installed in the library and dining rooms. Painting of the exterior of the
Administration building and Central Services building, as well as the interior
and exterior of two cottages have been accomplished. In subsequent years,
two cottages will be painted each year on a continuing basis. The previously
inadequate leased telephone system has been replaced with a new purchased
system which provides improved service and efficiency as well as greatly
reduced cost in future years. The new system enables direct calls to be made
and received by house-parents and children in each cottage, with appropriate
controls on toll calls. This feature is especially convenient in handling emergencies and also provides a more traditional home environment for the
children. Other benefits include the ability to make conference calls and to
transfer calls.
Much effort has been devoted to landscaping improvements. Concrete mow
strips have been poured around all of the cottages, and plans have been made
for the replacement or addition of shrubs. The hillside areas have been cleared
and planted with trees and the development of Rainbow Park has been
continued.
The Knights Templar Hospital, the only remaining building of the 1920
era, has been out of service for several years and has been deteriorating rapidly.
Various uses for the building were considered but the cost of renovation would
have exceeded the cost of more suitable new construction. Consequently, the
Board has decidep to demolish this building.
In conjunction with the development of a master plan for Union City, a
similar master plan is being prepared for possible future development of
facilities at Covina. The present facilities are well maintained and are a credit
to "the Fraternity. Improvements are continually being made for operational
efficiency as well as for the enjoyment of the residents and staff.

COVINA FACILITIES EXPANSION
By Kermit A. Jacobson, President
Our printed annual report pertains to work carried out during the fiscal
year ending June 30, 1985. However, in line with our desire to keep you informed, I give you this up-date on our present plans.
In addition to our recent renovation of two existing dormitories at Union
City named the Acacias, we have been studying the projected growth needs
for additional apartments and nursing facilities for our adults. Our needs
are reflected by our long waiting list and the increasing number of applications we continue to receive each month. We are at the point when we must
place approved applicants on a long waiting list due to the lack of available
space in our Residential and Skilled Nursing Areas.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Even though our Masonic membership continues to decline, our membership also continues to grow older. Thus as responsible Trustees, we must plan
for the anticipated increased need for housing for our adults. We carefully
monitor admissions to our Homes to insure that only those truly in need are
admitted.
Our Trustees have analyzed our projected needs for each level of care and
have determined that first we should expand our present level of skilled nursing
at Union City by another 120 beds. We are now working with our architect
to develop suitable plans for this expansion. At our request our architect has
also developed Master Plans for both Union City and Covina.
In our deliberations, we have concluded that at Covina where we have so
much undeveloped land we should consider reasonable use of that land. It
is our judgment that it would be desirable to have a facility strictly for ambulatory Adults in Southern California. There is no thought of duplicating
skilled nursing facilities at Covina. Furthermore, it is our opinion that to continue to use the Covina property to the exclusive use of our children is far
too expensive and not an efficient use of staff and facilities. Realizing that
children and the elderly easily develop an affinity for each other once they
are broughttogether, we are considering the use of the East half of the property at Covina for the development of adult housing. This plan is to provide, in several phases, the use of this unused land for our adults and still
protect the continued and uninterrupted program for our children. In so doing, we will be extending the use of this raw land to its best and most
economical use for both our children and our adults.
Currently, we are in the midst of this detailed Long Range planning. Part
of that study is to insure the availability of the funds for these expansions
as well as the availability of revenue to operate the expanded facilities at both
Homes. Assisting in these fiscal studies are the Investment Committee and
the Grand Treasurer. Detailed operating pro formas are being prepared based on the data provided by the several sources. With such data we will know,
with a reasonable degree of assurance, what our cash flow needs will be to
support these anticipated expansions.
The time between a decision to expand and the date of opening another
skilled nursing facility at Union City, or to commence building for our adults
at Covina, is approximately 30 to 36 months.

A program has been initiated at the Home to provide counselling and
guidance to high school juniors and seniors in preparation for their future
careers. It is recognized that students have varied interests and aptitudes; every
effort is being made to assist them in deciding upon an appropriate course
of action before they enter college or choose a vocation.
The staff of the Home is also placing additional emphasis on scholastic
achievement at all levels as part of a program to improve the educational accomplishments of the children.

During the past school year, ten alumni of the Masonic Home for Children

ADMISSIONS TO HOMES
by Jack R. Vickers and Ralph M Hinds,
Co-Chairmen Admissions Committee
The Admissions Committee was established in order to maximize efficiency in operations of the Board of Trustees. The Board meets monthly, alter-

nating in the North at the Union City Home and in the South at the Children's
Home in Covina. The Admissions Committee has co-chairmen: Ralph M.
Hinds from the North and Jack R. Vickers from the South. Five other
Trustees, selected from the North and South, comprise the balance of the
Committee.
During the last year and one-half it became necessary to establish a waiting
list for admission to Union City. In order to insure that those applicants with
the most need would be provided for first, the Board instituted a new concept. This concept, a point rating system, is used to rank the applicants and
provides the Board with a positive means to recognize the most needy and
place them in their proper place on the waiting list, regardless of when they
have been approved for admission. The system being used recognizes the three
levels of care; Residential, Personal Care and Skilled Nursing, and automatically positions the most needy in each category as space becomes available in
our Union City Home.
The rating system now being used is automatically reviewed every six months
and improvements are considered by the Board of Trustees. This process allows
the Board of Trustees to devote its attention to other critical matters involving the Homes Properties and their operations.
It has not been necessary to institute the rating system for our Covina Home
for Children since we are not operating near capacity. Each child's application is given comparable attention as that given to our adults in Union City.

LONG RANGE PLANNING
by Jack R. Vickers, Chairman Long Range Planning Committee
As a part of a continuing effort to insure care for our needy members and
their wives or widows, the Committee has continued its study of future needs.
This study began several years ago and continues as an active segment of the
Board of Trustees' effort.
This past year an in-depth look at our general membership was completed
and projections to the year 2000 were made. In 1973, Brother Bob Klinger
(now Grand Secretary) conducted a survey of the Lodges in this Jurisdiction.
Lodge Secretaries provided information on the general membership for the
fiscal year ending June 30, 1972. Data was obtained on 91.207o of the membership with respect to membership average age and age distribution.
As a part of the study, additional data with respect to deaths, dimits, suspensions, affiliations, reinstatements and candidates-raised was compiled. Computations were made and sensitivity analyses were conducted and an average
age of membership was established. This was then used as a baseline, and
projections (based upon trends during the last twenty-one years) were made
yearly up to the year 2000. These projections, supported by sensitivity analyses,
show that by the year 2000 our general membership will be approximately
45"7o of that for the fiscal year just ended and the average age of our membership will be 73 years. The study shows that our membership is declining at
an alarming rate. The study also shows that although the average age of
members is increasing, the number of members in the upper age brackets is
declining due to deaths and dimits which are not being replaced with
candidates and affiliations.
In summary, the study shows that an immediate requirement exists for additional facilities to provide for our needy members.

MAJOR GIFT PROGRAMS-POOLED INCOME FUND, WILLS,
BEQUESTS AND TRUSTS
by Adrian C. West, Director of Charitable Gifts
Through our Major Gifts Program many of our Brethren, their wives and
widows, have been assisted in preparing wills and bequests, establishing
charitable remainder trusts, and in various aspects of their estate planning.
While it is difficult to assess in advance the amount of such gifts, they are,
nevertheless, an important source of funds each year for Masonic Homes.
The Pooled Income Fund provides an attractive means of making a major
gift to Masonic Homes while still retaining a lifetime income benefit for the
donor. Due to the favorable treatment provided such gifts by present income
tax laws, it is often possible to increase current income for a donor through
a properly structured major gift to the Homes. Contributions of property
and cash added to the Pooled Income Fund during the past year amounted
to $548,486.47, which is the largest amount added to the Fund in a single
year since it was established in 1975.

various Lodge meetings, widow's nights, and other Masonic programs. Such

further information on our major gifts program, contact the Director of

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

REPORT OF THE ADMINISTRATOR
COVINA HOME

1984-1985
It is with continued pleasure that I submit this, my fifth, annual report to
the Grand Lodge.
This past fiscal year we have implemented, to full scale, the organizational
improvements recommended by and to your Trustees. Through these hard
working and dedicated Trustees, the Masonic Fraternity in this Jurisdiction
has provided the necessary working tools to manage this Home for Children,
a fine example of a pure Masonic philanthropy.
Space and time prevent me from listing the names of those special
individuals, Lodges, and Masonic bodies who have been especially supportive
of our Home for Children. Each of you know what special contribution you
have made which will go on forever in the lives of our children.
Through our Most Worshipful Grand Master, Roy J. Henville's special project fund, the Children's Home was able to purchase two Apple Ile educational computers with a printer. The children are not only learning to be computer proficient, but are enjoying this wonderful gift. Also, through this fund,
a number of attractive benches have been ordered. These benches will be
placed in various areas of the Masonic Home and Rainbow Park.
By and through your generosity we have served the following children:

Our current population consists of 35 boys and 20 girls, for a total of 55.
Our youngest child is four years of age and the oldest is seventeen. We'll have
12 elementary school students, 18 junior high students and 25 high school
students. Our children attend the public schools in the Charter Oak School
District.
I anticipate that applications for admission to the Masonic Home for
Children will increase. There must be more than the 55 children now at the

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
Your Masonic Homes Endowment Board is pleased to submit its 53rd
Annual Report covering the fiscal year ending June 30, 1985. Through the
enthusiasm and dedication of the Board Members and the continued commitment of the Brethren of this great Fraternity to the residents of our two
Homes, contributions to the Endowment Fund have well exceeded one and
one quarter million dollars.
INCOME FROM THE PERMANENT ENDOWMENT FUND

Income from the Masonic Homes Endowment Fund amounted to
$5,074,389.34 which was transferred to the operating account of our two
Homes. This income is an extremely and vitally important factor in providing
the Homes' ltustees with the funds necessary to maintain the exceptionally
high quality of care and services afforded to the residents of both of our
Homes.

HONOR ROLL TABS AND CERTIFICATES
For those Lodges which have attained Honor Roll status of $5.00 or more
average per member, tabs will be presented to the Lodge following the Annual
Communication, by a member of the Endowment Board. For those Lodges
which have attained Honor Roll status for the first time, certificates and tabs
will be presented in like manner.

Our sincere and grateful thank you to Grand Master Roy J. Henville and to
the Grand Lodge Officers and Committeemen , all of whom have been most
supportive of the Endowment Program. We also wish to thank the Masters,
Wardens and Secretaries of the Lodges for their efforts in furthering this
worthy program.
We extend a special thank you to the 89,072 Brothers who, through their
generosity, contributed $1,422,367.64 to the Endowment Fund during the past
year.
We appreciate the splendid assistance we have received from the Grand
Secretary's office under the leadership of Grand Secretary Robert A. Klinger
assisted by Assistant Grand Secretary Clare W. "Bud" Wilson, Jr., Brother
Fran Lewis and the Staff in the Homes Endowment Office at Grand Lodge.
My personal thank you to the members of the Endowment Board for their
dedicated efforts which have made this an outstanding year.

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE ON DISTRIBUTION

GRAND SECRETARY'S REPORT
We recommend that this report be referred to Committees as follows:
That portion relating to change of meeting place referred to the Committee on Charters.
That portion relating to Consolidation of Lodges be referred to the Committee on Charters.
That portion relating to the formation of new Lodges referred to the Committee on Charters and the Committee on By-Laws.
Exhibit ''A:.' concerning dispensations issued, referred to the Committee
on Jurisprudence.
Exhibit "B" concerning Amendments to By-Laws, referred to the Committee on By- Laws.
Exhibit "C'', Trial Records, referred to the Committee on Trial Review.

164

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
Your Committee on Distribution has examined the outstanding Message
of our Grand Master and wishes to commend him on his dedication to the
Craft.
GRAND MASTER'S MESSAGE
The Grand Master's Message contains four Decisions and five Recommendations, and we recommend that the subject matter be referred to the
following Committees:
Decision Number One, relative to restrictive use of Masonic insignia, be
referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence and the Committee on Policy
and General Purposes.
Decision Number Two, relative to York Rite Sovereign College be referred
to the Committee on Jurisprudence and the Committee on Policy and General
Purposes.
Decision Number Three, relating to C.M.C. Section 2050, be referred to
the Committee on Jurisprudence, the Committee on Policy and General Purposes and the Committee on Temple Properties.
On page 4 of the Grand Master's Message, reference is made to the restoration of recognition of the Grand Lodge of New Jersey. We recommend that
this item be referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence, the Committee on
Policy and General Purposes and the Committee on Recognition of Foreign
Grand Lodges.
Recommendation Number One, relative to C.M.C. Section 2050, be referred
to the Committee on Jurisprudence, the Committee on Policy and General
Purposes, and the Trustees of the Masonic Homes.
Recommendation Number 1\vo, relative to Pasadena Tournament of Roses,
be referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence, the Committee on Policy and
General Purposes, the Committee on Finance, and the Committee on Film
and Creative Projects.
Recommendation Number Three, relative to admission of children into the
Home at Covina, be referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence, the Committee on Policy and General Purposes, and the Trustees of the Masonic
Homes.
Recommendation Number Four, relative to removal of Lodge Master, be
referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence and the Committee on Policy
and General Purposes.
Recommendation Number Five, relative to C.M.C. Section 2048 and 2050,
be referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence and the Committee on Policy
and General Purposes.
GRAND TREASURER'S REPORT
We recommend that this report be referred to the Committee on Finance.

be referred to the Committees on Jurisprudence and Policy and General Purposes, and that part referring to budget be referred to the Committee on
Finance.

We recommend that this beautiful report of Masonic Charity in action be
referred in its entirety to the Committee on Finance.
MASONIC HOMES ENDOWMENT BOARD
We recommend that this outstanding report of Masonic Benevolene be

REPORT OF THE CALIFORNIA FREEMASON
PUBLICATION BOARD
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A.M. of California:
A Board comprised of the Grand Master, Grand Secretary, such advisors
as may be desirable, and an Editor- in-Chief, appointed by the Grand Master,
administer the quarterly editing and distribution of the California Freemason
the official publication of the Grand Lodge of California.
More that 19 million copies of the magazine have been distributed to the
members of California and Hawaii Lodges, to the Grand Lodges of other
jurisdictions, and to paid subscribers during its 33 year history. The magazine

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

166

is quoted from time to time in the publications of the American and foreign
Grand Lodges.
The primary purpose of the California Freemason is to inform the membe~s
of California and Hawaii Lodges of the activities of Grand Lodge, the Masomc
Homes of California, U.S. Constitution observances, California Masonic
Foundation, Public Schools Week and events within the constituent Lod~es
such as Hiram Awards, Widows' Nights, Layman's Nights, and more. Mamtaining the high principles of Freemasonry is a paramount goal of the
magazine.
.
.
.
.
A two-year subscription fee of only $2.00 will brmg the C,aliforma
Freemason to friends and families of California Masons. Such gift orders
are an excellent way to communicate the goals and purposes of Freemasonry
to the general public.
Respectfully submitted,
RALPH H. HEAD, Editor-in-Chief
ROY J. HENVILLE,
