REPORT OF THE SOJOURNERS COMMITTEE
To the Most Worship/ul Grand Lodge, F. & A.M. of California:
We of the Sojourners Committee are very enthusiastic and appreciative of
the excellent cooperation we have received from Most Worshipful Roy J.
Henville, the entire Grand Lodge Line, and especially Very Worshipful Robert
A. Klinger and his entire staff. Their effort~, guidance, and help has made
our job much more meaningful and productive. We wo~ld also hke ~o thank
the California High 1\velve Clubs who were very supportive of the S~Journers
program and promoted it in ·each one of the meetings. The Yor~ Rite, Sc.ottish Rite, and all other Concordant Bodies were all very helpful m supplymg
lists of known Sojourners.
This year we have endeavored to gather as many names and addresses of
Sojourners living in our two great States and pass them along to the Lodges
by Zip Code.
.
. .
.
Many Lodges have established Sojourners Committees withm their own
Lodges and some have been very successful. Vacaville Lodge 1':1<?· 134 re~orts
13 petitions, and Orange County Daylight No. 833 reports 9 petitto~s. ~eived.
Many other Lodges have reported significant gains from afflhat1on of
Sojourners.
Thanks to our Grand Secretary and Boulder City Lodge No. 37 in Boulder,
Colorado, we introduced the "Rusty Nail Degree" to the members of the
Sojourners Committee who in turn presented it to the individual Lodges.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

167

Although it did not get to the Lodges until later in the year, some Lodges
have reported outstanding results and new affiliations.
Reports estimate that there are over 70,000 Sojourners living in California
and Hawaii. If these figures are close to being right, you can see each of us
has our work cut out for us. However, if only half of these Sojourners affiliate with California/Hawaii Lodges, we would again enjoy the status of
Number 1.
The Grand Secretary's report will reflect our accomplishments for this year,
but in the words of a song, "WE'VE ONLY JUST BEGUN."
We have cultivated the ground, sown the seed, and with each Mason's help
we look forward to reaping a bountiful harvest of Sojourners. However, this
crop must be handled with much tenderness, compassion, and loving kindness. Just because the "crop" is not harvestable today does not mean it should
be discarded, but continually cultivated until it is ready. This "crop" may take
years to mature, but handled correctly we all will benefit from the abundant
harvest.
Thanks again to all who gave so much to get this program started, and
thanks to those who will keep it going in the future.
Respectfully submitted,
BRUCE CARMITCHEL, Chairman

REPORT OF TRUSTEES
CALIFORNIA MASONIC MEMORIAL TEMPLE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A.M. of California:
The Board of Trustees of the California Masonic Memorial Temple hereby
submits its 30th Annual Report.
At the close of the 1984 Annual Communication of Grand Lodge, the Board
of Trustees of the California Masonic Memorial Temple held its organiza-

PROCEEDIN GS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNI A

tion meeting as required by the California Masonic Code, nominating and
electing the following officers for the ensuing year:
STANLEY M . CAZNEAUX President
JOHN A. SICKENBERGER Treasurer
ROBERT 0. WEST, P.G.M. Vice President
ROBERT A. KLINGER Secretary

to donate $30,000.00 to the Masonic Homes Endowment Fund, in accordance
with our By-Laws.
The Board of Trustees would like to express its appreciation for an excellent
job done by Worshipful Loren Stritenberger, our Executive Vice President
and General Manager of the Temple. Under his direction the daily maintenance
is not only supervised but the entire rental and operation of the auditorium
and exhibit halls is achieved. In addition, he has responsibilities for our Pine
Street Properties and overall supervision of the Library and Museum. The
Trustees would also like to thank both our Grand Secretary and our Grand
Treasurer for their continued good counsel. Their expertise and advice to this
Board of Trustees has led to a very successful year. Your Trustees have
endeavored to discharge their duties, to the best of their ability, so that this
beautiful monument will continue to serve the needs of our great Fraternity
of Masons in the States of California and Hawaii.

168

The California Masonic Memorial Temple serves as a partiotic monument
and memorial, commemorating the members of the Armed Services of the
United States and of the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted
Masons of the State of California, who gave their lives in battle during World
War II. Our Temple is open to the public and attracts people from all o~er
the world. The Library sign-in sheets show visitors from the followmg
countries:
ARGENTINA, AUSTRALIA, 8ELGIUM,8RAZIL, CANADA, COLUMBIA, ENGLAND,
FINLAND, FRANCE, GREECE, HONG KONG,ICELAND, INDIA, ISRAEL, ITALY,
JAPAN.NEW ZEALAND, NORWAY,PHILIPPINES, SCOTLAND, SINGAPORE,
SO. AFRICA,SPAIN, SWITZERLAND, WEST GERMANY.

It continues to be the policy of the Trustees and of all the employees of
the Temple to maintain this building to the highest possible standards. Because
of our exceptional location and excellent facilities, ~e conti~ue to attract
stockholder meetings, concerts, lectures and graduation exercises. Some of
the large corporations who returned this year were Transamerica, McKesson
Corporation , P.G.& E., Levi Strauss, Bank of America, Che~ron and Crown
Zellerbach. Joining us for the first time were Earthquake Engmeers, San Francisco Life Underwriters, KQED, CBS and Nestle Corporation . Entertainm~nt
included the Berkeley Symphony, Miss Chinatown Pageant, Ebony Fas~1on
Faire, Andres Segovia, and Cary Grant. Using our Temple. for graduations
were the University of the Pacific, University of San Francisco and Golden
Gate University.
At the October 1984 Board of Trustees meeting, your Temple Board voted
to assume the funding of the budget for the Library and Museum C~mmit­
tee. Chairman C. John Bellman of the Library and Museum Committee requested and received a $25,000 budget retroactive to the start of the fiscal
year, July I, 1984. In a subsequent meeting the Library and Museum budget
for the 1985-1986 fiscal year was set at $17,500. Brother Harold R. Ecklund,
a professional librarian, has been hired to bring our records up-to-date and
then maintain this highly specialized Library and Museum for the study,
reference and enjoyment by the members of the Craft as well as our many
visitors to the Temple.
.
The Trustees are pleased to announce the continuation of our p~hcy of
providing free parking to our delegates during the official transactions of
Grand Lodge at the Annual Communica tions. In addition, we have also p~o­
vided decorative plants and additional seating in our Temple lobby durmg
Grand Lodge Week.
.
.
Although the maintenance of our Temple requires a conti~ued expe?d1ture
of monies, your Trustees are pleased to report that we are still able this year

REPORT OF CALIFORNIA MASONIC FOUNDATION
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A.M. of California:

The Trustees of the California Masonic Foundation report as follows:
The work of your Board is current and has been promptly and efficiently
dispatched. Your Trustees have worked diligently and effectively to achieve
the purposes of the Foundation, and to make them known to the Brethren
of this Jurisdiction and to encourage its support by contributions and
donations.
Your Trustees have made, during this reporting period, over 400 appearances
on behalf of the Foundation.
During this reporting period we have received donations and contributions
in the amount of $68,377. Appropriate acknowledgement thereof was made
to the donors, and to the families of those persons in whose memory many
of the contributions were made. Our income from investments was $111,903.
The investments, income, and expenses of the Foundation are set forth in
the report of the Grand Treasurer, and are not, therefore, repeated here. Direct
Trustee expense was 10.8 percent of the total income.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

The members of Grand Lodge should be aware that the Foundation has
not received any funds from Grand Lodge by way of per capita tax or assessment. They should also be aware that the Trustees have not expended any
capital funds. All awards, grants and expenses have been paid from the income or from contributions specifically designated for those purposes.
Grants for leadership training were made to the Northern and Southern
Jurisdictions, Order of DeMolay; Order of Job's Daughters; and the Order
of Rainbow, each in the amount of $2,000.00.
During this reporting period, we received 3,350 requests for scholarship
applications. 319 applications were returned for action by the Scholarship
Committee. We granted 183 scholarships in a total amount of $93,000.
In April 1984, the then Grand Master, E. Arthur Haglund, requested that
the Foundation undertake the solicitation of funds for the restoration of the
Statue of Liberty. The original request letter from the Grand Master was sent
in August 1984, and there have been two follow-up request flyers. The logistics
of handling this solicitation have been tremendous. Thousands of man hours
have been expended by your Trustees and a few other interested parties. A
special commendation should go to Sam Sheff, a member of the Grand Lodge
Week Activities Committee, for his unstinting help.
The Statue of Liberty Film has been shown in 77 Lodges with 3,966 in attendance. It has been shown in over 40 of our public schools with attendance
of over 5,500. It was also shown in meetings of Hi-12, York Rite, Scottish
Rite Order of the Eastern Star, and others.
I~dividual contributions have ranged from $1.00 to $1,000.00, with many
coming from our Home at Union City. Total contribution s for the reporting
period was $651,690 from 31,215 contributors.
Total contributions received to this date is $782,000 from 38,081
contributors.
Direct Trustee expense for the reporting period was one-half of 1 percent
of the total contributed.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
The Committee on Masonic Service Bureaus is pleased to submit its Annual
Report on the operations and conditions of the eighteen Masonic Service
Bureaus for the year ending June 30, 1985. The Committee is in its 58th year.
The Right Worshipful John W. Driskell, Deputy Grand Master, was appointed liaison officer. We appreciated his support and assistance during the
year.
The Committee is well aware of its responsibility in directing the operation
of the Bureaus in a uniform manner. The Service Bureaus assist the
Sojourners, their widows and orphans, operate blood banks, arrange and conduct funerals for deceased Masons, make investigations, assist in the applications for the Masonic Homes, visit sick and promote fraternal relations with
sojourners.
NEW COMMITTEE MEMBERS

We welcome back to our Committee A. Bruce Ivie, a member of Old West
Lodge No. 813, F. & A. M. after leaving the Committee to serve our Grand
Lodge as Senior Grand Deacon during the previous year. We also welcome
Jesse C. Canale, a member of Blackmer Lodge No. 442, F. & A. M., who
is serving the Committee as Secretary.
Delmar W. May was reappointed Chairman of the Committee by Most Worshipful Roy J. Henville, Grand Master.
NEW EXECUTIVE SECRETARIES

We were sorry to lose Paul M. Porter who resigned as Executive Secretary
of the East Bay Masonic Service Bureau after a long and outstanding term
as Executive Secretary. We are pleased that he has offered to stay until another
Secretary is elected with hopes that he will see fit to continue.
We also welcome Jack W. Hughes as Executive Secretary of the Santa Barbara Bureau who replaces Clarence A. Leslie who resigned after many years.
We also welcome John M. Mabel who replaces William H. Osborne as Executive Secretary of the San Francisco Bureau. William H. Osborne passed
away in 1984.
MEETINGS

The Committee held four meetings during the year. One was held during
Grand Lodge week which permitted members of the Bureaus and Lodge Officers to contact the Committee and receive help with their problems which
were applicable to their own areas.
A regional meeting was held in Oakland on February 23, 1985. Twentyeight members and guests of the Bureaus from Central California attended.
Very Worshipful Robert A. Klinger, Grand Secretary, was our speaker. Former
Chairman, Arthur R. Kirk, was our honored guest.

I73

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

A regional meeting was held in Los Angeles on April 13, 1985, 33 officers
and members of the Bureaus were present. Very Worshipful Robert A. Klinger,
Grand Secretary, was the speaker.
The Committee was honored with the presence of Very Worshipful Ron
Brinkman, Grand Secretary of the Grand Lodge of New Mexico and President of the Masonic Relief Association of the United States and Canada.
On June 11th, 1985 a meeting of the Committee was held in Pasadena at
the Scottish Rite Temple to review the Bureau's Annual Budget. The Most
Worshipful Roy J. Henville was the Committee's guest. His suggestions were
most helpful and appreciated.
A business meeting was held after all budgets were reviewed.

BLOOD BANKS
Several of our Bureaus operate Blood Banks for the benefit of the Masonic
Lodges' members and Sojourners. During the year 1,547 units of blood were
donated and over 1,706 units of blood were released to provide the important
life support to our members, their families and Sojourners. We compliment
the Bureaus and our members for supporting this worthy activity.
A problem has arisen since some of the Blood Banks have installed computers and so far have been unable to give an accurate count to the individual
Lodges who are members of their local Masonic Blood Bank. We feel this
will soon be worked out.

I72

TAXES
All Bureaus have filed the required information return to the Internal
Revenue Service on Form 990 and the State Franchise Board on either Form
199 or 199B. The Los Angeles Bureau prepares forms other than the 990 and
199. All Bureaus requiring tax returns have filed them on schedule.
BUSH MASONIC RELIEF FUND
Worshipful Ralph H. Head, President of the Bush Relief Fund, and the
Trustees provide the operating funds for the Bureaus located in the greater
Los Angeles area. The contribution from this fund amounts to 52 percent
of the total budget for the eighteen Bureaus. The Masters, officers and the
members of the Lodges join with the members of our Committee in expressing appreciation to the President and the Trustees of the Bush Masonic Relief
Fund for their generous contribution for the operations of the Bureaus in
the greater Los Angeles area.
MASONIC RELIEF ASSOCIATION OF THE U.S. AND CANADA
Our Grand Lodge now holds membership in the Masonic Relief Association of the United States and Canada. The Association has many functions
including the correlation of the various forms of Masonic relief throughout
the United States and Canada. Our California Bureaus are benefitting from
this membership.
We are pleased to report that the Executive Secretary of the Los Angeles
Bureau, Lloyd V. Smith, is a director of the Association.
The Committee had the pleasure of a visit from Very Worshipful Ron
Brinkman, Grand Secretary of the Grand Lodge A. F. & A. M. of New Mexico, who is the President of the Masonic Relief Association of the U.S. and
Canada, during our Los Angeles area meeting.

UNIFORM COMPACTS
New Compacts have been issued to Tri Lodge No. 595 F. & A. M. to join
the Los Angeles Masonic Service Bureau, also to Palms-Adams No. 512 F.
& A. M. to join the Santa Monica Bay Bureau, and to San Leandro-Brooklyn
Lodge No. 225 F. & A. M. to join the South Alameda County Masonic Service Bureau. A compact has been issued to Hermosa-Manhattan Lodge No.
557 F. & A. M. to join the Los Angeles Masonic Service Bureau, also Valle
de France Lodge No. 329 F. & A. M. to join the Pasadena Masonic Service
Bureau and to Conejo Lodge No. 807 F. & A. M. and Lynwood Lodge No.
600 F. & A. M. to join the Los Angeles Masonic Service Bureau. The new
Joseph L. Shell Daylight Lodge No. 837 has joined the San Diego Masonic
Service Bureau.
MASONIC HELP LINE
During the year Most Worshipful E. Arthur Haglund was Grand Master
he received a suggestion from a former Inspector that a Masonic Help Line
be instituted to better help Sojourners and needy Masons. He suggested that
the Committee on Masonic Service Bureaus study the suggestion and come
up with a plan for such a help line if it appeared to be warranted. With the
help of Right Worshipful Roy J. Henville, our liaison officer, and Worshipful Ralph Head a plan was worked out with the Los Angeles Masonic Service
Board to start such a plan under the supervision of the Los Angeles Service
Bureau for a 24 hour Hot Line. Stickers with the Help Line phone number
were handed out to many Masonic Service Bureaus. Although, directly, it has
not appeared to be used as much as we had hoped for, indirectly it has been
used and the Service Bureaus in the Southern California area have received
many calls which were directly related to the Help Line.
The Bay area Bureaus have picked up the idea and in a small way are
working out a way to implement their service by intercoupled phone lines
between Bureaus.
OPERATING EXPENSES
Total cost for operating the eighteen Bureaus for the year ending June 30,
1985 amounted to $144,039. Fixed expenses were $98,096; telephone, printing

REPORT OF INSURA NCE COMMITTEE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M of California:
The Insurance Committee met several times during the past year. All policies
were reviewed to be certain that all areas of potential for saving were not
overlooked. As professional Insurance Agents we were certain that the Grand
Lodge of California, the California Memorial Temple Association, and the
Masonic Homes of California would experience substantial increases in
premium costs. Effective July l, 1985 all insurance contracts were renewed

The Annual estimated Workers' Compensation premium for California and
Hawaii is projected to be $300,000. The 1985 experience modification is expected to be 87 percent.
The Health Insurance Program has been divided into two groups. The
Grand Lodge office staff, the employees of the California Memorial Temple
and the employees of the Masonic Homes at Covina are now underwritten
by Great West Life Insurance Company. The employees of the Masonic Homes
at Union City now have the option of being insured by either an HMO or
by a program sponsored by the California Association of Homes for the
Aging. By seperately underwriting these two groups we were able to reduce
our annual health premiums by approximately $20,000.
The members of this Committee experienced a deep loss by the passing
of Leland Peterson of Fresno. Lee's contributions were immeasurable. Much
of what was accomplished by this Committee was directly connected to his
hard work and valuable input. We will surely miss him.

been presented to the Lodge and before other groups in the area. Membership has increased approximately 40 percent to 67 members and attendance
and interest are maintained at a high level. Meetings are held quarterly, and
the Lodge is financially sound. We believe that this Lodge will be of benefit
to its members and a credit to Masonry in California. We, therefore, recommend that a Charter be granted.
Joseph L. Shell Daylight Masonic Lodge U.D. was granted a dispensation
on April 30, 1985 and was instituted on May 7, 1985 with 50 charter members.
The Lodge meets weekly at 10:00 A.M. for the benefit of those who work
night.s - or for reasons of retirement or age are not likely to attend evening
meetmgs.
From its beginning this Lodge has maintained a high level of attendance
and enthusiasm. Membership has increased by over 20 percent with 12 affiliations and 8 applicants for degrees. The Lodge is free of indebtedness and
has a financial balance of over $7,600.00. They have submitted all their books
and records covering the period of dispensation. We could find no reason
for adverse criticism, and for this we publicly congratulate them. We are
pleased to recommend that a Charter be granted.
We now have before us a petition from King Kalakaua Daylight Masonic
Lodge U.D., requesting that a Charter be granted. This Lodge was instituted
on July 11, 1985 with 45 charter members and has received applications for
five affiliations to date. They also meet in daytime at 11:00 A.M. to accommodate night workers and sojourners visiting in the Islands who wish to
establish Masonic contact. We saw a possibility of financial problems with
a very small net worth, and recommended a higher dues structure to provide
a better cash flow. To counteract this, the Lodge is free of debt and we saw
great enthusiasm and dedication. We felt that the considerable Masonic experience within the'membership could solve the potential financial difficulty. We recommend that the petition for Charter be granted.
Most Worshipful Grand Master, I move that Charters be granted and Lodge
numbers be assigned to:
Orange County Research Lodge U.D. in La Habra
Joseph L. Shell Daylight Lodge U.D. in San Diego
King Kalakaua Daylight Lodge U.D. in Honolulu

MORNING SESSION-Tuesday, October 15, 1985
At 9:00 A.M. the Grand Lodge was called on, the Grand Master presiding.
Grand Lodge was raised by Michael D. Sanders, Master of Reading Lodge
No. 254, using the gavel presented to the Grand Master at an outdoor Third
Degree conferred by the Oklahoma Indian Degree Team in Redding. Other
gavels used by the Grand Master during the Morning Session were presented
to him at the Mortgage Burning Ceremony of San Juan Lodge No. 732 in
Citrus Heights; gavel and sounding block presented to the Grand Master at
a Reception by the Aahmes Shrine Past Masters Unit in Oakland; at a
Breakfast Reception in Oakland by the East Bay Masonic Officers Association; at the Institution Ceremony of Joseph L. Shell Daylight Lodge U.D.
in San Diego; at the outdoor Third Degree conferred by the officers of the
160th Masonic District at the Jack Ladd Ranch in Brentwood; the Cornerstone
Ceremony for the new City Hall in Temple City by Camellia Lodge No. 612
and a gavel presented at the 125th Anniversary of Vitruvius Lodge No. 145
in Petaluma.
The Invocation was delivered by the Very Reverend Wayne B. Williamson,
Grand Chaplain.

Those entitled to travel allowances are the Master, or in his absence, the
ranking Warden, or in the absence of the Master and Wardens, the duly Elected
Representative in accordance with Section 1148, California Masonic Code.
However, no payment shall be allowed for the officers or representatives of
any Lodge, the dues of which have not been paid in full, or which shall be
reported by the Grand Secretary as having been delinquent in the transmission of Certificates of the Election and installation of officers of their respective Lodges. Past Grand Masters, not on committees, will be reimbursed as
provided in Section 1150, California Masonic Code. In accordance with Section 1148A, California Masonic Code, when a Master and Warden from the
same Lodge are present at an Annual Communication, and one of said officers
serves on a Grand Lodge Committee entitled to travel and expense reimbursement, he shall be reimbursed under Section 1150, California Masonic Code.
The other officer shall receive reimbursement under Section 1148, California
Masonic Code, as the officer representing his Lodge on the floor of Grand
Lodge.
Mileage from the various points within the State of California to San Francisco has been taken from the published records of the California State
Automobile Association. Mileage from points in the State of Hawaii to San
Francisco, has been taken from the published reports of air lines in accordance
with Section 1148, California Masonic Code. No compensation is allowed
to members representing Lodges in San Francisco and the immediate 30 mile
vicinity. Compensation of members from the State of California has been
computed on the basis of eleven (11) cents per mile, the rate fixed by the Committee on Finance. Compensation of members from the State of Hawaii has
been computed on the basis of published class of fare next below first class
round trip air rate of regularly scheduled major air lines, from Honolulu to
San Francisco, plus inter-Island air fare to Honolulu when necessary.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
The thrust of your Lodge Resources Development Committee this past year
has been two fold. We have worked with several Lodges in this Jurisdiction,
helping them strengthen and improve through program suggestions and officer
development. We have also continued to administer the Grand Master's
Achievement Award.
The major function of the Lodge Resources Development Committee is
to assist Lodges in developing their resources. These resources can range from
new Lodge Officers, program plans, advancement of candidates through the
degrees, to your members. Many Masters find themselves overwhelmed with
too many tasks - 3rd Degree Ritual, planning of programs, follow up to make
sure that they are done right (and of course the only way to be absolutely
sure is to do it yourself) and Stated Meetings just to name a few. Right? Wrong!
To be able to do the job right as Master you have to delegate! Many Masters
don't know how. The Lodge Resources Development Committee can help you
overcome this obstacle. Our committeemen have the background to work with
you, and to help you to develop your own programs and committees. We will
show you how to delegate easily and effectively. There are no overnight solutions, but results can be positive. How about you? Wouldn't you and your
Lodge benefit from some help in learning how to delegate and to revitalize
your programs?
This marks the second year for the Grand Master's Achievement Award.
More than twice as many Lodges participated in the program this year than
last year. The program consists of four basic areas: Lodge Officer Development, Programs, Masonic Responsibility, and Social Responsibility. Receipt
of the Award indicates that a Lodge is healthy and has a well rounded program for its members. Unfortunately, less than 15 percent of the Lodges in
this Jurisdiction have applied for and are qualified to receive the award at
the Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge in October.
The Award itself is not the important part of the program; it is only the
frosting on the cake. What is important is that the Lodge establishes a strong,
well rounded program for its members; one that involves the individual
members in their own Lodge activities.
If your Lodge is having trouble obtaining Lodge Officers, new members,
or getting your members to attend Lodge functions, don't overlook the benefits
this program offers. An attempt to comply with the requirements of the Grand
Master's Achievement Award will automatically begin to involve the membership of the Lodge, and start the Lodge on the way to strength and vitality.
The Brethren will find that if they sincerely try to accomplish the tasks outlined
in the application, the Lodge will begin to turn around, attendance will improve and Officers and new members will be easier to find.
Remember, a strong Lodge is an active Lodge, one that involves its members
in its activities. If your Lodge didn't earn, or apply for, the Award this year,

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

start working now for next year's Award. You'll find it well worth your while.
We were very saddened to hear of the passing of one of our members,
Brother William C. Leach. Soft and safe to thee, my Brother.
We would like to take this opportunity to thank the Grand Secretary, Very
Worshipful Bob Klinger, and his staff for all of the help that they have given
us this past year. Also, we would like to especially thank all of the many
Inspectors that took the time out of their busy schedules to review the
Applications from the Lodges in their District.
Our hats are off to all of you!

Of particular importance to the Masonic Homes is the Pooled Income Fund.
On June 30, 1985, the Fund had a market value of $2,380,222. The cash yield
was 9.2 percent. The Pooled Income Fund enables Masons and others in
California and Hawaii to establish a lifetime income for themselves and for
one-time designated beneficiaries. Certain tax advantages accrue to the
contributor.
The efforts of Masons and their friends have been responsibile for the rewarding accumulation of the assets in the several Grand Lodge funds. The
operations of the Masonic Homes at Union City and Covina are largely
financed through the income from Endowment and General Fund investments.
Other revenues furnish support for the charitable activities and educational
grants of the Grand Lodge of California.
Because the Investment Committee continues to exercise the utmost
prudence and care in the management of the funds, the investments rank
among the highest in quality. Although the investment policy has been conservative, the cash yield has resulted in a satisfactory total return.
During the year the Investment Committee, and indeed the entire Masonic
Fraternity, lost one of its most respected and venerable members, Past Grand
Master Guy Boyd Mize. "In the interchange of duty, honor and responsibility he has not sought the path of comfort, but has humbly faced the spur
of difficulty and challenge."
The Grand Master appointed B. Robert Malouf, Past Master of Henry
Knox-Westlake Lodge No. 392, to fill the unexpired term of Brother Mize.

REPORT OF THE INVESTMENT COMMITTEE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
It is the responsibility of the Investment Committee to report annually to
Grand Lodge on the financial condition of the funds of Grand Lodge and
its entities.
The Committee meets quarterly during the year with its investment
counselors. An independent investment firm reviews the performance of the
primary funds on a comparative basis with funds of a similar nature in the
United States.
The Committee is basically concerned with the preservation of fund principal and the highest rate of total return commensurate with safety. Three
funds: Masonic Homes Endowment Fund, Masonic Homes General Fund
and the Hugo M. Lorber Union City Home Fund constitute 95 percent of
the total investments.
The Committee also supervises other Grand Lodge funds: Grand Lodge
General Fund, California Masonic Memorial Temple, California Masonic
Foundation and Amaranth Fund, Pooled Income Fund and eighteen restricteduse funds of the Masonic Homes.
The market value of the total portfolio on June 30, 1985, was $148,789,770
compared to $ll4,540,165 a year earlier, an increase of 29.9 percent. The
1984-85 cash yield from the total invested funds was 9.85 percent.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON TEMPLE PROPERTIES
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
The Committee on Temple Properties hereby submits the Annual Report
of its activities for the 1984-1985 Grand Lodge Year.
The year has been a busy one. The Chairman wishes to express his deepest
gratitude for the cooperation he has received from the members of the Committee in replying promptly to the many requests we have had for advice, per

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

mission to proceed with projects, and general discussion relating to matters
of concern to Temple Associations of this Jurisdiction during the past year.
On a personal note, he wishes also to extend most heartfelt gratitude to our
Grand Secretary, Very Worshipful Robert A. Klinger, whose wise counsel and
assistance was invaluable in helping a new Chairman during the first few weeks
in office.
Your Committee suffered a great loss early in the year in the passing of
our veteran member, Brother Kenneth L. Wylie. His advice and expertise in
regard to the matters which arise in the course of the year have been sorely
missed.
On numerous occasions, individual members of this Committee have met
with various officers and members of Temple Associations and/or Lodges
in an effort to avoid situations which might arise, or solve those which had
arisen in the course of Temple business.
One of the problems with which this Committee is faced too often is the
tardiness of requests for approval of either long term leases, or the expenditure of funds in amounts exceeding the five thousand dollar limitation imposed by our Masonic Code. Section 1208 of the C.M.C. specifically states
that a Temple Association, or other Masonic entity which holds title to a
Masonic Temple Property, must obtain the consent of the Temple Properties
Committee before expending more than $5,000.00 toward the purchase of,
or entering into a contract for the repair or alteration of, or entering into
a lease agreement for over three years of a property belonging to a Masonic
Lodge or its Temple Association. Serious problems could arise for the local
Lodge or Temple Association if permission to proceed in such cases is not
obtained before any such contract is signed.
This Committee wishes to express its deep appreciation to our Grand
Master, Roy J. Henville, for his unflagging interest, cooperation and assistance
at any and all times when requested; to Deputy Grand Master John W.
Driskell, Senior Grand Warden Jack R. Levitt, and Junior Grand Warden
Leo B. Mark, the four members of the Executive Committee, who rendered
us wise and timely assistance whenever called upon; also to the Grand
Secretary, Assistant Grand Secretary and the entire staff of the Grand
Secretary's office, whose support and assistance throughout the year have been
invaluable.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M of California:
During the past year, there have been three reported incidents of the usage
of the "Square and Compass" in an unauthorized manner.
The owner of a patrol service in Carson used the emblem in advertising
in the yellow pages. On August 7, 1985, the Committee wrote the owner a
letter advising him that the use of the symbol was a misdemeanor under the
California Corporations Code as well as the Penal Code.
Since the yellow pages have not been published for this year, it is too early
to ascertain if the owner has complied.
In June, the Committee received a business card with the Square and Compass on it. Subsequent investigation revealed the business had ceased
operation.
An organization called the International F. and A. M. Masons, not
associated with our Grand Lodge, was using our emblem. Through correspond~nce, we informed the organization they were in violation of the
California Corporations Code. The Committee has received no response from
the organization.
Since the adoption of the revised Commercialism regulations, the question of what financial ventures Lodges can engage in has reoccurred. C.M.C.
Section 2070 prohibits Lodges from any collateral financial undertaking. In
current vogue are "Home Party Sales" by Lodges. The thrust of the plan
is for a Home Party salesperson to conduct a home party selling specific products. A portion of the commissions earned are guaranteed to the Lodge. On
its part, the Lodge must solicit the membership from the Lodge Roster. This
type of event is cpntrary to the Commercialism Regulations on two counts:
first, the Lodge is using the Roster for a non-Masonic purpose; and secondly, the Lodge is acting as nothing more than a "retail outlet" for a commercial venture.
Contrasted to the above, are the regulations governing Concordant Bodies.
A Concordant Body is not prohibited from engaging in a financial venture.
The only proscription is that the venture not be fraudulent, misleading,
unethical or illegal.
Any group, intending to sponsor any event where a profit potential exists
should discuss the event with its Inspector, well in advance of making any
commitment.
Respectfully submitted,
SHERWOOD C. KINGSLEY, Chairman

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON
U.S. CONSTITUTION OBSERVANCE

Respectfully submitted,

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
Your thirty hard working Grand Lodge committee members for the United
States Constitution Observance Committee have continued the excellent programs initiated in previous years. Although many new programs were
implemented, our emphasis this year has been to encourage many more nonMasons to attend our programs.
The year began at the 1984 Annual Grand Lodge Communication with
a most attractive red, white and blue exhibit booth which caught everyone's
attention. This handsome booth, staffed by knowledgeable Committeemen,
provided an excellent opportunity to further explain and promote Constitution Observance programs. Packets containing program formats and guidelines
for setting up local observances were distributed to all Senior Wardens.
Grand Master Roy J. Henville, the Deputy Grand Master and the Senior
Grand Warden, as well as Grand Secretary Robert A. Klinger and.his staff
have been of tremendous assistance to this Committee.
Shortly after our Annual Communication, the Chairman of this Committee, Sherman T. Wicker, entered the Celestial Lodge above, and Arnold C.
Happel was appointed as its Chairman by our Grand Master and, with the
Grand Master's permission, Maurice R. Crosby became Vice Chairman. Due
to the size of the State, this appointment will greatly improve the efficiency
of the Committee as we will now have Northern and Southern representation.
An active year was punctuated by three Committee meetings which were
held in Sacramento, San Jose and Lakewood, and judging from the response,
our booths, which we set up at various workshops, were very successful in
expanding Observance programs. The Committee members feel their efforts
were greatly rewarded. In addition, Grand Master Roy J. Henville proclaimed
the month of September as Constitution Observance Month.
The Observances enjoyed increased attendance this year as there were a
number of very fine programs held throughout the State. Burl Ives was the
Grand Marshal of the very large Sonoma County Lodge's parade and the
featured speaker was Grand Master Roy J. Henville whose subject was "The
Constitution." The San Francisco Masonic Officers Association promoted
an energetic U.S. Constitution Observance program for the San Francisco
School System. Many picnics, family nights, and special programs for Constitutional Observance were held with featured speakers such as Judges,
Generals, State Senators, Assemblymen, United States Congressmen, County
Sheriffs, and City Police Chiefs. Mayors of many cities issued proclamations
supporting the furtherance of Constitution Observance. Scottish Rite Valleys
and the Shrine supported and gave us special assistance which was greatly
appreciated. And of course, the interest generated this past year by our booths
was very rewarding.
We acknowledge with gratitude the generous assistance rendered by the
Grand Lodge Officers Corps and the Grand Lodge staff.

1983 GRAND MASTER'S RECOMMENDATION NO. 3
OPTIONAL USE OF A
"SHORT FORM" CWSING CEREMONY
The Committee on Jurisprudence:
Your Committee on Jurisprudence, to which this "Carry Over" Recommendation has been referred, reports as follows:
The Ritual Committee intends this Recommendation to implement Grand
Master Harry Maynard's Recommendation that an optional "Short Form"
ceremony be available for closing special meetings only of Constituent Lodges.
As this matter relates to ritual only, your Committee finds that no legislation is required.
Since this Recommendation is a "carry over,• a two-thirds affirmative vote
is required for adoption.
As the matter is already before Grand Lodge, no motion is required.

200

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
At the 1983 Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge it was then Grand
Master Maynard's recommendation that the Ritual Committee develop a
"Short Form" Closing Ceremony to be used by the Constituent Lodges as
an optional method of closing Lodges at Special Meetings.
The Ritual Committee did present such a "Short Form" closing ceremony
at the 1984 Annual Communication. The c;eremony presented for adoption
received a majority vote of the members of Grand Lodge present, but failed
the required five-sixths vote, hence it was carried over to this session.
Section 2690 C.M.C. says in part: "The Grand Lodge alone has power to
authorize any changes in the ritual for the purpose of having it remain as
it was handed down from time immemorial."
Please be advised that there is no authority in our law to change the ritual
other than for the express purpose quoted above: that of having it remain
as it was handed down from time immemorial. Nothing in our history indicates that there ever was an abbreviated form of ritual to be used at the
closing of a Lodge.
That being the case, we have no present authority to make such a change
in ritual until there has been a change in the law pertaining to ritual.
There should be no contention as to the interpretation of the law. The Ritual
Committee itself used the argument that change can be effected only to return
the ritual to its originally adopted form when, in 1983, they recommended
that the First Degree Lecture be returned to its original form.
The Committee on Jurisprudence is on record in past proceedings that
change in the ritual may be made only "for the purpose of having it remain
as it was handed down from time immemorial."
While Grand Masters, in some instances, use a short form of closing Grand
Lodges, their authority probably comes from Section 1032 C.M.C. which
grants discretionary powers to the Grand Master. These discretionary powers
belong solely to the Grand Master and cannot be transmitted to the Master
of a Lodge. Because Grand Masters may make more than one appearance
in a given day to open Grand Lodge and conduct its ceremonies, and ev~n
more frequently must travel considerable distance between events to meet daily
commitments to the Fraternity, it is understandable that they try to conserve
time wherever practical.
Timesaving in this instance, however, would not be nearly as great as the
form of closing used by Grand Masters. It is estimated that only 2 or 3 minutes
would be saved by the proposed "short form" closing ceremony.
Finally, ritual is of prime importance to candidates. It is the formality of
the manner in which we present our degrees at Special Meetings that makes
a lasting impression on most candidates. It is from their observation of closing
as well as opening ceremonies that the significance of our fraternal intentions are impressed upon their minds. We should not deprive them of that
great privilege for the sake of a few minutes. We must remember that the
proposed short form is for Special Meetings only and cannot be used at Stated
Meetings.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a "No" vote.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

201

1984 GRAND MASTER HAGLUND'S
RECOMMENDATION NO. 3
"PROFICIENCY FOR
CONCORDANT AND APPENDANT BODIES"
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Grand Master Haglund's Recommendation No. 3, in 1984, concerning the
waiver of the Proficiency Requirement in the Candidate's Lecture of the Master
Mason's Degree after a specified period of time, received a majority vote of
this Grand Lodge and is therefore before you again for your consideration.
Your 1985 Committee on Policy and General Purposes has carefully reviewed
the issue and finds no evidence for cause to deviate from the position taken
by the 1984 Committee. Accordingly, we reiterate the report given by them
at the last Annual Communication.

202

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Since October 1953, a Mason who applied and was elected to receive the
degrees of Masonry in a Lodge of this Jurisdiction first was required to give
satisfactory evidence in open Lodge, that he was proficient and qualified in
the Candidates Lecture of the Degree of Master Mason before he was able
to apply and be elected to a Concordant or Appendant Masonic body; and
then only and until after the lapse of one year from the date he received the
degree of Master Mason.
Grand Master Haglund's Recommendation No. 3 would, in essence, remove
the Proficiency requirement after a period of five years from the date on which
the Candidate received the Degree of Master Mason.
As the foregoing Proficiency requirement did not exist prior to October,
1953, when it was first adopted, Grand Master Haglund's Recommendation
would make our law in this regard, except for the waiting period, the same
as it originally was; for it seeks to allow the Masons, who have not complied
with the present regulations of Section 2635 of the California Masonic Code,
to petition and be elected to a prerequisite Masonic body without restriction
by our Grand Lodge.
Many of our Brethren, for reasons of their own, have failed to comply with
our present law; and if after five years from the date they received the Third
Degree of Freemasonry they have not passed the present required Proficiency in that Degree, your Committee on Policy and General Purposes believes
that they should no longer be restricted from expanding their Masonic
horizons in a Concordant or Appendant Body if they wish to do so.
We, therefore, recommend a "Yes" vote on Grand Master Haglund's Recommendation No. 3.
Not Approved.

the auspices of the Film and Creative Projects Committee and some forty
Hiram Award Programs were held by Lodges in this Jurisdiction. An attractive Hiram Award certificate was designed and made available for presentation to the recipient.

'unsung hero' of every Lodge such as the volunteer who makes the coffee
at each meeting, the one who sets the tables or arranges the furniture and
ornaments in the Lodge room, the painter, the gardener, the handyman, the
organist, the program chairman or any number of outstanding Brethren who
consistently donate their time and talents to our beloved Fraternity or who
have brought credit to the Craft by their community activities."

confusion or the lack of specific guidelines. In his annual message to the Grand

AFTERNOON SESSION-Tuesday, October 15, 1985

than any other. Operative Masonry began to die in the Seventeenth Century
when cathedral building slowed. It was then that men in increasing numbers
were admitted to Masonry to study or speculate on the moral and
philosophical lessons associated with the working tools and techniques of
the operative stonemasons, and our Fraternity expanded once again. Masonry
expanded to this country, arriving with the Colonists. However, in the 1820's,
many blamed the Masons for the disappearance of a William Morgan who
had published an alleged expose regarding the secrets of Freemasonry. The
public's reaction was so severe against Masonry that in New York alone over
a four year period the number of Lodges dropped from five hundred to eightytwo and the number of members from over twenty thousand to fewer than
three thousand. After the Civil War, the growth of Freemasonry was rapid
and permanent with only a temporary setback during the Great Depression
and the hopefully temporary setback which commenced about twenty years
ago. Over many centuries, therefore, the size and vitality of Masonry has been
cyclical.
The second overriding principle of civilization from which we can take comfort and consolation can be summarized as follows: institutions with a message
or a truth on the essence of Man never die. They adapt to changing times
but the truths taught remain the same. Man has certain basic beliefs in common, regardless of background: a belief in a Supreme Being and respect for
Nature and all things beyond his control. These are the only means of make
sense of an often senseless world. Therefore, the greatest and most enduring
ideas of Man are those which use these basic instincts to explain the mysteries
of life.
All great institutions have survived because they address Man's basic instincts with a ti~less message. Christianity began as a small sect of Jews
who believed that the Messiah had come and would return in a few years in
a second coming to save all people. Christianity has developed into a worldwide
religion. Although its adherents cannot agree on the time of the second
coming, they all agree that each person should lead his life as if that second
coming and each individual's personal Judgment Day can come at any
moment. Christianity has survived because its basic truths - faith in a loving
God, hope of personal salvation and commitment to personal inprovement
- transcend all ages and have been interpreted by each age to apply to the
problems of the time.
Consider our American system of government. Our United States Constitution, with a fragile start, has endured, from a rural, homogeneous,
agrarian society of less than four million people in 1790, when communication between Massachusetts and South Carolina could take weeks, to an urban,
diverse, industrial society of 200,000,000 people, with instantaneous communication available to the vast majority. Our system of government has survived because its basic truths - the guarantee of liberty for all; free, public
education which equips people to rule themselves; and, most importantly,
the personal vigilance of every American in preserving our Constitution and
never countenancing any person who would abridge its liberties for anyone

"MASONRY FOR THE TWENTY-FIRST CENTURY"
R. STEPHEN DOAN, Grand Orator

Most Worshipful Grand Master, distinguished visitors and Brethren of this
Grand Lodge:
Masons are builders. Legendarily, we built King Solomon's Temple.
Historically, we built the great Gothic cathedrals in Europe during the Middle
Ages. We built our Fraternity from a guild, or a labor union, if you will, of
operative stonemasons to a speculative society of non-operative Masons
accepted to study and put into practice the philosophical principles of the
ancient stonemasons' craft, the moral and philosophical lessons associated
with the working tools and practices of our operative forebearers.
Because Masons have always been builders, some of us are uncertain as
to how we can reverse the recent decline in our Fraternity. Our membership
has eroded steadily since the middle of the 1960's; Lodges consolidate but
still cannot find officers. As builders, we have never been trained to defend
against those forces of our contemporar~ world'. sometimes more interes~ed
in destroying than building on the foundations which have supported Mankmd
for eternity.
We can however find comfort and consolation in two overriding principles
of civiliza~ion. First, as with the tides, all things ebb and flood. Life is cyclical,
moving back and forth, pulsating, in a cycle. It does not necessarily move
on a continuum to one goal.
Consider the vitality of Masonry over the centuries. Our historical beginnings can be traced to the construction of the great Gothic cathedrals in
the late Thirteenth Century. Operative Masonry thrived and expanded as every
population center with a bishop sought to build a cathedral more impressive

207

209

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

- have been embraced by each generation and interpreted as needed to resolve
America's problems at the time.
Masonry likewise possesses timeless truths. They are the truths which
distinguished Masonry as an operative guild during the Middle Ages and
allowed it to transform itself into a speculative society in the Seventeenth and
Eighteenth Centuries. They are the truths by which Masonry survived the
Morgan affair; they are the truths by which Masonry survived the Depression; they are the truths which will permit us to reverse our present decline.
We can reverse this recent decline in membership, this inevitable ebb tide in
the continuing cycle of our Fraternity's existence, by redefining those universal truths about Mankind which Masonry teaches to meet the needs of our
time. We must ready ourselves for the next inevitable flood tide by determining
how Masonry can best exemplify its universal, timeless truths to answer Man's
questions on life in the 1\venty-First Century.
What are the universal truths of Masonry that survive all ages? The answer
is so self-evident that we might otherwise overlook it. They are so fundamental
to Masonry that they were explained to you on the very night that you became
a Mason; they are the principal tenents of Masonry; they are: brotherly love,
relief and truth.

ciple of brotherly love, a member can find friends among strangers wherever
he or she might travel. A member can travel to a new location, without family
or any established friends, and immediately find friends and therefore support in strange surroundings at the local Masonic Temple. But, what are we
doing to encourage this? What activities do we plan so that Masonry's practiced truth of brotherly love can help solve these problems of the TwentyFirst Century?
In order to make Masonry's brotherly love important for the 1\venty-First
Century, we must dispel the myth that Masonry arbitrarily discriminates in
its membership. We rightfully possess and inspire the reputation of being selective in that only good men and true may join us, but this has sometimes been
unfortunately viewed as selection based upon class or particular sectarian
belief. There are no restrictions on membership in our Fraternity other than
a belief in a Supreme Being and an expectation of personal salvation. No
religious or political belief consistent with these two requirements for membership in Masonry bars any man from membership. There are no racial barriers
on membership. There are no barriers based on the countries from which
one's ancestors came.
We must dispel the myth about membership in our Fraternity whenever
the opportunity arises. When someone asks us about Masonry, there is a great
deal that we can tell him and, indeed, there are only a few things about
Masonry which are 'secret': a few of our methods of recognizing one another
and certain of our legends are secret and cannot be disclosed. At the same
time, we should remind the questioner that there is absolutely no religious
nor any other barrier to becoming a Mason, if the applicant believes in God
and a future existence.
More importaptly, we must make Masonry attractive. It should encourage
and inspire men to join and share in its brotherly love and affection once
they know that it is open to them. What can your Lodge do to make Masonry
more attractive? Does your Lodge have a Layman's Night Program at least
annually? There is no better way to acquaint the uninitiated who may have
expressed an interest in Freemasonry with the Principles of our Fraternity
and at the same time increase the knowledge and interest and therefore the
enthusiasm of our present members. Lodges routinely have received from two
to ten petitions as a result of a Layman's Night Program.
What social activities does your Lodge have? Some Lodges have achieved
success as essentially an all-men's organization with minimal involvement of
wives and family. This is certainly the exception and not the rule. For the
most part, Lodges with programs and activities of interest to the Mason, his
wife and children are the Lodges with no membership problems. My own
Lodge has a family potluck dinner at every Stated Meeting. Many Lodges
accompany their Stated Meeting dinners with programs for the wives while
the men are in their meeting. When a man comes home on the night of his
Stated Meeting, his wife will not encourage him to go to Lodge in most
instances if it means that she must stay home alone. However, if going to
a Stated Meeting means that she is going out to dinner and will meet with
her friends while her husband is in the meeting, you can guess where that
Mason will have dinner that night!

208

Brotherly Love

By brotherly love, Masons are taught to regard all human beings as members
of one family, regardless of power or wealth. As we believe that we are all
children of God, we are, by definition, all brothers, obligated to aid, support
and protect one another. Masonry unites people of diverse backgrounds
because, having expressed a belief in God, all of us were brothers even before
initiation into our Fraternity. In the medieval Masonic Lodges of operative
stonemasons, brotherly love was essential to maintain harmony among a large
group of relatively uneducated workers whose political allegiances and struggle
for personal survival might be in conflict. Also, the medieval stonemasons
traveled to whatever political jurisdiction had work available. Because it was
often necessary to travel to strange lands with unfamiliar customs, a
stonemason was expected to commence work immediately in harmony and
concord with people who theretofore might have been complete strangers.
Masonry, of course, in the Twenty-First Century will not build stone
cathedrals in Europe. However, many characteristics of the 1\venty-First
Century will not be unlike the Middle Ages. There is a greater mobility in
society today. Men and women are often transferred several times in their
economic career to different geographical locations as part of their work.
There is also an unfortunate increase in economic inequality among people.
While we in America have historically relied on the family to a certain extent
for economic and psychological support, the family institution has declined
with the increasing number of broken homes as well as the strain on family
ties caused by people moving around the country as part of their work.
Masonry can supply the answer to this problem. Whether by membership
in Masonry, Eastern Star, a Masonic youth group or any of the other Masonicaffiliated organizations, each of which is founded upon the Masonic prin-

210

PROCEEDIN GS OF THE

My Lodge has had family activities: picnics, baseball games and the like,
that include children of the members and our local Masonic youth groups.
When I served as Master of the Lodge, at the age of twenty-five, I had more
than a dozen members of my Lodge younger than I was who joined as a result
of those activities involving the members of my Lodge and my DeMolay
Chapter. Some churches say that families that pray together stay together. In
this instance, Masonic families that play together stay together because the
Masonic youth, even if their parents do not belong to Masonic organizations,
through social activities with the members of the Masonic Lodge become their
friends and naturally want to be a part of them when they become eligible.
I have one more thought with respect to the impression which we give to
the uninitiated. Never judge a book by the cover, we may have learned as
a child, but a tattered, dirty cover on a book is much less appealing to the
potential reader than a well-kept and clean cover. What does your Masonic
Temple look like? My brother lives in a town which was a small, rural, farming
community when its Masonic Lodge began. However, it is now a relatively
affluent suburb of a major city. When asked if he had had any success in
attracting his friends in the community to Masonry, my brother logically
responded: these people are successful and live in nice houses. They do not
want to go to a run-down, old Lodge Hall like that. Lodge Halls do not have
to be architectural monuments but even the most modest Masonic Temple
will create a far better impression if maintained clean and in good repair.
Relief

To relieve the distressed is a duty which all men possess, but particularly
Masons because of the indissoluble links between us of brotherly love and
affection. Among our medieval stonemason ancestors, Masonic relief was of
tremendous importance. The Gothic cathedrals constructed by the operative
Masons reached almost forty stories in height, a feat not duplicated before
or in any period afterward until many centuries later. The work was dangerous.
In addition to working at great heights, the workmen were required to cut
stones and move them to the building site. In an era when there was no
workmen's compensation insurance nor public welfare system as we know
it today, there was no established means to assume responsibility for a
stonemason injured on the job or for assistance of his widow and orphans
should he be killed on the job. This responsibility was assumed by the
stonemasons. A man upon becoming a stonemason could rest assured that,
should any calamity befall him, he would be taken care of, as well as those
dependent upon him, by his brother Masons. To aid and assist the distressed,
worthy brother Mason, his widow and orphans thus became one of the first
lessons a man learned upon becoming a stonemason.
As the operative stonemasons' actual building activities declined during
the Seventeenth Century, the need for the relief of an injured brother or the
family of a deceased brother declined also. This did not diminish the Masons'
charitable concerns. So engrained in the philosophy of Masonry was the
teaching of relief that the Masons extended their charitable endeavors beyond
their own circle of members and families to the public at large. A fundamental

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNI A

211

impetus to the creation of the Grand Lodge of California was the tremendous need for Masonic charity caused by the sudden influx of people at the
time of the Gold Rush in 1850. The crowning glories of California Masonic
charity today are our Masonic Homes.
. With Social Security, welfare, Medicare and Medi-Cal, we sometimes lose
sight of the need for Masonic charity. Unlike governmental programs, however,
Masonry gives charitably with a human face. Our Masonic charities, such
as our Masonic Homes and the Shriners' Hospitals for Crippled Children
and Burns Institutes, just to name a few, admit regardless of economic means
and, in the case of the Shriners' Hospitals and Burns Institutes, regardless
of affiliation with Masonry. Our Masonic charities care in a family environment, with respect and without the impersonal, sometimes uncaring, approach
of many governmental assistance bureaucracies.
How is this relevant for the Twenty- First Century? While the government
assumes a bulk of the social welfare responsibilities in society, we are only
too aware that this is and will continue to be an era of limitations. As life
expectancies increase and as government programs continue to be limited
there will remain a significant proportion of society, particularly the elderly'.
serviced at only a bare minimum by government and then only with an impersonal rather than the personal approach of Masonic charity.
What can your Lodge do? Of course, your Lodge as well as any of the
concordant bodies to which you belong can continue to support the organized charities of the Grand Lodge and of the governing body of your concor~ant orga!1iz~tions. But, eac~ Lodge and concordant body can put charity
mto practice m the commumty on a personal, individual basis. During the
early history of California Freemasonry, it was not uncommon for a Masonic
Lodge to assume all of the responsibilities for the relief of a distressed member
including payment of all food and housing bills and medical expenses. Ther~
are countless examples of this Masonic charity in the early history of our
Jurisdiction, which on many occasions was extended beyond our Masonic
family to tho~e in the community who were in need. We can do that today.
Every Lodge 1s probably near an old folks' home. What is your Lodge doing
for them? While charity clearly begins at home, there are many opportunities
for us to extend charity to the community at large, opportunities to show
those who may not be Masons one of the truths of our Fraternity and to
turn our words into deeds by displaying Masonic Charity in relieving those
who may be less fortunate.
Truth

Truth is a divine attribute and the foundation of every virtue. In this sense,
truth means sincerity, honesty of expression and plain dealing. Our medieval
stonemason ancestors taught their apprentices to be truthful because they
wished to maintain the reputation of their craft and to assure any potential
employer that honest work would be received for wages paid.
Over the centuries, however, this sense of truth has broadened into a wider
meaning. A real objective of Freemasonry today is the search for truth, that
search for perfection of thought and conduct which God had in view when
He originally created us in His image. Clearly, the search for truth will be

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

as relevant in the Twenty-First Century as it has been in every century before
as Man never has and probably never in this life will achieve perfection; but,
the perhaps impossibility of the goal should not dissuade any of us from the
necessity of the search.
How can we help ourselves and others in the Twenty-First Century in the
search for truth? For those who are Masons, the ritual of our Fraternity is
the foundation for our search. The great philosophers of different ages who
have become Masons have extolled its symbols, allegories and legends as the
means by which any reflective member could discover the pathway to personal perfection. What are you doing as a Mason to discover the pathway
to perfection through our ritual? Do you simply parrot the ritual by rote,
or do you attempt to understand what it means? If you are a Master, what
kind of Masonic education program do you have for your members? During
this year, I have directed my orations to both members and non-members
of the Fraternity in an attempt to help them understand the philosophy of
Masonry and how it may apply in their daily lives. Even some of your Grand
Lodge officers, Inspectors and Committeemen, including myself, have been
surprised by some of the philosophical aspects of our Fraternity which I have
discovered in preparing for these orations.
Do you help your new candidates learn the philosophy of life upon which
they have embarked by becoming Masons? Do you motivate members who
may have belonged for some time to increase their Masonic knowledge and,
therefore, their interest in our Fraternity? Do you have a five to ten minute
talk at every meeting about a subject of interest regarding our teachings? A
member assigned to report on something of interest in Mackey's Revised
Encyclopedia of Freemasonry, still in print and easily available, could report
for several years in such a manner before duplicating any material.
Our search for truth should extend beyond our membership. Masons believe
very strongly that each individual should have the freedom to search for truth
in his or her own way so long as that search does not interfere with the rights
of another to pursue similarly his or her search for truth. Masons therefore
support the United States Constitution and should make the observance of
its anniversary in September of each year a prominent feature of a Lodge's
program because it is our Constitution which is the best guarantee of each
one of our searches for personal truth. In addition, Masons support free public
schools as only an educated citizenry can, through elections and public service, guarantee that our constitutional system of liberties will be preserved and,
therefore, that we and future generations will have our Constitution in a
democratic society available to preserve our search for personal truth.
What is your Lodge doing to support the Constitution and public schools?
Do you have a Constitution and public schools observance? Do you invite
the general public and explain the importance of the Constitution and public
schools and why Masonry does and each citizen should support them? One
Lodge in this Jurisdiction has sponsored an annual public essay contest among
local public school students to increase their awareness of these institutions.
My own Eastern Star Chapter this last year awarded a $400.00 scholarship
to a local high school senior as its contribution to the continuation of an
educated citizenry.

In the Winter 1984 edition of the California Freemason, one of our
Hawaiian Brethren reports a conversation in the late 1960's with an officer
of the Grand Lodge. In response to an inquiry by our Hawaiian Brother as
to what was being done to stem our membership decline, our Hawaiian Brother
was shocked to receive the response: There is no need for concern, since
membership numbers are cyclical in nature and we need only to ride this out.
Our Hawaiian Brother observed: Ride out to what? Oblivion?
Institutions are cyclical and their truths can endure. But, institutions and
their truths do not survive without the active support of each of their
adherents. Masonry will survive and can be an important force in the TwentyFirst Century only if we are committed to those actions necessary to make
its truths relevant for the Twenty-First Century and an important part of the
lives of all people, whether Masons or not. We must do something. I have
given you some thoughts, but how best they can work in your own circumstances can only be determined by you on reflection on what your Lodge
and its community needs.
The social critic Eric Hoffer observed that most of us are frightened by
change: the more dramatic the transition, the more dramatic our reaction.
Uncertainty with respect to the future of our Craft in a rapidly changing world
is particularly troublesome because Masonry's truths have, to date, survived
the test of time. However, as with all institutions, our Fraternity must grow,
adapt to change, or stagnate. We must increase our commitment to
Freemasonry and understand how its truths should be adapted to a changing
world or we will stagnate.
The most important, the fundamental tenents of Freemasonry are brotherly
love, relief and truth, but there will be no Freemasonry if it does not serve
the current needs of Mankind. Freemasonry will survive only if we make its
tenents responsive ·to the needs of the Twenty-First Century. What will you
do to help?

STREAMLINING OPENING CEREMONIES CONSTITUENT LODGES
(85-3)
The proponent of this Resolution seeks to streamline the opening ceremonies
by eliminating that portion of the ritual which is known as the "jewel march"
and directing the Ritual Committee of the Grand Lodge to adopt a suitable
procedure in lieu thereof.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, the ritual of the three degrees of Freemasonry is intended to
impart the lessons of our Craft and focus attention on the building of a
spiritual Temple within the hearts and souls of each Mason; and
WHEREAS, any superfluous action which tends to detract from the real
meaning of the ritual should be avoided; and

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

WHEREAS, the so called "jewel march" in which the officers receive their
jewels and take their stations is time consuming, and regrettably in some instances poorly executed, thereby detracting from the real meaning of the opening ceremonies and setting a poor example as to what is to follow; and
WHEREAS, the Grand Lodge in its opening ceremonies has no similar
ceremony.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that the Ritual Committee of
this Grand Lodge propose in place of the ceremony known as the "jewel
march:' a procedure, to be approved by this Grand Lodge, for officers of a
Lodge to take their stations at the opening of the Lodge.

If the "jewel march" is properly executed, which practice and proper rehearsal can assure, the "jewel march" can be very impressive, interesting and highly
important in setting the tone of the meeting which is to follow.
The "jewel march" is a part of the ritual for the opening of a Masonic
Lodge. !his Resolution is another attempt to modify and change our ritual;
and while the Grand Lodge under Section 2690 of the California Masonic
Code has that authority, such change can be made only for the purpose of
having the ritual remain as it was handed down from time immemorial. This
Resolution does not meet that criteria.
Therefore, your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends
a "No" vote on this Resolution.

to Masonry in those areas; and
WHEREAS, there are also other areas of this Jurisdiction that have facilities
capable of accommodating future Annual Communications.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

"Sect. 150. ANNUAL COMMUNICATION. The Grand Lodge shall hold
an Annual Communication for the transaction of its regular business commencing at 9 o'clock A.M. on the second Monday of each October and
commencing with the year 1986 and every fourth year thereafter it shall

and retype the many committee reports, etc. Perhaps these logistical problems
could be worked out, but there are other and more important and basic reasons
why this Resolution should not be adopted.
Many years ago, in 1947, the Grand Master and other great Masonic leaders
of this Jurisdiction had the wisdom and foresight to consider the building
of a great and beautiful Masonic monument, a new and permanent home
for the Grand Lodge of California.
This magnificent California Masonic Memorial Temple, dedicated to our
Masonic Brethren who died in the cause of freedom, is admired by Masons
throughout the world.
In the 1958 Dedication Issue of the California Freemason, Editor Newcomb
Condee stated, "We must ever keep in mind the simple truth that the magnificent edifice on Nob Hill is only the symbol of Freemasonry in our State. It
is the beacon which symbolizes the truth which must be kept burning in our
hearts and minds. Temples made of stone may be destroyed and devastated,
but the spirit of free men searching for God's truth is indestructible. This
truth will eventually triumph over those forces which seek to enslave the minds
and bodies of men spiritually or politically."
Shouldn't each of us, as members of Grand Lodge, keep the faith with those
dedicated Masonic leaders of years past; those who dreamed the impossible
dream and saw that dream become a reality. Certainly they deserve more than
to have the Annual Communications held in this Temple only once in every
four years.
The requirement of a five-sixths vote to determine the location of the Annual Communication in the intervening years leaves unanswered the following questions:
Who .would present such a Resolution?
Would a Special Communication be called for that purpose?
Who would determine the proposed location?
How far in advance would such legislation be proposed?
If the proposed legislation fails to receive a five-sixths affirmative vote,
where would the Annual Communication be held?
These are only a few of the questions the proponent has not answered and
your Committee on Policy and General Purposes is not able to answer them
for you.
This Temple should be the permanent home for every Annual Communication of the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a "No" vote.

The proponents of this Resolution seek to codify and standardize the manner of voting when considering Resolutions aimed at altering, adding to or

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, Resolutions seeking to alter, add to or delete language from
sections of the California Masonic Code have been, in the past, subjected
to a written ballot to determine their disposition, at least at the initial consideration; and
WHEREAS, such written ballot has not always been required in subsequent consideration of such Resolutions when carried over to the next following Annual Communication; and
WHEREAS, if such a Resolution warranted a decision by written ballot
at its initial consideration, such written ballot should be taken at subsequent
considerations; and
WHEREAS, the manner of balloting by other methods than written is subject to some interpretation due to the fact that each voice, hand or standing
person is accorded a full vote when, by statute, Past Masters are accorded
only a fractional vote; and
WHEREAS, the use of written ballots is nowhere mandated in the California Masonic Code when considering amendments to the Constitution and/or
Ordinances of this Grand Lodge.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that both Sections 500 and 4000
of the California Masonic Code be amended by striking from each the last
sentence and substituting in their places the words, "When the report of said
Committee is presented, a written vote shall be taken on the amendment."
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that both Sections 504 and 4004 of the
California Masonic Code be amended by inserting the word "written" in line
six of each such section immediately preceding the word "votes."
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that Section 250 be amended by adding
thereto the words "or amendments to this Code" after the word "officers"
so the beginning of said section shall read, ''All questions of the Grand Lodge,
except election of officers or amendments to this Code, shall be decided ...."
Respectfully submitted,

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 85-5 seeks to standardize the manner of voting when considering resolutions aimed at altering, adding to or deleting language from
the sections of the California Masonic Code.
The proponents state that initial considerations of any change in the Code
are made by written ballot, but that if that consideration does not receive
the necessary votes and is carried over, a written ballot is not always required,
and argues that the requirement should be the same in both instances - namely,
that the written ballot rule should apply.
They also suggest that a ballot by a method other than written is subject
to interpretation, as opposed to being exact, because of the fact that each
voice, hand or standing person is accorded a full vote, when legally, a Past
Master is entitled to a fractional vote only.
They therefore ~ropose that Sections 500 and 4000, having to do with initial considerations of resolutions, be altered to read in part, ''A written vote
shall be taken:• and that Sections 504 and 4004, having to do with carry-over
voting be likewise altered. Further, to alter Section 250 so that all questions
except election of officers or amendments to this Code shall be decided by
voice, hand, a rising vote or written ballot, thereby eliminating amendments
from being decided by any other method than written.
The overriding objection to this Resolution is that there is a safeguard written into the voting process in that California Masonic Code Section 250 allows
that, even should a ballot other than written be called for, 3 members may
demand, before the announcement of the result, that a written ballot be taken.
This Resolution is attempting to write into the California Masonic Code
a practice which is, in essence, already in existence.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes, therefore, recommends
a "No" vote on Resolution No. 85-5.
Not adopted.
