To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, R & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, the proponent of this Resolution believes that Grand Lodge
is operating under "regulations established in the Seventeen Hundreds", and
California Lodges are restricted from raising funds; and
WHEREAS, the majority rule has in government and business been the
recognized way which votes are decided on issues; and
WHEREAS, the present rule of requiring a "five-sixths vote" makes it difficult to pass needed legislation, and to reduce the vote required to "twothirds" is realistic and closer to the true majority rule.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that Section 502 be amended
to read:
"Sect. 502. VOTE REQUIRED. Upon the report of said committee, if twothirds of the vote shall be in favor of such proposed amendment it shall
be declared adopted; and, from and after the close of that Communication, it shall become a part of the Constitution."
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that Section 4002 be amended to read:
"Sect. 4002. VOTE REQUIRED. Upon the report of said committee, if
two-thirds of the vote shall be in favor of such proposed amendment it
shall be declared adopted; and, from and after the close of the Communication, it shall become a part of the Ordinances."

221

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponent of Resolution No. 85-6 seeks to reduce the required vote
to effect amendments to our Constitution from five-sixths of the votes cast
in favor to two-thirds of the votes cast.
Similar proposals have been presented to the Grand Lodge with some degree
of regularity during its modern history. Obviously none of these proposals
has been approved by the Grand Lodge. Some of these proponents withdrew
their resolutions before balloting. In some instances the proposed resolutions
received a majority vote and were held over until the next Annual Communication whereupon they failed to attain the required two- thirds vote of passage.
The various proponents of the resolutions to change the required vote have
indicated that our law was virtually unchangeable because of the size of the
majority required to approve change. The many annotations to our Constitution and Ordinances indicate that desired change can be accomplished.
One of the great strengths of our Fraternity is its stability--stability in the
manner in which we conduct our business, receive candidates, present our
ritual, endorse public education, and support our National Constitution to
name only a few.
Traditionally, and by the requirements of law, a unanimous vote is required
in Constituent Lodges to elect candidates for degrees or members for
affiliation.
All of us recognize that a temporary emotional appeal can be felt upon
the presentation of arguments pro or con on any proposal, but adequate time
for reflection giv~ each of us the opportunity to make our determination
upon fact rather than emotion.
The founders of our Fraternity recognized that harmony would be a
necessary requirement to perpetuate our organization. In a great part, harmony comes from unanimity or near-unanimity of opinion. No harm has
ever come to our Fraternity by the exercise of caution. Preserving the fivesixths majority vote is an exercise in caution.
If a given proposal has such appeal to the members of Grand Lodge that
even though it fails the five-sixths majority but exceeds a simple majority,
our law provides that it be held over to the succeeding Annual Communication, at which time the required vote for passage has been reduced to the twothirds proposed in the present resolution.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes favors the preservation
of caution and stability and recommends a "No" vote.
Not adopted.

Secretary, will provide all information necessary for verification of the
Brother's Masonic membership.

California Masonic Code, to read as follows:
"Sect. 2001. PHOTOCOPY OF DUES RECEIPT. Wherever this Article requires a dues receipt be submitted to the office of the Grand

LEONARD L. TODD, SR., PM No. 832

The proponents of this Resolution seek to permit the selling or serving of
liquor, wine or beer as incidental to the operation of a restaurant located in
a building also housing a Masonic Lodge.

Referred to Committees on Jurisprudence, Policy and General Purposes
and Charters.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, C.M.C. Sections 2048 and 2050 prohibit Masonic Lodges (or
organizations the prerequisite of membership wherein is that a person be a
Master Mason) from holding Stated or Special Meetings in, or owning or
renting a building, or being a tenant in a building, containing a bar or liquor
store; and
WHEREAS, C.M.C. Section 2048 does permit a tenant in such a building
engaged primarily in the sale of other merchandise, to sell bottled (packaged)
liquors incidental to the sale of such other merchandise, provided that there
shall be no advertising of liquor on the exterior of such building which
dominates the advertising of other business conducted therein, or is in such
location or form as to make such building undesirable for use by a Masonic
Lodge or Masonic related organization; and
WHEREAS, Section 2048 does draw some line of distinction between a
bar, liquor store and a store selling packaged liquor as a secondary item (like
drug stores and grocery stores); and
WHEREAS, Section 2050 permits Masonic Lodges and other Masonic
related organizatidns to hold meetings of a social nature or other social events
at which liquor, wine or beer may be used or served in hotels, restaurants,
dining rooms, clubs, convention halls, picnic areas or other establishments
not a Masonic Temple or building or structure owned or operated by a
Masonic Lodge or prerequisite organization; and
WHEREAS, other Masonic jurisdictions permit Masonic Lodges to meet
in mid-rise and high-rise buildings in which liquor is sold such as restaurants
and clubs; and
WHEREAS, a restaurant serving liquor should not be in the same classification as a bar or liquor store.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that Sections 2048 and 2050
of the California Masonic Code be amended to read as follows:
"Sect. 2048. MEETING PLACE LIMITATIONS. A Masonic Lodge, or
organization the prerequisite of membership wherein is that a person be
a Master Mason, shall not hold a Stated or Special Meeting in, or own
or rent a building, or be a tenant in a building, containing a bar, liquor
store or establishment, except that a tenant in such a building engaged
primarily in the sale of other merchandise and, except that a Masonic Lodge
or prerequisite organization may own or rent a bulding or be a tenant in
a building or have a land-lease agreement in a mid-rise building of three
stories or more, in which a tenant or other occupier in such building engag-

Secretary, a photocopy thereof, duly certified by the Secretary of any
Lodge in this Jurisdiction, may be substituted."

The Committee on Jurisprudence·
Your Committee on Jurisprudence, to which Resolution No. 85-8 has been
referred, reports as follows:
The proponents of this Resolution seek to allow the use of a duly certified

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponents of this resolution seek to allow the use of a duly certified
photocopy of a dues receipt, rather than the original, in a petition for dispensation to form a new Lodge.
Current technology produces photocopies which are of excellent quality
and clearly legible.
When certified by the Secretary of a Lodge in this Jurisdiction, a photocopy
would serve Grand Lodge's requirements equally well as the original dues
receipt.
As the C.M.C now stands, a member would not be able to visit a Lodge
while his dues receipt is in the possession of Grand Lodge. The use of a
photocopy in this instance would allow a member to retain his dues receipt
necessary for purposes of Lodge visitations.
Your Policy and General Purposes Committee recommends a "Yes" vote.
The Committee on Charters:
The Committee on Charters recommends a "Yes" vote.
Adopted.

The Committee on Jurisprudence:
Your Committee on Jurisprudence, to which Resolution No. 85-9 has been
referred, reports as follows:
The proponents of this Resolution seek to permit the selling or serving of
liquor, wine or beer as incidental to the operation of a restaurant located in
a mid-rise building of three stories or more also housing a Masonic Lodge.
Your Committee finds that the legislation as distributed by the Grand
Secretary to the constituent Lodges is adequate to carry out the intent of the
proponents, except that due to clerical oversight, the following interlineations
must be made:
1. On page 2, in the first paragraph of Section 2048, line 8, following the
word "merchandise;' add: "may sell bottled liquors incidental to the
sale of such other merchandise."
2. On page 2, in the second paragraph of Section 2048, the next to last
line, following the word "liquor" add: ", wine or beer."
3. On page 3 in the next to last line, following the word "liquor" also add:
", wine or b'eer."
With the foregoing amendments, the legislation is now in order and requires a 5/6 affirmative vote for adoption.
To place the matter before the Grand Lodge, we move the adoption of the
Resolution.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 85-9 proposes to amend existing law which governs and
places limitations on meeting places of Masonic Lodges and related Masonic
organizations.
The substance of the Resolution is to "permit a Masonic Lodge or prerequisite organization to own or rent a building or be a tenant in a building
or have a land-lease agreement in a mid-rise building of three stories or more,
in which a tenant or other occupier in such building engaged primarily in
the restaurant business may sell or serve liquor, wine or beer incidental to
the operation of such restaurant business, provided that such restaurant is
not on the same floor as is the Masonic Lodge or prerequisite organization
meeting place."
Section 2048 of the C.M.C. as it is currently written, states in part: "A
Masonic Lodge, or organization the prerequisite of membership wherein is
that a person be a Master Mason, shall not hold a Stated or Special Meeting

228

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

in, or own or rent a building, or be a tenant in a building, containing a bar,
liquor store or establishment, except that a tenant in such a building engaged
primarily in the sale of other merchandise may sell bottled liquors incidental
to the sale of such other merchandise; provided, however, that there shall be
no advertising of liquor on the exterior of such building which dominates
the advertising of other business conducted therein, or is in such location
or form as to make such building undesirable for use by a Masonic Lodge
or Masonic related organization."
The proposers of this Resolution have attempted to include sufficient
safeguards to protect the integrity of California Freemasonry, however, a
thorough analysis of the Resolution, and the possible situations that could
arise, causes serious concern among the members of the Policy and General
Purposes Committee. What will be the criteria used in determining which
is the primary business where both food and liquor are sold? Who will make
the initial judgment? Since only mid-rise buildings are considered, will it be
of general benefit to our Fraternity or is it single interest legislation?
In considering such legislation our first thought is to look at the ideal arrangement, such as, a family type restaurant on the ground floor on one side
of the building, with the Lodge room or meeting place on another level on
the opposite side of the building. This could be the rare exception. The word
"restaurant" could very well be a substitute for "nightclub." Have you ever
been assigned the hotel room immediately above the restaurant and been lulled
to sleep by a jazz band? Picture yourself as Master of your Lodge giving the
third degree lecture accompanied by such dinner music.
The words "or other occupier" used in the Resolution also offer some interesting possibilities. A caterer engaged primarily in the restaurant business
could become the occupier of such building for the purpose of a dinner reception or celebration at which liquor, wine or beer could be sold. This event
could also have a host patron where the liquor, wine or beer would be free
to the guests, further compounding the situation. To carry it one step further, all of this could occur with the Lodge room or meeting place on a
separate floor, as required by the Legislation, with the social hall or banquet
room of the Masonic Lodge or related organization on the same floor and
contiguous to the activity or event.
The challenges to and interpretation of this proposal are as broad as your
own imagination.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes has thoroughly examined this Resolution for the broad benefits to the Fraternity. At very best we
find it to be of limited or special interest legislation.
We, therefore, recommend a "No" vote.

SERVING ALCOHOLIC BEVERAGES
IN MASONIC TEMPLES AT NON-MASONIC FUNCTIONS
(85-10)
The proponents of this Resolution seek to allow liquor, wine or beer to
be served in banquet rooms of Masonic Temples rented to others provided
that no charge be made for such beverages and provided that no Masonic
or Masonic related function is taking place in the building at the time.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, increased costs have made it difficult for Masonic Lodges to
maintain and improve their Temples; and
WHEREAS, many Masonic Temples maintain a banquet room that is
separate and distinct from the Lodge Room; and
WHEREAS, these banquet rooms and facilities represent a potential source
of rental income~ and
WHEREAS, prospective renters for non-Masonic functions seek facilities
which allow the serving of alcoholic beverages with refreshments.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED THAT, Sections 2048 and 2050
of the California Masonic Code be amended to read as follows:
"Sect. 2048. MEETING PLACE LIMITATIONS. A Masonic Lodge, or
organization the prerequisite of membership wherein is that a person be
a Master Mason, shall not hold a Stated or Special Meeting in, or own
or rent a building, or be a tenant in a building, containing a bar, liquor
store or establishment, except that a tenant in such a building engaged
primarily in the sale of other merchandise may sell bottled liquors incidental
to the sale of such other merchandise. Further, a Masonic Lodge or prerequisite organization may own or lease space in a building and may allow
the serving of liquor, wine or beer in banquet rooms which are separate
and distinct from and not used as Lodge rooms during such time that such
banquet rooms are rented to others for non-Masonic functions; and provided that no separate charge may be made for such liquor, wine or beer;
and provided further that such liquor, wine or beer may only be served
in such banquet rooms during the time that no Masonic or Masonic related
function is taking place within such building.
It is further provided that there shall be no advertising of liquor, wine
or beer on the exterior of such building which dominates the advertising

The Committee on Jurisprudence:
Your Committee on Jurisprudence, to which Resolution No. 85-10 has been
referred, reports as follows:
The proponents of this resolution seek to allow liquor, wine or beer to be
served in banquet rooms of Masonic Temples rented to others provided that
no charge be made for such beverages and provided that no Masonic or
Masonic related function is taking place in the building at the time.
Your committee finds that the legislation as distributed by the Grand
Secretary to the constituent Lodges is adequate to carry out the intent of the

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 85-10 marks the eleventh time in the last 22 years that legislation, in one form or another, regarding the serving of alcoholic beverages
in Masonic social halls or banquet rooms has been presented to this Grand
Lodge. In every case the issue has been either withdrawn or rejected.
This resolution seeks to amend Sections 2048 and 2050 of the C.M.C. by
adding to each the following words: "A Masonic Lodge or prerequisite
organization may own or lease space in a building and may allow the serving
of liquor, wine or beer in banquet rooms which are separate and distinct from
and are not used as Lodge rooms during such times that such banquet rooms
are rented to others for non-Masonic functions; and provided that no separate
charge may be made for such liquor, wine or beer; and provided further that
such liquor, wine or beer may only be served in such banquet rooms during
the time that no Masonic or Masonic related function is taking place within
such building."
The arguments against such proposals have been both eloquent and exhausting. Your CQmmittee on Policy and General Purposes chooses to draw
on those words in responding to this resolution.
It is difficult to perceive any way in which moderation in the use of alcoholic
beverages could be controlled and assured. By providing Masonic facilities
for non- Masonic events at which the stimulus of intoxicants might lead to
some of those in attendance becoming noisy or unruly could certainly result
in the conclusion in the minds of neighboring residents or passers-by that
Masons did not entirely observe the limits of good conduct.
Our present regulations concerning the presence of liquor in our Lodge
halls were made after much careful study and consideration and it is the belief
of this committee that many people, Mason and non-Mason alike, feel that
one of the things that distinguishes Masonry from other fraternal orders is
the abstinence from serving alcoholic beverages in our meeting places. We
believe that distinction to be important.
We believe also that preserving the sanctity of our Lodges, the dignity and
serious purposes of Masonry and the recognized quality of the institution
is of far greater value than the suggested financial and economic gains.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a "No" vote.
Not adopted.

MEMBERSHIP IN ORGANIZATIONS REQUIRING
MASONIC MEMBERSHIP AS PREREQUISITE
(85-11)
The proponents of this Resolution seek to clarify the provisions of our Code
prohibiting membership in certain organizations whose members must be
Master Masons.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, this Grand Lodge at its Annual Communication in 1957 expressed concern that certain organizations which require directly or indirectly, Masonic affiliation as a condition of membership, were failing to
acknowledge the supremacy of this Grand Lodge; and
WHEREAS, Section 332.1 (now Section 2068) was added to our California Masonic Code precluding a Mason from the jurisdiction from joining
any organization of Masons not existing in this jurisdiction on September
27, 1957; and
WHEREAS, as a result of a decision of our Grand Master in 1958, the
section was amended to specifically exclude clubs organized for the purpose
of instituting new Lodges; and
WHEREAS, the said amendment thus precludes the creation of any other
new Masonic clubs or other new organizations of Masons including Past
Master Associations and Masters and Wardens Associations; and
WHEREAS, the intent of the legislation as disclosed by Section 2068a of
our Code was to preclude the creation of new organizations purporting to
confer degrees or to utilize a ritual other than that adopted by our Grand
Lodge.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that Section 2068 of the California Masonic Code be amended to read as follows:
"Section 2068. MEMBERSHIP IN PREREQUISITE BODIES. A Mason
residing within this jurisdiction shall not become a member of any organization, or subdivision thereof, by whatsoever name or character, the prerequisite of which is that a person be a Master Mason, unless such organization existed in this jurisdiction on September 27, 1957. This section shall
not be construed as a recognition of any such pre-existing organization;
nor shall it be construed as prohibiting clubs organized for the purpose
of instituting a new Lodge; nor to organizations or associations of Past
Masters, or Masters and Wardens of a Lodge or Lodges of this jurisdiction; nor to organizations or associations of Masons which do not confer
degrees, and except for ceremonies of installation, do not have a ritual
other than the established ritual of this Grand Lodge."
Respectfully submitted,
HARLAN P. HUEBNER, PM No. 445

RICHARD L. RIEMER, PM No. 778

The Committee on Jurisprudence·
Your Committee on Jurisprudence, to which Resolution No. 85-11 has been
referred, reports as follows:
The proponents of this Resolution seek to clarify the provisions of the
California Masonic Code prohibiting membership in certain organizations
whose members must be Master Masons.
Your Committee finds that the legislation as distributed by the Grand
Secretary to the Constituent Lodges is adequate to carry out the intent of
the proponents.
To place the matter before Grand Lodge, we move the adoption of the
Resolution.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 85-11 has been proposed by members of the Jurisprudence
Committee who also were active on the Committee which designed the present California Masonic Code.
The Resolution, if adopted, would clarify those provisions of our Law concerning membership in organizations whose members must be Master Masons
and to the formation of such bodies. A strict interpretation of the Law as
it is now written might, for example, prevent the formation of Past Masters
Associations and membership therein.
The proposed Resolution should be considered as a housekeeping measure
to prevent misinterpretation of the Law.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a "Yes" vote.

ORGANIZATION
OF MASONIC TEMPLE ASSOCIATIONS
(85-12)
The proponents of this Resolution seek to clarify the provisions of the
California Masonic Code relating to the investment of Lodge funds in a
Masonic Temple Association and to establish specific regulations dealing with
the formation, organization and operation of Masonic Temple Associations.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, the California Masonic Code requires each Lodge to retain
the control of its own funds and property, yet many Masonic Temple Associations are organized such that no such control exists; and
WHEREAS, many Masonic Temple Associations are organized such that
they do not qualify for exemption from Federal and State income taxes on
their net profits.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that the authority of each Lodge
in this jurisdiction over the government of any Masonic Temple Association

234

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

in which it holds an ownership interest be clarified by amending the California Masonic Code as follows:
"Sect. 2304. ADDITIONAL INVESTMENTS. A Lodge, after first obtaining the consent of the Grand Lodge Committee on Temple Properties, may
also invest its funds in or maintain an investment in:
1. Memberships or shares, as the case may be, in a Masonic Temple
Association (organized and to be operated in accordance with the provisions of this Code) wherein a Masonic Lodge or Masonic Lodges, collectively, hold a majority of memberships or shares or wherein such a
controlling interest shall be acquired by such investment. Such Masonic
Temple Association shall be one:
a. which owns real estate embracing a building suitable for the occupancy in whole or in part by a Masonic Lodge, or
b . which owns land upon which it is proposed to erect such a building, or
c. which is formed for the purpose of acquiring such real estate and/or
building.
2. A loan evidenced by:
a . A duly executed promissory note amply secured by a first lien against
property of a class described under paragraphs l(a) or l(b) above, or
b. A promissory note duly executed by a Masonic Temple Association
in which the Lodge owns a controlling interest."
A new Section 2305 be added to the California Masonic Code to read
as follows:
"Sect. 2305. MASONIC TEMPLE ASSOCIATION. All Masonic Temple
Associations shall be organized and shall operate as follows:
1. A Masonic Temple Association may be organized either as a non-profit
or as a general law corporation under the laws of the state in which
it owns or is to acquire real estate, land or a building.
2. The exclusive purpose for which a Masonic Temple Association may
be organized is to hold title to property, collect income therefrom and
turn over the entire amount thereof, less expenses, to its members or
shareholders, all of whom must be organizations described in Section
50l(c) of the Internal Revenue Code of 1954. A Masonic Temple Association shall not engage in any activities or exercise any powers that are
not in furtherance of this exclusive purpose. No part of the net earnings of a Masonic Temple Association shall inure to the benefit of any
member or private shareholder, as defined for purposes of Section
50l(c)(7) of the Internal Revenue Code of 1954.
3. Uniform Articles of Incorporation and By-Laws for Masonic Temple
Associations shall be promulgated from time to time by the Grand Lodge
Committee on Temple Properties, with the approval of the Grand
Master, and shall be adopted for use by each Masonic Temple Association. Any amendments to such uniform articles and/or by-laws, as promulgated from time to time by the Grand Lodge Committee on Temple
Properties, with the approval of the Grand Master, also shall be adopted
for use by each Masonic Temple Association. All such articles, by-laws
and any amendments thereto shall be approved by the Grand Lodge

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

235

Committee on Temple Properties and the Grand Master before they shall
become effective. Uniform articles and by-laws shall be promulgated
for a Masonic Temple Association organized as either a non- profit or
as a general law corporation under the laws of the state of its incorporation. Appropriate revisions to the uniform articles and by-laws may
be authorized by the Committee on Temple Properties for Masonic Temple Associations with more than one member or shareholder.
4. A Masonic Lodge shall exercise its rights as a member or shareholder
of a Masonic Temple Association, including its right to elect or remove
directors, pursuant only to the authorization of a majority of members
of the Lodge present at a duly called meeting of the Lodge at which
a quorum is present. Such authorization shall be conclusively presumed
by written instruments, executed by the Worshipful Master or Secretary
of the Lodge, filed with the Secretary of the Masonic Temple Association. In addition, the Worshipful Master of the Lodge, or any person
authorized by proxy or power of attorney duly executed by him, is
authorized to execute any documents and to vote the Lodge's membership or shares at any members' or shareholders' meeting of the Masonic
Temple Association in accordance with the terms of any action previously authorized by the Lodge.
5. Annually on or before the fifteenth day of July, each Masonic Temple
Association shall transmit to the Grand Secretary a full and correct
report of its transactions for the twelve months preceding the first day
of July in such form as may be provided. Such report shall include a
statement of assets, liabilities and net worth as of the end of such twelve
month period. Masonic Temple Associations formed during such twelve
month period shall transmit a report from the date of incorporation."
Respectfully submitted,

This Resolution seeks to amend an Ordinance and requires a five-sixths

To place the matter before the Grand Lodge, we move the adoption of the
Resolution.

The Committee on Taxation:
This Committee was active in the preparation of this Resolution. The
reasons for proposing it can be summarized as follows:
I. Control: Adoption of Resolution No. 85-12 would clarify the right of
a Masonic Lodge to elect and remove directors of the Masonic Temple
Association of which it is a member. It would also clarify how a Lodge
may vote its ownership interests.
It has come to the Committee's attention that there are some Masonic Temple Associations in this Jurisdiction whose officers and directors believe that
they are beyond the control of the Masonic Lodge which owns the Temple
Association. Section 2300 of the California Masonic Code already requires
a Masonic Lodge to retain the control of its own funds and properties. This
legislation would reaffirm that control. This legislation would also set forth
how a Lodge exercises that control by the vote of its membership in a Masonic
Temple Association: it would be done pursuant to the authorization of a majority of the members of the Lodge present at a duly called Lodge meeting
at which a quorum is present.
2. Tax-Exempt Status: By adoption of this legislation, Masonic Temple
Associations could become exempt from the payment of federal and
state taxes on their net income. This is accomplished by providing that
the exclusive business of a Masonic Temple Association must be to hold
title to property, collect income from the property and annually turn
over the entire amount of such income, less expenses, to the Masonic
Lodge which owns it. This is the requisite for tax exemption for Masonic
Temple Associations under federal and California law. Internal Revenue
Code Sections 50l(a), 50l(c)(2), (10). California Revenue & Taxation
Code Section 2370lh. By requiring all Masonic Temple Associations in
the Jurisdiction to have uniform articles of incorporation and by-laws,
the Grand Lodge may then apply for and maintain the federal tax-exempt
status for all complying Masonic Temple Associations within the
Jurisdiction, such as Grand Lodge now does for all Masonic Lodges
within the Jurisdiction. Revenue Procedure 80-27, 1980-1 C.B. 677.
There is at least one Masonic Temple Association in this Jurisdiction which
has paid significant sums in taxes to the federal and state governments in recent years because it was not organized as a tax- exempt entity. Also, the
government has been increasingly vigorous in challenging the basis upon which
some Masonic Temple Associations have claimed exemption in prior years.
The adoption of this legislation and operation of the Masonic Temple Association in accordance with its requirements would significantly reduce the risk
that a Masonic Temple Association must pay income tax on its net profits.
3. Limited Liability: There are still some Masonic Temple Associations
in this Jurisdiction which are not separately incorporated from their
Lodges. Thus, any uninsured liability arising with respect to the Temple property could be assessed against each member of the Lodge. This
legislation would require each Masonic Temple Association to incorporate, thereby lessening this risk.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponents of this Resolution seek to clarify the provisions of the
California Masonic Code relating to the investment of Lodge funds in a
Masonic Temple Association and to establish specific regulations dealing with
the formation, organization and operation of Masonic Temple Associations.
Your Policy and General Purposes Committee has reviewed and carefully
considered this proposed Resolution and believes that the provisions thereof,
and the suggested procedures recommended therein, are appropriate and
necessary and will prove of benefit to the Masonic Lodges and Masonic Temple
Associations of our Jurisdiction. This Resolution clarifies and spells out in
detail what should be the investment policy of Masonic Lodges when investing
in Masonic Temple Associations, and it, also , sets forth certain needed limitations, requirements, and action to be taken by both Masonic Lodges ~nd
Masonic Temple Associations when considering the formation, operation,
and management of a Masonic Temple Association.
The primary purpose of this Resolution is to insure that Masonic Temple
Associations are non-profit corporations, so that the tax benefits in regard
thereto will inure to all Masonic Temple Associations. Masonic Temple
Associations already formed may simply amend their Articles of Incorporation and By-Laws in order to obtain that benefit; and Masonic Lodges forming Temple Associations in the future may obtain that benefit by following
the procedure outlined in this Resolution.
The Policy and General Purposes Committee, therefore, recommends a
"Yes" vote on this Resolution.

AFFILIATION AS A MULTIPLE MEMBER
(85-13)
The proponent of this Resolution seeks to eliminate the requirement of

of a Lodge of another Grand Jurisdiction.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, there appears to be a conflict between the annotation at Section 2692a and Section 2402, Paragraph 2, regarding the requirements of
residence for affiliation in this Grand Jurisdiction as a dual member; and
WHEREAS, the current practice in this Grand Jurisdiction is that residence
within this Jurisdiction is not a requisite to become a dual member.
NOW, THEREFOR E, BE IT RESOLVED, that Section 2402, Paragraph
2 of the California Masonic Code be amended by deleting the phrase, "if
residing in this jurisdiction" so that said paragraph would thus be amended
to read as follows:
"A member of a Lodge of any other Grand Jurisdiction which allows dual
membership may affiliate with one or more Lodges under this Grand Lodge
while retaining his membership in such other jurisdiction. He becomes a
dual member."
Respectfully submitted,

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponent of this Resolution seeks to eliminate the requirement of
residence in this Jurisdiction for affiliation as a dual member by members
of a Lodge in another Grand Jurisdiction.
Section 2402, Paragraph 2, of the California Masonic Code, states, "A
member of a Lodge of any other Grand Jurisdiction which allows dual
membership may, if residing in this Jurisdiction, affiliate with one or more
Lodges under this Grand Lodge while retaining his membership in such other
jurisdiction. He becomes a dual member."
Section 2692a states, "The requirements of residence do not apply to applicants for affiliation. Thus a Master Mason residing in and holding membership in another jurisdiction which recognizes dual membership may affiliate
with a Lodge in our Jurisdiction either on a dimit or as a dual member."
Ross, G.M. 1931 pp. 467, 731.
Since there is an obvious conflict in these two Sections it seems necessary
to change one or the other, either to permit dual membership by affiliation
in a California Lodge regardless of place of residence, or to limit affiliation
for dual membership in our Lodges to residents of this Jurisdiction.
The proponent of this Resolution seeks the former course of action and
proposes to amerfd Section 2402, Paragraph 2 by deleting the phrase, "if
residing in this Jurisdiction:• so the paragraph would be amended to read
as follows:
''A member of a Lodge of any other Grand Jurisdiction which allows dual
membership may affiliate with one or more Lodges under this Grand Lodge
while retaining his membership in such other jurisdiction. He becomes a
dual member."
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes concurs with the proponent of the Resolution and recommends a "Yes" vote.
Adopted.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponent of this Resolution seeks to provide that suspension or expulsion in another Grand Jurisdiction of a Mason who holds dual membership in this Jurisdiction, shall cause his suspension or expulsion in all Lodges
in this Jurisdiction, in which he holds dual membership.
Section 2402 of the California Masonic Code provides that, "Suspension
by a Lodge in the Jurisdiction of this Grand Lodge for non-payment of dues
of a multiple member shall immediately and of itself, suspend his membership in all Lodges in this Jurisdiction, and the Secretary of any Lodge suspending such a member shall immediately notify the Grand Secretary and also
every other Lodge in which the multiple member holds membership." Provision is also made for notice of reinstatement, if such should occur, and for
a sixty day prior Notice of Intention to Suspend during which period such
other Lodge may contact the member in an effort to avoid such suspension.
Section 2402 does not provide for automatic suspension of a member of
a Lodge in this Jurisdiction if he is suspended for non-payment of dues in
another Grand Jurisdiction. The proponent intends to correct this by adding
the following paragraph to Section 2402, Paragraph 6:
"Suspension by a Lodge in any other Grand Jurisdiction for non-payment
of dues sh~l forthwith suspend his membership in all Lodges in this
Jurisdiction but shall be handled in the same manner as provided above
in this section for members suspended by a Lodge in this Jurisdiction by
giving sixty days notice, and provided further, that the restoration of such
a member shall be in the same manner as provided in this Code."
To deal with suspension or expulsion of a multiple member for other than
non-payment of dues, the proponent proposes to amend Section 2404,
Paragraph 10, to read as follows:
"Suspension or expulsion by a Lodge in the Jurisdiction of this or any
other Grand Lodge, for other than non-payment of dues, of a multiple
member shall forthwith suspend or expel his membership in all Lodges
in this Jurisdiction, ...."
The amended paragraph goes on to provide that proper notice be given
of such suspension or expulsion as well as in the case of restoration of
membership.
As presently written, Paragraph 10 provides that if a multiple member is
suspended or expelled by a Lodge in another Jurisdiction and notice thereof
is received by a Lodge in this Jurisdiction, the Master of such Lodge shall
cause such action to be taken by that Lodge or charges are to be preferred

242

PROCEEDIN GS OF THE

against such multiple member as the facts shall require under the laws of the
Grand Lodge of California.
Adoption of this Resolution would eliminate the necessity for action by
a Lodge in this Jurisdiction other than the automatic suspension or expulsion of the member in accordance with the action taken by a Lodge in another
Jurisdiction.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a "Yes" vote.
Failing a 5/6 affirmative vote, but receiving a majority vote, the Resolution will be held over for consideration at the 1986 Annual Communication.

PAST MASTER S' ASSOCIA TIONS
(85-15)
The proponent of this Resolution seeks to modify the Code so individual
Lodges may have Past Masters' Associations and these Associations may accumulate funds and transact appropriate business.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, the California Masonic Code Section 2544 recognizes the probable existence of voluntary Past Masters' Associations; and
WHEREAS, Section 2544 does not attempt to define or specify the purpose(s) for which an Association is formed, provided the activities are
amenable to all the laws, rules and regulations of the Fraternity.
NOW, THEREFOR E, BE IT RESOLVED, that Section 2544 be amended
to read:
"Past Masters' Associations are voluntary associations of Masons and are
not directly amenable to the supervision of Grand Lodge except through
the power of the Grand Lodge to regulate and govern the activities of each
member as an individual Mason. As such they are amenable to all the laws,
rules and regulations of the Fraternity.
Past Masters from an individual Lodge may form such an Association
for such purposes, consistent with the above, as they determine. The
Association shall be autonomous in character and nature, have the authority
to accumulate funds and transact business appropriate for its established
purposes."
Respectfully submitted,

The proponent of this Resolution seeks in the case of an Application submitted by a Past Master of this Grand Lodge for plural membership (in
another Lodge in this Jurisdiction), to modify the requirement of a unanimous

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, members of the Grand Lodge consist of the Grand Lodge
Officers, and the-Constituent Lodges' Past Masters, Masters, and Wardens;
and
WHEREAS, the members of the Grand Lodge have studied Masonic Law
and ritual as a requirement for governing a Lodge; and
WHEREAS, the knowledge thus gained can be a valuable asset in assisting
in the government of, not only their own Lodges, but also other Lodges in
this Jurisdiction; and
WHEREAS, the desire of a Grand Lodge member to become a plural
member of a Constituent Lodge requires that he meet the same balloting requirements that a non-Mason must meet; and
WHEREAS, this requirement permits an unknown member, for personal
and possible unmasonic reasons, to prevent a qualified, upright and well informed member of Grand Lodge from becoming a plural member of a Constituent Lodge in this Jurisdiction; and
WHEREAS, members of Grand Lodge, by virtue of the fact that they are
members of the governing body of the Fraternity, should be shown special
consideration; and
WHEREAS, Grand Lodge has set a precedent by providing for restoration
to membership in a Lodge by other than a unanimous ballot under certain
conditions as shown in Sections 2820 and 3512 of the California Masonic
Code.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that Section 2651 be added to
the California Masonic Code to read as follows:
"Section 2651. BALLOT REQUIRED ON APPLICATION FOR PLURAL
MEMBERSHIP BY A PAST MASTER. In the case of a Past Master of
a Constituent Lodge of this Grand Lodge who submits an application for
affiliation, as a plural member, to another Lodge of this Jurisdiction, upon
a favorable report of the Investigating Committee, a secret ballot shall be
held and an affirmative vote of two-thirds of the members voting shall
be required to elect said Past Master for affiliation with the Lodge."

section provides for restoration to membership in the Lodge of which he had
been a member, and not to membership in a different Lodge. There is no
relationship between Sections 2820 and 3512 C.M.C. and the new Section 2651
proposed by the proponent in Resolution No. 85-17.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recognizes the service
rendered by Past Masters. However, it is of the opinion that all applications
for affiliation to membership, whether for plural membership or otherwise,
would be by an unanimous ballot. There should be no distinction for Past
Masters.
The proponent states, "That Past Masters should be shown special consideration." It is the opinion of your Committee that to give special consideration to Past Masters in the voting procedures for election to Plural Membership in a Lodge in this Jurisdiction is contrary to the policy of this Grand
Lodge.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a "No" vote.
Not Adopted.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 85-19 seeks to have Grand Lodge approve the use of the
Ritual of the second section of the Master Mason Degree used by Le Progres
de I..:Oceanie Lodge No. 371.
This Hawaiian Lodge has a beautiful and impressive history and use of
this Ritual has been a tradition since 1843.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes understands the reasoning
behind the proponent's Resolution.
However, compliance to Section 1114 C.M.C. is necessary for the continuation of the adopted California Ritual in this Jurisdiction.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a "No" vote.
The Committee on Ritual:
In October, 1984 it became necessary for your Grand Lecturer to reaffirm
decisions relative to the conformity of the ritual.
It was brought to my attention that one of our Lodges deviated from the
adopted ritual in the second section of the third degree.
Lodge Le Progres de I..:Oceanie was originally under dispensation by the
Supreme Council of the Ancient and Accepted Scottish Rite of France in 1843
and received their charter in 1850. After floundering somewhat and being
considered a clandestine Lodge for a period of time, Lodge Le Progres
petitioned the Grand Jurisdiction of California in 1860, but was denied and
remained under the jurisdiction of France and its Scottish Rite heritage until
its acceptance into this Jurisdiction in September, 1905. Lodge Le Progres
was under the control of the Supreme Council of the Ancient and Accepted
Scottish Rite of France for a period of 57 years before its affiliation with
this Jurisdiction.
Lodge Le Progres did indeed include in its petition to the Grand Lodge
of California in 1904 a request to retain its work of the second section of
the third degree. However, I must point out to you, my Brethren, that the
Committee on Jurisprudence did not include any reference to the retention
of work that deviated from our adopted ritual in its report and recommendation to this body. Therefore, Lodge Le Progres is in error when they attempt to lead you to believe they were given this permission. They would also
lead you to believe that there are only slight differences in the second section
of the third degree. These differences in the eyes of many Grand Lecturers
and Grand Masters are much more than slight and apparently can be changed
at the whim of the Lodge because there is no control of the chain of instruction as now takes place and has taken place since 1916 through the Ritual
Committee and the Inspectoral Corps.
Grand Masters and Grand Lecturers have wrestled with this problem since
Le Progres first became a chartered California Lodge in 1905.
This Resolution would lead you to believe that it has been allowed 69 years
of peaceful practice of its cherished work without any interference by any
Inspector, Grand Lecturer or Grand Master. These are not the facts. I have
in my possession copies of letters sent between the Lodge and various Grand

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

251

Masters and Grand Lecturers that repudiate the so-called facts. It did indeed
strike an agreement in 1958 with the then Grand Master Leo E. Anderson
and Grand Lecturer Elbert Davis wherein it would conform to our ritual in
its entirety and then following the end of the California work, they would
be able to add a small portion of their own work. Apparently Le Progres
would not accept this agreement and continued to do their work as before
in defiance of this agreement. In 1959 it presented a Resolution to the Grand
Lodge similar to the Resolution before us now, requesting the authority to
continue the "French Scottish Rite" work. Another agreement was struck in
1959 with the then Grand Master Phil N. Myers and Grand Lecturer Elbert
Davis whereupon it would conform and be allowed to add its portion at the
end of the California work. It withdrew the Resolution and again did not
conform, but continued to do the work as it had in the past.
The work does not resemble that which has been adopted by this Grand
Jurisdiction, and this continued practice is a violation of our Code. It is my
duty as Grand Lecturer to require Lodges to conform to the ritual in order
that there will be uniformity of the ritual throughout this Jurisdiction. The
work it has been trying to perpetuate from year to year is in and of itself
a violation of the Master's obligation - "that it is not in the power of any
man, or body of men, to make innovations in the body of Masonry." Grand
Lodge alone has the power to authorize any changes in the ritual for the purpose of having it remain as it was handed down from time immemorial.
"Each degree conferred and all lectures in this Jurisdiction must be in conformity with the ritual now or hereafter taught by the Grand Lecturer and
recognized by the Grand Lodge, and such must be adhered to by all Lodges
and Masons in this Jurisdiction, except that the Lodges in this Jurisdiction
whose long- establi§hed ritualistic work is in part a departure from the uniform
ritual of this Jurisdiction, may continue to perform, insofar as the same may
not be disapproved by the Grand Master and the Grand Lecturer ...." Section 2688 allows some exceptions for those Lodges working in a foreign
language and a note which states: "Parfaite Union No. 17, Valle de France
No. 329, Hermann Lodge No. 127 are the excepted Lodges." While these excepted Lodges work in a foreign language, they do not deviate in any way
from our ritual of the Third Degree. Le Progres does not work in a foreign
language nor has it worked in a foreign language since becoming a part of
this Jurisdiction.
Section 2530. Duties of Master. It shall be his duty "to confer or have conferred all degrees in strict accordance with the ritual which has been, or may
hereafter be, ordained by the Grand Lodge."
Section 1114. It shall be the duty of the Grand Lecturer: "To supervise and
direct the Assistant Grand Lecturers and the Inspectors in the performance
of their duties, and to require conformity with the adopted ritual and work
and to see that the Inspectors examine all officers who are required to produce
certificates of proficiency at their installation in accordance with these ordinances."
Accordingly, I reaffirm my position as Grand Lecturer that Lodge Le
Progres de I..:Oceanie No. 371 must not be permitted this special privilege.

Temple is shown on four different occasions. It is screened in a small

The Temple is open to visitors on Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday and Friday
from 10:00 A.M. to 3:00 P.M .. Masonic Lodges pay a $45.00 rental fee per
night. Masonic youth groups are charged $25.00 for Saturday morning dates.
Nine Masonic organizations rented the Temple during the year for degree
work. We have one permanent tenant, Plaza de Los Angeles No. 814 which
meets every Thursday night.
Lodges renting the Temple are afforded free parking after 6:00 P.M. directly
across North Main Street in West Lot No. 2.
Hundreds of new visitors will visit the Old Temple when the Ancient Arabic
Order, Nobles of the Mystic Shrine hold their Imperial Sessions in Los
Angeles, June 30 through July 4, 1986. Illustrious Thomas M. Boles, Potentate
during 1985 of Al Malaikah Shrine Temple, is a booster of the Old Temple
and has made plans for visiting Shriners to visit the historic building. Nearly
25,000 Shriners are expected to visit Los Angeles from all over North America.
The Old Temple is air conditioned and has a modern heating system. It
has been recently painted and several old-fashioned facilities replaced. It can
accommodate 60 persons in the main room.
Reservations can be made by contacting the Chairman or the Custodian,
Oliver Celaya, at (213) 626-4933. Incidentally, Brother Celaya will be Master
of William D. Stephens Lodge No. 698 in 1986. This is the Blue Lodge of
Potentate Boles and also of Illustrious Walker Sanborn Kisselburgh, 33rd
Degree, who is the Imperial Potentate of the Shrine of North America.
The Committee is grateful to Ralph H. Head, editor of the California
Freemason for including the Temple on the front cover of the December 1985

issue.

in 1985. Our sincere thanks to the Grand Secretary, Very Worshipful Robert
A. Klinger, for his interest and courtesy in allowing us space on "G" Floor
for our exhibit.
We look forward to a memorable year during 1986.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON
OLD MASONIC HALL AT LOS ANGELES
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
In tha mainstream of California Freemasonry, the Old Masonic Hall at
Los Angeles enjoyed a most active year and charted plans for an epoch-filled
1986.
Visitors to the birthplace of Masonry in Southern California set an alltime record of 2,480 for the year ending on September 24, 1985.
The reason for the increased activity is that the historic Temple is located
near Olvera Street, which attracts more than 2 million people a year, making
it one of Southern California's top tourist attractions.
The Temple is located at 416 1/2 North Main Street, occupying the first
site in the Pico-Garnier block, consisting of pre-1900 buildings as part of El
Pueblo de Los Angeles State Historic Park. The Old Plaza has been landscaped and paved with brick. There are viable plans to erect hotels, restaurants,
gift shops, museums and entertainment centers. Developers would manage
the refurbished area. However, the Old Plaza, where the Old Masonic Hall
is located, would remain unchanged, under State supervision.
The interior of the Temple underwent a number of much needed improvements during the last year. Heading these improvements were two new
10 feet by 12 feet display cases. For the first time, valuable relics that have
been kept under lock and key have surfaced and are being displayed in walnut
cases, which can be illuminated for night use.
Spreading the historical role the Old Temple plays in the area is an 18 minute
movie, entitled, "Welcome to the Old Plaza Area" in which the Masonic

Our Committee's objectives and goals, as enumerated in our last year's
report, were reinforced and reemphasized by the Elective Line with the added
responsibility of observing and monitoring the extent to which the educational pamphlets and pamphlet holders in each Masonic Temple in our Grand
Jurisdiction are being used.
These holders were distributed to the various Temples late last year, including

received in sufficient quantity to enable your Chairman to render an opinion
concerning the success or failure of this method of distributing such pamphlet material throughout our Grand Jurisdiction.

the leadership seminars held this past year. Our committee material and
pamphlets were again eagerly sought by those in attendance.
We had scheduled a joint mini-seminar with the Inspectors of the Fifth
and Sixth Masonic Divisions during June 1985, but were forced to cancel same
due to a breakdown in communication and a conflict of dates.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON
REVIEW OF PROCEEDINGS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
In 1984-85 your Committee reviewed some 22 publications from Grand
Jurisdictions in amity with the Grand Lodge of California. Of these, 18 were
from Grand Lodges in the United States, and 4 from foreign jurisdictions.
Our annual report does not attempt to detail the activities of these bodies
but rather to present information as to the position of Freemasonry in the
United States as well as the world. We do not attempt to give detailed data
on membership, finances, committee actions and similar matters except as
they may be of an unusual nature.
Diminishing membership is one thing every jurisdiction seems to have in
common. Pennsylvania has adopted a program which is known as King
Solomon II for the purpose of increasing membership. It seems to be working.
Other jurisdictions have asked permission to use part of it and further develop
it for their areas .•
Colorado has an interesting Grand Lodge Committee known as the Armed
Forces Welfare Committee. Their responsibility is to have volunteers put in
over 5000 hours of regular visits to the Veteran's Hospital in Denver and Grand
Junction.
Some of the jurisdictions use advertisement in their magazines to generate
much needed revenue - New Zealand, Indiana, Vermont, Rhode Island, just
to name a few.
In New Zealand 5 Lodges combined recently to purchase a baby respiration monitor for use in their area. Another Lodge donated a laerdal cardiac
rhythm simulator to a hospital. This is Masonry in action, and it is something
we in this Jurisdiction could do for further exposure.
Iowa is studying the feasibility of a plan for keying Grand Lodge and local
dues to the economy, indexing them every few years.
The per capita tax has been raised in every one of the jurisdictions reviewed.
Some have been substantial increases. For instance, South Dakota where it
jumped from $2 to $5 annually and in British Columbia where all members
were assessed $5 in 1984 and $1 per year thereafter.
Education is of interest in all of the jurisdictions reviewed. Some feel that
we need more education on Masonry for Lodge members and leadership
workshops for officers.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON TAXATION
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
The Grand Lodge Committee on Taxation renders advice on matters of
taxation when requested by the Grand Lodge, subordinate Lodges and ot~er
organizations under their jurisdiction. Our assistance has been requested with
respect to matters of income, property, sales and employment taxes. Our work
includes this annual report which discusses items of current interest in the
taxation of fraternal organizations.
This year's report is a summary of the overall tax treatment of Masonic
Lodges and Temple Associations which Masters, Secretaries and Temple
Boards members may use as a handbook. Because this is a summary, this
material does not address all possible issues in detail. A competent tax advisor may be required in some circumstances.
Masonic Lodges
Masonic Lodges are exempt from all federal and California income taxes,
regardless of the amount of income from dues, interest, dividends or income
from other investments, with certain exceptions, discussed in the next
paragraph. The Internal Revenue Service has officially recognized that t.he
Grand Lodge of Californi":.and its subordinate Lodges are exe~pt from mcome tax under Internal Revenue Code Section 501(c)(10). It 1s Group Exemption No. 0214, memorialized in a letter dated July 11, 1.972 ~rom ~~e I.~.S.
to the Grand Lodge, which letter had the followmg 1dent1f1cat1on:
T:MS:EO:R:l. (This classification may be important for other purposes. For
example, you may be asked to prove your exempt status in or?er t~ receive
authorization from the U.S. Postal Service to mail at the special third-class
bulk rate.)
A Lodge is taxable on income from a trade or business which is unrelated
to the fraternal purposes of the Lodge. For example, net income from a working oil interest would be taxable because such an interest is consi.dt;:red a trade
or business. To constitute a trade or business, however, the act1v1ty must be

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

regularly carried on. This does not include periodic events. Operating a
restaurant constitutes a trade or business. Holding periodic dinners does not
constitute a trade or business. In addition, income from events conducted
by tax-exempt fraternal organizations, such as Masonic Lodges, are not taxable if substantially all the labor required to hold the event is performed for
the Lodge without compensation.
While there may be no income tax consequences, there are potential California sales and use tax consequences to certain Lodge events. A sales tax is assessed upon the sale of tangible personal property. The sale of tangible personal
property includes furnishing meals as well as supplying merchandise at garage
sales or bazaars, for a purchase price, even if the purchase price is labeled
a "donation".
There is one exemption to the tax available to Lodges, however. Social clubs
and fraternal organizations, such as Masonic Lodges are not subject to the
sales tax on their receipts from furnishing meals if the meals are furnished
exclusively to members and are furnished less frequently than once a week.
Both these requirements must be met. If the Lodge furnishes meals to nonmembers, all receipts from meals are subject to tax, whether the meals are
furnished to members or non-members. However, meals paid for by members
are considered furnished to the members and are therefore not subject to the
sales tax even though consumed by guests who are not members. The Committee suggests that tickets for non-members who attend Lodge dinners should
be purchased by members of the Lodge. The Lodge need not thereafter concern itself with whether the member obtains any reimbursement from the
guest.
Any other transfers of tangible personal property by the Lodge, such as
at garage sales or bazaars, are subject to the sales tax. If the Lodge is subject
to the sales tax, it must apply for a California Seller's permit. These can be
obtained from the local office of the State Board of Equalization.
Some Lodges have been asked to pay sales tax when they purchase from
printers their completed trestleboard or other Lodge bulletin for distribution
to members. As discussed above, with respect to Lodge dinners and other
events, the sale of tangible personal property is subject to the sales tax. A
printer's charge for printing the Lodge's bulletin is considered the sale of tangible personal property: the bulletin. However, the law provides an exemption
for the sale of "periodicals". A periodical is a publication issued at stated
intervals, which publication contains news or information of general interest
to a particular organization. A Lodge bulletin which is no more than a notice
of upcoming meetings does not qualify as a periodical containing "news or
information of general interest". However, a Lodge bulletin which contains
articles and other information in addition to upcoming events has been ruled
exempt from the sales tax. If your Lodge bulletin does contain news and information other than upcoming dates, and you are paying sales tax to your
printer for printing the bulletin, you should advise the printer that the bulletin
is exempt as a periodical. If the printer is unwilling to recognize this exemption, the State Board of Equalization or your Committee should be contacted.

A Lodge is required to withhold payroll taxes from the wages of its
employees. Generally, a Lodge's employees would include persons such as the
Secretary, custodian or anyone else who receives compensation for services
rendered to the Lodge, although there are exceptions if wages do not exceed
$100 a calendar quarter ($100 a month in the case of elected or appointed
officers). Withholding may be required even if the Lodge calls the payments
"mileage" or some other form of expense reimbursement. Because these rules
are detailed and beyond the scope of this summary, a competent tax advisor
should be consulted before such payments are made.

264

265

Masonic Temple Associations
A Masonic Temple Association, even if separately incorporated from the
Lodge, can be tax-exempt, just like a Masonic Lodge. In order to be exempt
from the payment of federal and California taxes on the net income of a Temple Association, wholly owned by a Lodge, the exclusive business of the Temple
Association must be to hold title to property, collect income from the property and annually turn over the entire amount of such income, less expenses,
to the Lodge which owns it. Internal Revenue Code Sections 50l(a), 50l(c)(2),
(10). California Revenue and Taxation Code Section 2370lh. If this is not done,
the Temple Association will lose its exempt status. The articles of incorporation for a Temple Association should include this exclusive purpose. (Temple
Associations can qualify for exempt status even if not wholly owned by a
single Lodge, but the satisfaction of the requirements to obtain exempt status
may be more difficult.)
In determining the amount of net income which must be turned over to
the Lodge, any expense incurred by the Temple Association reduces the amount
of income requirecLto be remitted to the Lodge. The term "expense" includes
not only out-of-pocket expenditures but also reasonable additions to depreciation reserves. See Rev. Ru!. 66-102, 1966-1 C.B. 133; Rev. Ru!. 67-104, 1967-1
C.B. 120. Because of possibly differing interpretations of what is reasonable,
the Committee recommends that a Temple Association turn over its entire
net cash profit for the year to the Lodge which owns it. If the Temple Association in future years requires additional cash, the Lodge can then return the
money to the Temple Association. Of course, any reinvestment of funds in
the Temple Association should not be done without obtaining the consent
of the Grand Lodge Committee on Temple Properties. California Masonic
Code Section 2304. Should the property owned by the Temple Association
be sold subsequently, the net income distribution rule would require the Temple
Association to dissolve and transfer its remaining assets to the Lodge.
The Grand Lodge does not maintain a group exemption for individual Temple Associations as it does for Masonic Lodges, discussed previously. Application for recognition of exempt status should be made to the 1.R.S. on
Form 1024 and to the State of California on FTB 3500. Detailed instructions
are published with these forms regarding their proper completion.
Generally, a Masonic Temple Association's receipt of rents from real property is not taxable if rents attributable to personal property leased with the
real property are IO percent or less of the total rents and if the determination

266

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

of the amount of the rent does not depend on the net income or profits derived
by the tenant. Rental based upon a fixed percentage of gross receipts or sales
is permitted, however. Internal Revenue Code Section 512(b)(3). Thus,
regardless of how a Masonic Temple may be leased, if the rental payment
is a fixed amount or a fixed percentage of the tenant's gross receipts and no
significant amounts of personal property are leased with the building, the
Temple Association will not be taxed on its rental income. No distinction is
drawn between rentals to retail stores and rentals to other fraternal
organizations.
If services are rendered by an exempt organization for the convenience of
the tenant (such as maid services), other than those usually and customarily
rendered in connection with the rental of space (such as heat and electricity),
the rents would be taxable. U.S. Treasury Regulation Sections l.512(b)- l(c)(2),
(5). Thus rents from the operation of a hotel, boarding house, motel,
warehouse or parking lot are generally taxable. But, they are taxable only if
conducted directly by the exempt organization. For example, if a Masonic
Temple Association leased property to a hotel and collected rent at a fixed
monthly rate or at a fixed percentage of the hotel's gross receipts, then the
rental income of the Masonic Temple Association would not be taxable: the
Temple Association did not perform the services and did not participate in
the net income of the entity performing those services. The Internal Revenue
Service has ruled that income derived by an exempt organization for the use
of its meeting hall is not taxable if the only services provided are utilities and
janitorial services. Revenue Ruling 69-178, 1969-1 C.B. 158.
It is possible for a Masonic Temple Association to be taxable upon part
of its rental income if the property is "debt-financed" property, i.e.: there is
a loan against the property. See Internal Revenue Code Section 514. However,
because the Temple Association would be entitled to deduct interest and
depreciation, no tax would be due in most circumstances. In any event, if
a tax is due, it is paid by the Masonic Temple Association itself. The Lodge
should not be liable.
Temple Associations are not exempt for California property tax purposes.
Temple Associations are not exempt from any other taxes, such as California
sale and use taxes, or from the requirement to withhold and pay employment
taxes with respect to employees. (See the discussion of these taxes in the discussion of Masonic Lodges.)

all Lodges comply. As discussed subsequently, the Federal Form 990 is due
only if the filing entity has a certain amount of total gross receipts for the
year. There is a significant penalty for failure to file a return if indeed one
is due. If the difference between filing and not filing a return is the amount
of these contributions held in trust, the Committee would strongly recommend that the Lodge include them in gross receipts and file the return to
eliminate any risk of the failure to file penalty. In any event, it is important
for us as Masons in our fraternal activities to comply with regulatory requirements until changed.
Lodges and Temple Associations with gross receipts not in excess of $25,000
are excused from filing Federal Form 990 and California Form 199. However,
Lodges and Temple Associations with annual gross receipts of $25,000 or less
are required to file the simplified information return, California Form 199B.
If a Lodge or Temple Association is required to file Form 990 with the Internal Revenue Service or Forms 199 or 199B with the California Franchise
Tax Board, a penalty of up to $10 a day (to a maximum of $5,000) is imposed
on each such exempt organization which fails to file such an annual information return or files a late return without reasonable cause. The returns are
due by the fifteenth day of the fifth month after the end of your accounting
period. Thus, if a Lodge or Temple Association uses a calendar year, its returns
are due on the following May 15th.
Although there can be no assurances for the future, the Committee has
been successful in the past in proving reasonable cause. We encourage all
Lodges and Masonic Temple Associations to file their returns in a timely
fashion. If for any reason the return is filed late and a penalty is assessed,
we ask that you seek competent tax advice, including any member of this
Committee, immeqiately upon receipt of a notice assessing such a penalty
and before paying it.
Certain payments made by Lodges and Temple Associations totaling $600
or more during a calendar year must be reported to the Internal Revenue Service on Form 1099 and the Franchise Tax Board on Form 599 prior to March
Ist of the following year. Such information returns are required for payments
in the form of wages, salaries, rent premiums, annuities, compensation,
remuneration or otherwise in amounts of $600 or more in a single calendar
year. If the payments are dividends or interest, the dollar threshold for reporting is reduced to $10 a year. No such reporting is required for payments
made to an employee whose wages are properly reported on Form W-2. Failure
to comply with these rules could subject the paying Lodge or Temple Association to a $50 fine from the Internal Revenue Service and a $10 fine from the
State of California for each failure to file. It should be noted that a Form
1099 and a Form 599 need not be filed if the payee is a corporation. Thus,
no filing would be required with respect to payments by a Lodge to an incorporated Temple Association.
Periodically, the tax returns of Masonic Lodges and Temple Associations
are audited. Usually, the agent is only verifying that you are exempt, that
the Lodge or Temple Association does not engage in political activity (which
would jeopardize exempt status) and that there is no income from advertising
in Lodge publications (which income is taxable). As part of the review, the

Those forms call for the Lodge or Temple Association to report "total gross

Are Contributions to a Masonic Lodge or a Masonic Temple Association Tax
Deductible?
While a Masonic Lodge is not taxable on its income from dues and investments, it is not the type of organization which can receive gifts which
are deductible for income, gift or estate tax purposes unless the funds are
transferred to the Lodge with the express request that they be redirected to
a charity which is qualified to receive such tax deductible contributions, such
as the Masonic Homes of California. Internal Revenue Code Section 170(c)(4).
Also, contributions to a Temple Association for its exclusive use are not deductible for income, gift or estate tax purposes.
Contributions by an individual to a domestic fraternal order operating under
the Lodge system, such as Masonic Lodges, are deductible for income tax
purposes only if the contributions will be used exclusively for religious,
charitable, scientific, literary or educational purposes, or for the prevention
of cruelty to children or animals. Internal Revenue Code Section 170(c)(4).
For example, a charitable purpose is the support of elderly and indigent
members of the order who live in a home owned by the order. LT. 3261, C.B.
1939-1, 122. Thus, contributions to the Homes Endowment Fund for the support of the Homes at Union City and Covina are deductible even though given
to the Lodge for transmittal to the Homes Endowment Fund rather than sent
directly to the Fund. However, contributions given to a Lodge for the use
of a local blood bank are not deductible unless the blood bank's operations
qualify it as a charitable organization. TYpically, this would require the blood
bank to limit its aid to poor and distressed members of the Fraternity and
their families. Because most blood banks do not so operate, it is unlikley that
contributions to the Lodge for the use of the local blood bank would be
deductible.
Periodically, Lodges and individuals are asked for proof that contributions
to the Masonic Homes Endowment Fund are deductible for income, gift or
estate tax purposes. California Masonic Code Section 1406b provides that
the Masonic Homes Endowment Fund is an asset of the Masonic Homes of
California. The Masonic Homes of California is listed as an I.R.C. Section
501(c)(3) organization in Publication 78, Cumulative List of Organizations
described in Section 170(c) of the Internal Revenue Code of 1954. This
Publication together with the California Masonic Code should be sufficient
evidence of the exempt status of the Masonic Homes Endowment Fund and
sufficient evidence that contributions to such Fund are deductible for income,
gift and estate tax purposes. Again, even if individuals make such contributions through Lodges, the contributions are still deductible if given to the
Lodge with specific iqstructions that the contributions be forwarded by the
Lodge to the Masonie Homes Endowment Fund.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON YOUTH ORDERS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
Your Committee on Youth Orders has been active this year in a continued
effort to support and promote the health and general welfare of our Masonic
Youth Orders. At the direction of the Grand Master, the Committee was expanded to forty (40) members in an effort to increase its activity and visibility among our Lodges and the various Youth Orders. This, we think, has been
successful enough that it should be continued.
The two major problem areas for the Youth Orders remain a declining
membership and a lack of enough qualified adult leaders and workers.
It is gratifying to note the rate of loss of members appears to be slowing
and, while it seems too early yet to predict, there is encouragement that it
might actually level off and start upward in the next few years.
It is the belief of this Chairman that the changes and trends in our general
society today are, for the first time in some twenty (20) years, favoring the
ideals and principles promoted by the Masonic Fraternity. This, we feel, will
in turn make it more fashionable and acceptable to join and belong to our
Orders. These changes are in the direct path of increased membership, and
we feel this will lij)pear first in our Masonic Youth Groups, then ultimately
in our own Fraternity.
The primary concerns of this Committee with regard to the relationship
between the California Grand Lodge and the various youth organizations continues to center around the lack of understanding on the part of our Lodges
and our Masons as to who the youth organizations are and how they fit into
the Masonic family. As a corollary to this, the youth organizations continue
to need a larger number of qualified, dedicated adult leaders to support the
youth in their organizations and activities. This is not to say that there are
not many outstanding examples of superior relationships between Lodges and
local Assemblies, Bethels and Chapters. Nevertheless, we continue to learn
of gross examples of misunderstanding and little or no Masonic support in
certain localities.
On August 18, 1985, a meeting was held under the auspices of this Committee between the Executive Committee of the Grand Lodge and the Adult
Heads of the various Masonic Youth Orders in California. The primary purposes and accomplishments were:
A. To promote a greater acquaintanceship and understanding between the
various entities and their leaders.
B. To openly discuss the problems and needs of each of the groups and
exchange beneficial ideas.

270

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

C. To exchange rosters and calendars to promote the inter-action between
.
the groups and their members.
D. To open and maintain lines of communication between the vanous
organizations and their leaders.
A similar meeting has already been scheduled for next year, and we recommend they be continued.
This year the Committee again made available a single-page flyer for Lodges
to include in their Trestleboard mailing asking Masons to recommend young
people for membership in appropriate Masonic Youth ?rder~. Similarl~, an
article and accompanying cut-out type coupon was published m The California Freemason. Our Lodges asked for approximately 110,000 of the flyers
and it is presumed all those were mailed. The result of both these efforts was
some 150 names being received and forwarded to the appropriate Youth Order.
While it is difficult to track the exact results, we are aware of a number of
new members in our Masonic Youth Orders as a result of this project. We
recommend it be continued and extend our thanks to The California
Freemason and Brother Ralph Head, Editor, for his support of this effort.
Grand Master Henville has been most diligent and enthusiastic in his personal support of Masonic Youth. He has been present at the a.nnual me~ting
of each group in California, or sent a member of the Executive ComI?1.t~ee
as his Representative, and has personally attended many events and act1V1t1es
of local youth groups. He has continued the recent practice of offering some
reimbursement of expenses to the Youth Leader of each group attending Grand
Lodge. This is well received by the Youth Orders as a tangible expression of
Masonic Recognition of and support for their Orders.
This Committee continues to staff an information booth on "G" Floor
during this Grand Lodge Communication for the benefit of our Lodges in
general and particularly for Senior Wardens regarding their including youth
activities in the Lodge calendar for the coming year.
Having served as Chairman of this fine Committee now for five (5) years,
this Chairman has asked not to be reappointed. This is out of a conviction
that five (5) years is long enough to serve on any Committee in consideration
for the Committee and the cause being served. New leadership always brings
new energy, activity and ideas. So, I leave this post with a deep sense of thanks
and appreciation to each of the Grand Masters under whom I have had the
pleasure of serving, to the Very Worshipful Robert A. Klinger, Grand Sec~tary,
and the fine staff in the Grand Lodge office, to the wonderfully dedicated
members of this Committee over the years and to the various youth and adult
leaders of the Youth Orders with whom I've had an opportunity to associate
and work. I leave, most of all, with a renewed conviction that in the success
of our Youth Orders lies the success of our entire Masonic Fraternity, both
immediately and in the future, and I pray for greater support and understanding for them by the Grand Lodge, local Lodges and all Masons.

Respectfully submitted,
GLENN D. WOODY, Chairman
